At its 69th Ordinary Session held virtually from 15 November to 5 December 2021, the Commission considered the Communication and declared it admissible.

On 28 March 2022, the parties were informed that the Communication had been considered at the 69th Ordinary Session and declared admissible. By the same notification, the Complainants were requested to send their observations on the merits to the Secretariat of the Commission within a period of sixty (60) days from the date of the notification.
On 26 May 2022, the Complainants wrote to the Secretariat to request an extension of 14 days under Rule 98(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.
On 18 July 2022, the Secretariat of the Commission received the Complainants' submissions on the merits.

On 09 August 2022, a Note Verbale was sent to the Respondent State to transmit to it the Complainants' arguments on the merits. By the same Note Verbale, the Secretariat invited the Respondent State to submit its observations on the said arguments within a period of two (2) months upon receipt of the notification.

By a Note Verbale of 16 November 2022, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State that to date, it had not yet received its observations on the merits and that consequently it was obliged to take a default decision during its subsequent sessions.

The Complainants maintain that the Communication satisfies the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter. With regard to the requirement laid down in Article 56(1) relating to the identity of the authors of the Communication, the Complainants indicate that the Communication was submitted to the Commission by three organizations representing the victims, which are clearly identified in the Complaint with their contact details.

Concerning the requirement laid down by Article 56(2) on the compatibility of the Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter, the Complainants maintain that they attach capital importance to all the principles conveyed by Article 4 of the Constitutive Act of the African Union. They maintain that the present Complaint aims at respect for these principles, notably the promotion of gender equality, respect for human rights, the rule of law, respect for the promotion of social justice as well as the sanctity of human life and condemnation and rejection of impunity. They state that the Communication alleges only violations of rights recognized by the African Charter and the Maputo Protocol on the rights of women in Africa, respectively ratified without reservation by the Democratic Republic of the Congo on 28/07/1987 and 09/02/2009. They indicate that the alleged violations are thus subsequent to the entry into force of these two instruments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

With regard to the requirements of Article 56(3) of the African Charter, the Complainants indicate that the Communication does not convey insults against the State concerned, its institutions or the African Union. They stress that the Complainants hold the Democratic Republic of the Congo and all the organs of the African Union in great respect. Thus, they made sure that the present Communication does not utter disparaging remarks towards the Respondent State and its institutions or towards the African Union and its organs, notably the Commission which has seized itself of this Complaint.

To prove compliance with the provisions of Article 56(4) of the African Charter, the Complainants put forward that the present Communication is not based on information disseminated by the media. They maintain that they have at their disposal tangible and irrefutable evidence gathered during the various investigative missions they carried out successively to Fizi-Centre, the locality where the violations alleged in the Complaint were committed, then to Kinshasa where the High Military Court sits, as well as the testimonies gathered from the victims or their beneficiaries. Also according to the Complainants, the allegations contained in this Communication are based notably on judgment RP 043 of the Military Court of South Kivu, on the statements of the victims, on witness depositions and on the documents contained in the file under RPA 47 pending before the High Military Court.

With regard to the requirements of Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Complainants recall that the African Charter lays down the rule of exhaustion of local remedies if they exist, unless it is obvious to the Commission that the procedure for these remedies is unduly prolonged. The Complainants note that the African Charter admits an exception to the principle of exhaustion of local remedies, that of their being unduly prolonged. The Complainants observe that through its constant jurisprudence on the illusory and futile nature of exhausting domestic remedies when the procedure had proved to be unduly prolonged.

The Complainants rely on this exception derived from the undue prolongation of the procedure of local remedies to pray the Commission to exempt them from exhausting them and to declare the Complaint admissible. In support of this request, the Complainants observe that the violations alleged in the present Complaint took place on the night of 01 to 02 January 2011. The Military Court of South Kivu rendered its decision on 21 February 2011 convicting the culprits of the violations alleged in this Complaint to sentences of penal servitude while sentencing them jointly and severally with the Congolese State to make pecuniary reparation for the harm suffered by the victims. The Complainants indicate that on the same date of 21 February 2011, the accused lodged an appeal against this decision before the High Military Court.

The Complainants allege that since then, the case has remained pending. They state that the reasons put forward by the High Military Court to adjourn the case indefinitely include notably the absence of a member of the bench who had travelled to Kisangani for another case on 29 July 2015, the date of public hearing communicated by the Court to the parties, as well as the lack of notification and/or appearance at the public hearings of 19 and 26 August 2015 by the accused (Commander Bahati Lisuba Chance) who had been acquitted by the Military Court of South Kivu and by the State of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the civilly liable party. They further allege that at the time the Court had rendered a judgment by default of appearance, thus allowing the proceedings to advance without the presence of the accused acquitted at first instance, the lawyers of the State of the Democratic Republic of the Congo did not regularly appear at the hearings and the Complainants cite as an example the failure of the civilly liable party to appear at the hearing of 24 February 2016.

The Complainants observe that the DRC not only contributed to the delay of justice for the victims by being absent from public hearings, but it also disregarded the request of the victims who asked, at the hearing of 26 August 2015, that the Court hold mobile hearings (audiences foraines) in the locality where the violations were committed, reiterating that it was practically impossible for the victims to appear or to be represented at the hearings held in Kinshasa.

The Complainants indicate that the procedure unduly prolonged by adjournments of hearings manifestly constituting dilatory manoeuvres in the trial by the High Military Court continues to plunge the victims, some already in a situation of extreme vulnerability, into desolation.

They further lament that the expedited procedure which must be reserved for cases relating to the sexual violence alleged in the present communication was not applied although provided for by the Code of Criminal Procedure. They stress that the High Military Court has been seized of the appeal for more than seven years without being able to rule on the merits of the case, which renders this remedy ineffective and practically non-existent for the victims when their specific situation is taken into account.

The Complainants state that at the time the Commission was seized, more than seven years had elapsed without the case in the present Communication being tried because of the interminable adjournments of hearings, to which is added the geographical remoteness of the High Military Court, which generate the undue prolongation of the procedure before the High Military Court and which make it inaccessible and consequently inefficient, ineffective and insufficient for the victims who are physically, morally and financially vulnerable. This state of affairs makes repeated air travel to Kinshasa to appear or to be represented at the trial practically impossible for them. For the Complainants, only people in good financial circumstances can effectively use it; this is the reason why the Commission declared admissible the Communication Purohit & Moore v. The Gambia when it observed that the remedies that existed in The Gambia might be available to wealthy people and were neither real nor practical for victims of modest and indigent backgrounds.

The Complainants, relying on the Commission's view in the Communication Dawda Jawara v. The Gambia and taking into account the situation of the victims, observe that the High Military Court in Kinshasa is not a remedy capable of redressing the violations they suffered. They conclude that the present application satisfies the requirement laid down in Article 56(5) of the Charter on exhaustion of local remedies.

With regard to the requirement of submitting the Communication within a reasonable time after exhaustion of local remedies as provided for in Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainants indicate that in the present case, the High Military Court not having yet ruled on the appeal, the calculation of time from the exhaustion of local remedies does not apply. They indicate that in the absence of exhaustion of local remedies, the date of notification of the unavailability and undue prolongation is taken as the reference point in calculating the reasonable time, as was the Commission's position in the Communication Tsatsu Tsikata v. Ghana. They allege, however, that in the present case, the High Military Court has not yet notified the victims of the outcome of the appeal brought by their torturers in 2011 and that, in the absence of such notification, they had hope of seeing a decision of the High Military Court. The Complainants state that the present Communication concerns a case still pending before the High Military Court, which implies that until the date of seizure, the reasonable time for seizing the Commission had not begun to run. Consequently, they pray the Commission to consider that the present Communication was submitted within a reasonable time.

With regard to the requirement laid down by Article 56(7) of the African Charter, the Complainants indicate that the violations alleged in this Complaint have never been the subject of a judgment beyond the borders of the DRC and no international court has yet rendered a decision on this case.
As indicated above, the Respondent State has not submitted its observations on the admissibility of the Communication despite the multiple requests made to that effect by the Secretariat.

The present Communication was submitted on the basis of Article 55 of the African Charter which gives the Commission competence to receive and consider "Communications other than those of States Parties". The said Communications must, in order to be declared admissible, fulfil the requirements provided for in Article 56 of the African Charter.

Under the provisions of Rule 105(2) of its Rules of Procedure, the Secretariat transmits to the Respondent State the arguments submitted by the Complainants. In this case, the Commission notes that the Secretariat complied with all the requirements of its Rules of Procedure as to the transmission to the Respondent State of the Complainants' observations on admissibility within the prescribed time limits. As the procedure shows, numerous notification and reminder correspondences were sent to the Respondent State during the period from 20 August 2018 to 10 May 2021, notably Notes Verbales referenced CADHP/COMM/686/18/RDC/1232/18, CADHP/COMM/686/18/RDC/616 /19, CADHP/COMM/686/18/RDC/1136 /19 and CADHP/COMM/686/18/RDC/1359 /19, CADHP/COMM/686/18/RDC/603 /20 and CADHP/COMM/686/18/RDC/437/21, by which the Secretariat of the Commission invited it to submit its observations on the admissibility of the Communication. Despite observance of the relevant procedure, the State did not transmit its observations. On the basis of these findings, the Commission decides to examine the Communication on the basis of the elements in its possession, in accordance with its practice.
The Respondent State having not produced a brief on Admissibility, the Commission will proceed to an examination of all the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter.

Under Article 56(1) of the Charter, Communications submitted to the Commission must "indicate their authors even if the latter requests anonymity". The Commission notes that the Communication clearly identifies its authors, who are the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa (IHRDA), Equality Now and the Association of Women Lawyers Defenders of Human Rights (AFADDH for short), whose full addresses as well as all the information establishing their identities are on file. The Commission further notes that the present Communication was submitted in the name and on behalf of 54 victims, including one man.

As regards compliance with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter, which requires that Communications be compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter, the Commission recalls that the requirement is understood as compatibility ratione personae, ratione materiae, ratione temporis and ratione loci of the Communication with the Constitutive Act of the African Union and the African Charter. In this case, the Commission notes that the Communication is submitted by Complainants having standing to do so. The Communication is directed against the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for violations of the rights protected by Articles 1, 5, 6, 7, 14, 15 and 16 of the African Charter, which the State ratified on 20/07/1987. The Commission further notes that the Communication also alleges the violation, on the territory of the Respondent State, of the rights protected by Articles 3, 8, 12, 14, 24 and 25 of the Maputo Protocol, ratified by the Respondent State on 9 June 2008. The Commission also notes that neither the arguments invoked nor the requests formulated are contrary to any of the principles contained in the African Charter and the Constitutive Act of the African Union. The Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

With regard to compliance with the provisions of Article 56(3), Communications must not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the OAU/AU. The Commission notes, in light of its jurisprudence, the Commission notes that the Communication under examination contains no term that could be characterized as insulting or disparaging towards the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union. It therefore considers that the requirement under Article 56(3) of the African Charter has been fulfilled.

Article 56(4) of the African Charter only proscribes Complaints brought before the Commission under Article 55 of the same Charter that "are based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media". The Commission notes that this requirement is met since the Communication contains, notably, judicial documents relating to the file RPA 47 pending before the High Military Court, statements of the victims and testimonies gathered during the investigative missions they carried out successively to Fizi-Centre, the locality where the violations alleged in the Complaint were committed, and to Kinshasa where the High Military Court sits.
Under Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Communication must be submitted after exhaustion of local remedies, unless it is obvious that the procedure is unduly prolonged.

The Commission recalls that the objective of this requirement is to avoid turning international courts into courts of first instance. Furthermore, its application enables the Respondent State to become aware of the facts alleged against it and, where appropriate, to remedy the situation within its judicial system. The Commission notes, however, that the local remedies whose exhaustion is thus required must meet the criteria of availability, effectiveness and sufficiency enshrined in the case of Jawara v. The Gambia. In that landmark decision, the Commission elaborated on the meaning of these criteria by deciding that a remedy is considered available when it can be pursued without impediment by the petitioner, that it is effective if it offers a prospect of success and that it is sufficient when it is capable of satisfying the complainant and redressing the alleged violation.

The Commission notes that, in the present communication, the Complainants allege the undue prolongation of local remedies on the basis of the time elapsed since the commencement of the judicial proceedings at the domestic level and their ineffective and insufficient nature owing to the geographical remoteness of the High Military Court.

The African Charter does not define an unduly prolonged procedure under Article 56(5). There are therefore no standard criteria used by the Commission to determine whether a process has been unduly prolonged.
In its jurisprudence, the position adopted by the Commission is that the prolongation of local remedies must be assessed taking into account the nature and the circumstances surrounding each case.

Thus, in the case of Modise v. Botswana, the Commission held that local remedies lasting more than ten years were unduly prolonged. In its decision Odjouoriby Cossi Paul v. Benin, the Commission considered that an appeal lasting three years at the national level is a remedy unduly prolonged.

The Commission notes that the arguments invoked by the Complainants and the evidence provided indicate that, following the various human rights violations that occurred on the night of 1 to 2 January 2011, the Senior Military Prosecutor's Office of South Kivu began its investigations on 26 January 2011 and the Military Court of South Kivu rendered its decision on 21 February 2011 imposing sentences of penal servitude on the culprits while sentencing them jointly and severally with the Congolese State to make pecuniary reparation for the harm suffered by the victims. The Commission further notes that on the same day, the accused lodged an appeal against the said decision before the High Military Court of Kinshasa, which is pending to date.

The Commission notes that in the present Communication, a period of more than 5 years and 8 months elapsed between the date of seizure of the national courts in January 2011 and that of seizure of the Commission in October 2016. It further notes that since the appeal lodged by the accused before the High Military Court, the file has remained at the same stage and no follow-up has been given to the Complainants owing to the repeated adjournments.

The Commission also observes that the relevant norms of the domestic law of the Respondent State, notably the Code of Criminal Procedure applicable before military courts and those of ordinary law, prescribe the expedited handling of cases relating to sexual violence. It provides that, without prejudice to the legal provisions relating to the flagrante delicto procedure, the preliminary investigation in matters of sexual violence is carried out within a maximum period of one month from the seizure of the judicial authority and that the investigation and delivery of judgment are carried out within a period of three months from the seizure of the Judicial Authority. In application of these provisions of Congolese law and in light of the above developments, the Commission finds that the local remedies, which lasted more than 5 years for a case alleging sexual violence, were unduly prolonged.

Turning to the ineffective and insufficient nature of the remedies alleged by the Complainants, it can easily be deduced from the foregoing that remedies that were thus prolonged manifestly could not have been effective. In addition, the Commission notes that the geographical remoteness of the High Military Court, which requires the Complainants to travel by air from South Kivu to appear at the hearings, renders it inaccessible and consequently inefficient, ineffective and insufficient for the victims who are physically, morally and financially vulnerable. The Commission further notes that the refusal to hold mobile hearings in the locality where the violations were committed constitutes an obstacle for the Complainants to obtaining justice at the national level.

The Commission recalls its jurisprudence in the Communication Gabriel Shumba v. Zimbabwe where it concluded that the remedies provided for in Zimbabwean law posed, given the circumstances of the case, impediments to their being exhausted, thus becoming unavailable to the complainants. The Commission is of the view that seizing the High Military Court in Kinshasa is not a remedy capable of redressing the violations suffered by the Complainants. Consequently, the Commission finds that the local remedies were not effective, without any need to rule on their sufficiency. In view of the foregoing, the Commission concludes that the Communication complies with the requirements of Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

According to the wording of Article 56(6) of the Charter, the Communication must be submitted within a reasonable time from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter.

In the present Communication, it emerges from the analysis of Article 56(5) made in the preceding paragraphs that local remedies were not exhausted because they were unduly prolonged and proved ineffective. Referring to the jurisprudence of the Commission in the case of Tsatsu Tsikata v. Ghana, the Complainants observe that in the absence of exhaustion of local remedies, the date of notification to the Complainant of the unavailability and undue prolongation is taken as the reference point in calculating the reasonable time. They indicate that the present Communication was submitted within a reasonable time following the lack of notification relating to the outcome of the case which is still pending before the High Military Court.

The Commission recalls that the requirement under Article 56(6) remains applicable to all Communications because it aims to instil reasonable diligence and vigilance and to discourage future Complainants from registering delays in seizing the Commission. Thus, the Commission declared Communication 305/05 - Article 19 and others v. Zimbabwe inadmissible, because the Complainant should have seized the Commission as soon as it saw that its efforts to secure a remedy at the national level "had reached a dead end".
In the present Communication, the time for seizure cannot be calculated "from the time local remedies are exhausted" but rather "from the date the Commission is seized of the matter".

In this regard, the question to be settled is whether in this case the seizure of the Commission was made within a reasonable time. The Commission, drawing inspiration from the practice in the Inter-American and European human rights systems, which consider the six-month period as a "standard norm", has accepted in its jurisprudence that the determination of the "reasonable time" for submitting a Communication must be made on a case-by-case basis, according to the circumstances of each case. The Commission held that 2 years and 5 months in the case of Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan and 1 year and 3 months in the case of Dr Farouk Mohamed Ibrahim v. Sudan were not reasonable periods, on the ground that the Complainants had submitted the Communication well after the point that could have been considered reasonable but also gave no compelling reason for the long wait before seizing the Commission.

By contrast, in the case of Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and others v. DRC, the Commission considered that the three-year period taken before seizing it was justified, given the reasons advanced by the Complainants, namely the physical inaccessibility of the courts, the lack of notification of the judgment of the High Military Court as well as the serious and massive nature of the alleged violations.

In the present Communication, the Commission notes that the Military Court of South Kivu rendered its decision on 21 February 2011. On the same day, the accused lodged an appeal before the High Military Court of Kinshasa against the judgment that sentenced them jointly and severally with the Congolese State to make pecuniary reparation for the harm suffered by the victims.

The Commission further notes that the High Military Court scheduled public hearings during which the case was always adjourned sine die, notably on 29 July 2015, 19 and 26 August 2015, the most recent of which is that of 24 February 2016.

The Commission considers the latter as the date from which the time for its seizure should begin to run. It notes that the Complainants submitted their Complaint on 4 October 2016, that is 7 months after the last action recorded in the context of the present Communication. In accordance with its jurisprudence, the Commission finds that this time for seizure is reasonable and that the requirement under examination is fulfilled.

Finally, under the provisions of Article 56(7), the Communication must not deal with cases which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter. The Commission recalls that these provisions require the Communication to respect the principles of res judicata, lis pendens, and non bis in idem.

In this case, the Commission relies on the elements submitted by the Complainants to find that the facts alleged in the present Communication have been brought only before national courts. No international or regional human rights body has examined a Complaint concerning the same facts, nor has the case been settled before another forum applying the principles recalled supra. The Commission therefore finds that the Communication does not concern a case which has been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations or the Constitutive Act of the African Union, or the African Charter and concludes that it respects the requirement laid down by the provisions of the said article and consequently fulfils the admissibility requirements laid down in Article 56
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with Article 56 of the African Charter;

It follows from the Complainants' own admission and even from the procedure described above that the Complainants were notified of the decision on admissibility on 30 March 2022 and therefore had to file their submissions on the merits within the period of 60 days in accordance with Rule 108(1) of the Commission's 2010 Rules of Procedure, that is by 30 May 2022. On 26 May 2022, that is four (4) days before the expiry of this required period, the Complainants requested an additional period of 14 days to finalize the arguments on the merits.

The Complainants admit that although this extension was granted to them, they were unable to finalize the brief within the period. They claim that this is due notably to the fact that the verification of certain information required communicating directly with the victims whom they found it difficult to reach, notably because they do not have modern means of communication such as the internet or telephones. They then implore the Commission to exempt them from the rigour of the texts in the interest of justice for the victims.

In the Communication Mouvement du 17 Mai v. Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Commission noted that the purpose of time-limit requirements in a procedure is to guarantee the expeditiousness of justice and to ensure that it is rendered within a reasonable time. The Commission considers that the notion of expeditiousness of justice implies that the procedure must be conducted promptly without loss of time. However, the Commission is also convinced that this notion is not limited merely to speed; it also includes a degree of quality in the procedure.

Under this second aspect, it is the interest of justice that comes into play. Thus, for example, in the case of Collectif des familles de disparu(e)s v. Algeria, at its 16th Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Kigali, Rwanda, the Commission decided, "for the proper administration of justice, to admit the Respondent State's observations on the merits", which had been transmitted to it six (6) months after the submission of the complaining party. In particular, in that case, whereas the complainant's observations on the merits had been transmitted to the Respondent State on 25 September 2013, the latter waited until 3 April 2014 to submit its arguments.

In the present case, the Commission observes that the case involves about fifty victims. In analyzing the submissions, the Commission notes that the Complainants give a detailed description of the harm suffered by each of them, accompanied by their individual testimonies and their identity documents. The Commission shares the Complainants' view that the collection of such individualized information undoubtedly required sufficient time to enable the Complainants to reach each of the victims directly.

In this sense, the Commission considers that the delay of one month (the Complainants having submitted their arguments on 18 July 2022, that is 1 month after the expiry of the extension granted to them) in the Complainants' submissions on the merits is justified and decides to admit them.

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 5 of the African Charter and of Article 3(1) of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women (Maputo Protocol). They consider that the right to life is a fundamental right which all human beings must enjoy without any discrimination and that consequently the exposure of the victims to suffering and personal indignity violates the right to human dignity.

Referring to the Convention against Torture, the Complainants conclude that the blows and injuries inflicted on the 52 victims of Fizi constitute torture. In support of their conclusion, they consider first that the suffering inflicted on the victims was severe and intentional and that the agents of the State's armed forces committed rapes and gang rapes against 51 women. They add that many of these gang rapes were committed in the presence of the victims' relatives, in particular their husbands and children (e.g.: victims Nos 1, 15, 18, 19, 22, 24, 26, 27, 29, 31, 39, 41, 47, 50 and 51). The soldiers also struck the victims with rifle butts (e.g.: victims Nos 17 and 18). According to the Complainants, these acts necessarily cause severe suffering and can only be intentional because they were used as tools of punishment and humiliation against the victims and their relatives. They add that, moreover, these acts were inflicted on the victims as punishment for their alleged role in the death of Petro. Finally, the Complainants stress that the perpetrators of the acts are soldiers, members of the armed forces of the DRC.
They thus request the African Commission to find a flagrant violation of Article 5 of the African Charter and of Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainants maintain that Articles 6 of the African Charter and 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol were violated. In particular, they point out that the arrests and imprisonments of the 52 victims were carried out without regard to any legal text in force in the DRC. They stress, above all, that all 52 victims were arrested by soldiers and that all the victims, with the exception of one person (Eric Ntalindwa), were arrested followed by rape before being left in their homes or in the bush.

By way of example, they point to the situation of one victim, Bora Ezéchiel (victim No. 52) who was, in addition, forced to spend the night in a military camp in Fizi on 31 December 2011. They indicate that she was detained there with her children and that she was released the next day following the intervention of the administration in Fizi (See Annex 52).

They insist that, moreover, the soldiers had no legal power to imprison civilians. In support of their allegation, they point out that the 52 victims were all civilians who were arrested and detained as collective punishment following the death of Corporal Ndaisaba Petro. They indicate that this was confirmed by the Military Court of South Kivu in convicting nine soldiers for crime against humanity by imprisonment or other severe forms of deprivation of liberty.
Consequently, the Complainants pray the African Commission to find a violation of Article 6 of the African Charter and of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 7(1) of the African Charter and 8 of the Maputo Protocol which protect the right to a fair trial and the right of access to justice. The Complainants stress that the right to a fair trial is paramount in any democratic State because respect for this right enables the implementation of the other rights guaranteed by the African Charter.

To explain the notion of reasonable time, they rely on the jurisprudence of the European Court which indicates that this notion must be assessed according to the circumstances of each case, the conduct of the applicant, the conduct of the Respondent State and what is at stake for the applicant. According to them, the case in question has nothing complex about it insofar as the accused were identified. As to the conduct of the parties, the Complainants recall that the victims requested on several occasions that the High Military Court hold mobile hearings in Fizi because it was practically impossible to appear or to be represented at the hearings held in Kinshasa.

They insist that, moreover, the slowness of the procedure is attributable to the Congolese State. The Complainants allege that the reasons advanced by the High Court to adjourn the case indefinitely, notably the travel of a member of the bench to Kisangani on the date of the sitting as well as the lack of notification and/or appearance of an accused at the public hearings, do not hold. In particular, they insist that the State bears responsibility for this absence from the public hearings because it has the public powers to compel the accused to take part in the hearings. They indicate that, moreover, the Congolese Code of Criminal Procedure provides that, without prejudice to the legal provisions relating to the flagrante delicto procedure, the preliminary investigation in matters of sexual violence is carried out within a maximum period of one month from the judicial seizure and that despite this provision, the appeal has been pending before the High Military Court since 21 February 2011.

Hence they pray the African Commission to hold that all the irregularities that have marred the procedure before the High Military Court since 21 February 2011 violate Article 7.1 of the African Charter and Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol.

The Complainants allege that the Congolese State violated Article 14 of the African Charter and Articles 16 and 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol. They indicate that even if the right to property is not absolute under the African Charter, a State Party must prove that any interference with this right was made in the public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws.

They reiterate that the looting carried out by the FARDC caused the destruction of houses and numerous goods as well as the loss of houses by many inhabitants of Fizi together with all the effects they contained. They add that the attacks caused several infringements of the right to property including thefts, extortions, malicious destruction, damage to or deterioration of property, the destruction of shops whose contents were carried off, and the extortion of telephones and sums of money found on the victims.

Referring to the SERAC case in which the African Commission held that the destruction of the houses and villages of the Ogoni people constituted a serious violation of the right to housing implicitly protected by Article 14 of the African Charter, they conclude that the destruction of the houses of the inhabitants of Fizi by the security forces constitutes on the part of the DRC a violation of the right to property and the right to housing of the inhabitants concerned.

The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 16 of the African Charter and 14(1) of the Maputo Protocol. After defining the rights protected by these provisions, the Complainants allege that the physical and psychological suffering that the victims endured implies the violation of these rights. In particular, they recall that 51 of the 52 victims were victims of rapes or gang rapes perpetrated by agents of the armed forces which left indelible physical and moral after-effects. They add that although the State was able to cover certain care at the Fizi hospital, the victims received no assistance from the State after leaving the hospital despite the multiple lingering sufferings. They reiterate that some victims have already succumbed to the gravity of these physical and psychological sufferings.

The Complainants stress that the situation of the survivors is aggravated by the lack of means to obtain medical care. They reiterate that some victims suffer from paralysis of the lower limbs, others are sterile and others traumatized because they were raped in their homes in front of their children and husbands. They also say that the victims are stigmatized by the community, which calls them "Wakubakwa" to designate a raped person. The same is true of the children who are ostracized at school.

The Complainants maintain that by ratifying the African Charter, the DRC undertook to take all measures to prevent the violation of the rights it sets out and, where appropriate, to remedy their disregard by its agents or by any other person under its authority. They reiterate that by violating its obligations arising from the various provisions of the Charter and the Maputo Protocol, the State violated Article 1 of the Charter
The Respondent State has not submitted its observations on the merits despite multiple reminders from the Secretariat of the Commission inviting it to do so.

As indicated above, the Respondent State has not submitted its observations on the Complainants' allegations. In the absence of these observations, the Commission will pursue its analysis on the basis of the elements at its disposal; this in accordance with its already established jurisprudence.

Before any analysis on the merits of the Complainants' allegations, it is important for the Commission to establish the scope of its competence under the Charter. Indeed, in the present Communication, in addition to the allegations of violation of the African Charter, the Complainants invite the Commission to find the violation of the provisions of the Protocol to the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights on the Rights of Women in Africa, known as the Maputo Protocol. It is therefore incumbent on the Commission to verify its competence to interpret this Protocol.

Article 27 of the Maputo Protocol on its interpretation indicates that "the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights shall be seized with matters of interpretation arising from the application or implementation of this Protocol". This provision implies that in the event of a conflict of interpretation of the Maputo Protocol, it is the Court that is competent to decide. However, this does not mean that the Commission is not competent to interpret this instrument for the protection of women's rights in Africa.

Indeed, by its expression "Protocol to the Charter", the Maputo Protocol is a supplement to and consequently forms an integral part of the African Charter. This follows even from Article 66 of the Charter which provides for the adoption of special protocols or agreements, if necessary, to "supplement the provisions of the present Charter". In particular, the Maputo Protocol finds its raison d'être or legal basis in the provisions of Article 18(3) of the Charter which requires all States to eliminate all forms of discrimination against women and to ensure the protection of women's rights, as stipulated in international declarations and conventions. It therefore supplements the Charter in its Article 18(3).

The status of the Maputo Protocol as a supplement to the Charter is also deduced from its Article 26 which requires States to incorporate in their periodic reports submitted in accordance with the terms of Article 62 of the African Charter, indications of the legislative and other measures they have taken for the full realization of the rights recognized in the Maputo Protocol.

Thus, the Commission being vested with the power to interpret the principal instrument that is the Charter, it follows that it is also so vested for the document that supplements it, namely, therefore, the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission observes that in reality, all the Complainants' allegations are linked to the ineffectiveness of the appeal made by the convicted persons before the High Military Court. Indeed, the Commission notes that whereas the 1 Judge had admitted the violations alleged by the Complainants and had convicted the accused, the procedure before the High Military Court (appellate court) has been indefinitely long. In particular, although there were several hearings in 2015, the Commission notes from the Complainants' submissions that many others were postponed and no decision on the merits has been rendered. Also the victims are and remain drowned in dilatory procedural manoeuvres preventing them from having the first judge's convictions enforced. It is for this reason that it proposes to analyze first the allegation of violation of the right of access to justice and the right to a fair trial

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 7(1) of the African Charter and of Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol. 106.Article 7(1) provides: "1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal." 107.In the case of Kevin Mgwanga Gunme et al v. Cameroon, the Commission indicated that respect for the rights set out in Article 7 is a fundamental principle in any democratic State. The Commission considers that it is through respect for these rights that the other rights guaranteed by the Charter can be realized. Thus, it is important that States take rigorous measures to ensure their application or to enable their respect. 108.The right to be tried within a reasonable time includes the expression "reasonable time" which needs to be clarified in order to understand its scope and content. Unfortunately, the Charter does not give its meaning. However, the Commission first notes that this expression contains a juxtaposition of two terms: that of "time" and that of "reasonable". In essence, the term "time" means an interval of time during which an action occurs. Thus, it can be deduced that, in the context of judicial proceedings, "time" means an interval of time in which a trial, a judgment or a judicial decision takes place. 109.As for the qualifier "reasonable", it refers to what is logical and satisfactory. It follows that the term "reasonable time" as intended by the Charter refers to an interval of time that is neither surprisingly long nor abusively short. In other words, the Charter wants the duration of the trial to be of an acceptable length or not excessively long or else the trial to be concluded without excessive delay.

However, it remains important to determine what represents a delay that is not excessive. In its Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa adopted in 2003, the Commission indicated that to determine the possible existence of excessive delay, account must be taken notably of the complexity of the case, the conduct of the parties, the conduct of other participants in the proceedings, the conduct of the competent authorities, whether or not a person is in pre-trial detention and the interest of the person concerned in the proceedings. The Commission therefore considers that the circumstances of the case, notably the complexity of the case, the conduct of the authorities and of the trial in general, are an important element in determining whether the length of a trial is reasonable.

In the case under analysis, the Commission observes that the Military Court of South Kivu had convicted the perpetrators on 21 February 2011. The latter lodged an appeal on the spot the same day, that is to say the 2011 before the High Military Court. However, the Commission also notes that at the time of receipt of the Complainants' observations on the merits on 26 July 2022, that is about 10 years after it was seized, the High Military Court had not yet rendered its decision although hearings had taken place in 2015.

The Commission notes that there were no particular circumstances that contributed to such a delay as defined above. In this sense, it considers that this waiting period is not reasonable. This violation of the right to a remedy thus led to the actualization of all the other violations alleged and admitted by the first judge. The State therefore took back with one hand what it had granted with the other.
Hence the violation of Article 7(1) of the Charter On the violation of Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol

Article 8(a) and (e) of the Maputo Protocol provides that "women and men are equal before the law and shall have the right to equal protection and benefit of the law. States shall take all appropriate measures to ensure: a) effective access by women to legal and judicial assistance and services; e) equitable representation of women in the judicial institutions and those responsible for law enforcement". This provision advocates the right of access to justice and the right to equal protection of women before the law.

The Commission considers that this right preaches the non-discrimination of women before the law. In particular, the right of access to justice and to equal protection of women before the law consists in the right of women or any other person to have access to the courts and to be treated or protected in the same way by the law and the courts. Thus, this provision prevents protection by the courts or the law from being denied to women on the pretext that they are women while men benefit from it. The Commission considers that, for there to be a violation of Article 8(a) and (e), it must be demonstrated that women did not benefit from the same protection as men from the courts or the law.

In this case, the Commission does not find in the Complainants' submissions elements that show that women were victims of treatment different from that of men before the courts or the law. In particular, it is not demonstrated that the excessive delay or unreasonable time taken by the High Military Court to decide on the situation of the victims was due to their social status as women. More specifically, that legal assistance or legal or judicial services were denied to the women victims of these attacks for the sole reason of belonging to the category of "women".

In the absence of this proof, the Commission concludes that Article 8(a) and (e) was not violated. On the alleged violation of the right not to be subjected to torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment and the right to dignity

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 5 of the African Charter and of Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol. Article 5 of the Charter guarantees respect for human dignity and prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment in these terms: "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited". As for Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol, it provides that "Every woman shall have the right to dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition and protection of her human and legal rights."

The Complainants allege that the blows and injuries inflicted on the 52 victims of Fizi constitute torture within the meaning of the Convention against Torture. It is important for the Commission to understand the content and meaning of Article 5 of the Charter and of Article 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

The Commission observes that the two provisions are interconnected and complement each other in that they both contribute to respect for human dignity. Indeed, whereas Article 5 advocates respect for the dignity of every individual, Article 3(1) of the Protocol is specific because it advocates the dignity of women. Article 5 of the Charter lists certain attitudes that lead to the violation of human dignity including, among others, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment which are alleged by the Complainants in the present communication. The Commission is of the view that dignity is a concept around which the prohibition of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment is founded. Indeed, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity.

Neither the Charter nor the Maputo Protocol defines the notion of torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In the absence of such a definition by the Charter, the Commission can only draw inspiration from other international human rights instruments under Articles 60 and 61 of the Charter. Thus, Article 1 of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment indicates that the term "torture" "means any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for such purposes as obtaining from him or a third person information or a confession, punishing him for an act he or a third person has committed or is suspected of having committed, or intimidating or coercing him or a third person, or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind, when such pain or suffering is inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity. It does not include pain or suffering arising only from, inherent in or incidental to lawful sanctions".

Thus, the Commission notes that this definition contains three cumulative conditions in order to be able to conclude that torture exists. First, torture involves the intentional infliction of severe suffering which may be physical or mental. This is what the United Nations Human Rights Committee emphasized in its general comment No. 20 in interpreting Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights which prohibits torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment. In that general comment, the Committee indicated that this article "relates not only to acts that cause physical pain but also to acts that cause mental suffering" Next, this infliction must be administered by a public official or any person acting in an official capacity or at his instigation or with his express or tacit consent, and finally the infliction must be done for a specific purpose.

As for the notion of "cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment", the Commission, in the case of Media Rights v. Nigeria, stressed that "the expression 'cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment' is to be interpreted so as to extend to the widest possible protection against abuses, whether physical or mental".

In this case, from the Complainants' submissions and the testimonies at its disposal, the Commission notes that physical and mental violence was indeed inflicted on the victims. These notably include "gang rapes imposed on women in the presence of their husbands and children, extortions, malicious destruction, damage to or deterioration of property, blows with rifle butts or daggers on targeted persons.....". 125.The Commission shares the Complainants' view that these acts were intentional, because it is manifest that the perpetrators (that is, the soldiers) administered them to the victims as punishment for their alleged role in the death of Pedro. It follows that all these inflictions were made only for the purpose of punishing the victims following the death of Corporal Pedro. The Commission also notes that these acts were inflicted by a public authority, namely the Congolese law enforcement forces, in particular the soldiers. Moreover, in its general comment No. 4, the Commission expressly referred to acts of sexual and gender-based violence as a form of torture and ill-treatment because of the specific, traumatic and gender-specific impact of sexual violence on the victims, including at the individual, family and collective levels. 126.It follows that all the conditions are met to conclude that there was torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and, consequently, an infringement of the human dignity of the victims who are the women in the present case. 127.The Commission concludes that Articles 5 of the Charter and 3(1) of the Maputo Protocol were violated 128.Under this allegation, the Complainants invoke the violation of Article 6 of the African Charter and of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 6 of the Charter which stipulates that: "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The provisions of this article protect both the right to liberty of the person and the right to security of the person. Both rights are fundamental.

Indeed, the enjoyment of these two rights plays an important role in that it influences the enjoyment of other rights. This was, moreover, emphasized by the United Nations Human Rights Committee in its general comment No. 35, indicating that liberty and security of person are precious in themselves and also because the deprivation of liberty and the denial of the right to security of person have at all times been means of impeding the enjoyment of other rights.

In the case of Amnesty International and Others v. Sudan, the Commission indicated that Article 6 must be interpreted so as to permit arrests only in the exercise of the powers normally devolved on law enforcement in a democratic society. Likewise, in the case of Liesbeth Zegveld and Mussie Ephrem v. Eritrea, the African Commission stressed that all detentions must respect fundamental human rights principles. There should be no incommunicado detention and States must indicate that someone is detained by specifying the place of detention. In the Communication Purohit and Moore v. The Gambia also, the African Commission pointed out that the deprivation of liberty must be authorized by law and must be compatible with the obligations of States Parties to the African Charter.

It follows from these assertions of the Commission that the right to liberty and security of person within the meaning of Article 6 means that arrests and detentions must be carried out in strict compliance with the law. However, compliance with the law is not sufficient in itself, it is also necessary that these laws be acceptable in a democratic society.

In this case, after analysis of all the documents and the various testimonies, the Commission first observes that almost all the victims were subjected to unlawful arrest and detention in their homes and in the bush by the soldiers deployed to avenge the death of Corporal Pedro. During these arrests, these victims were raped, some of them in front of their husbands and their children. Others were beaten to force them to accept sexual relations.

From the foregoing, the Commission concludes that the arrests to which the victims were subjected did not comply with the law, since not only were they carried out in their homes and in the bush, but they were also accompanied by acts of rape and human rights violations.
It follows that Article 6 of the Charter was violated. On the alleged violation of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol which stipulates that "every woman shall be entitled to respect for her life, her physical integrity and the security of her person. All forms of exploitation, punishment and inhuman or degrading treatment shall be prohibited". This provision protects the right to life, to physical integrity and to the security of women.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee has emphasized that "the right to life concerns the entitlement of individuals to be free from acts and omissions that are intended or may be expected to cause their unnatural or premature death, as well as to enjoy a life with dignity". As for physical integrity, the Commission considers that it is infringed when acts of torture, inhuman or degrading treatment or any kind of barbarity are inflicted on a human being. This implies that respect for physical integrity ensures the protection of the human body and of human life. The right to human security, for its part, protects the human person against any serious and widespread threat.

Thus, through its Article 4(1), the Maputo Protocol wants the life, physical integrity and security of women to be respected in all respects. As the Commission has already indicated in the case of Geneviève Mbiankeu v. Cameroon, States are bound not only by the obligation to respect the rights of their citizens but also to protect them against violation by third parties. Thus, in the case of World Organisation Against Torture and African Zone League for the Defence of the Rights of Children and Students (on behalf of Céline) v. Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Commission considered that the acts of physical violence and gang rape perpetrated against the victim undoubtedly constitute a violation of her physical and moral integrity.

In the present communication, as demonstrated above, the victims faced acts of torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment resulting from the gang rapes inflicted on them. This constitutes an infringement of physical integrity.
It follows that Article 4(1) of the Maputo Protocol was violated
The Complainants allege the violation of Article 14 of the Charter and of Articles 16 and 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol.

This article provides that "The right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws". On analysis of the provisions of this article, the Commission observes that the latter establishes two aspects of the right to property: that is, the principle of the right to property and peaceful enjoyment of goods on the one hand; and the possibility and conditions of this right to property on the other hand.

The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights defined the right to property by indicating that, in its classical acceptation, this right comprises three elements, namely the right to use the thing which is the object of the right (usus), the right to enjoy its fruits (fructus), and the right to dispose of it, that is to transfer it (abusus). It is in this sense that the Commission considers that the right to property includes not only the right to have access to one's property and to prevent the invasion and encroachment of the said property, but also the right to possession, and use as well as control in complete tranquillity of this property, as its owners desire.

However, Article 14 of the Charter recognizes that States are permitted, in certain circumstances, to control notably the use of property in accordance with the public or general interest, by applying the laws they consider necessary for this purpose.

Thus, in the case of George Iyanyori Kajikabi v. Arab Republic of Egypt, the Commission observed that the chaotic circumstances in which the victims were displaced did not allow them to take their personal effects and that they were forced to abandon them behind them. It also noted that, since the valuables were not returned to them and adequate compensation in respect of the destruction of their personal effects was not granted to them, the State violated Article 14 of the Charter.

In the present communication, the Commission observes that the looting and the attacks carried out by the FARDC caused the destruction of houses, shops and numerous other goods including thefts, extortion of telephones and shops, malicious destruction, deterioration of property. The Commission is of the view that all these acts are such as to impede the right to use the thing that is the object of property and do not allow the owners to enjoy its fruits peacefully. The same is true of the right to dispose of or transfer goods over which the victims had the right of property. Indeed, the appropriation of the victims' goods by the perpetrators in the present case contradicts the right to dispose of the thing over which one has the right of property because it is done without the consent of the victims. Thus, the Commission concludes that the right to property as described above was violated in all its aspects.
It follows that Article 14 of the Charter was violated

Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol stipulates as follows: "Women shall have the right to equal access to housing and to acceptable living conditions in a healthy environment. To ensure this right, States Parties shall grant to women, whatever their marital status, access to adequate housing". This article protects the right to housing for women on an equal footing with men.

In its Principles and Guidelines on the Implementation of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter, the Commission defined the human right to adequate housing as "the right of everyone to gain and sustain a safe and secure home and community in which to live in peace and dignity". In the SERAC case, the Commission indicated that at a bare minimum, the right to housing obliged the Nigerian government not to destroy the houses of its citizens.

It thus considered that the obligation to respect housing rights requires that the State, and therefore all its organs and agents, abstain from carrying out, sponsoring or tolerating practices, policies or legal measures violating the integrity of individuals or encroaching on their freedom to use this material or other resources available to them, in the manner they find most appropriate to satisfy the housing needs of the individual, family, household or community. Within the meaning of Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol, women must be protected against such practices, policies and legal measures that block the use of their homes in any way.

As explained in the SERAC case, the right to shelter goes even further than a roof over one's head and encompasses the right of every individual to be left alone and to live in peace whether under a roof or not. In the present case, it emerges from the testimonies and the Complainants' submissions that some of the victims' houses were burned, others demolished. As indicated above, all these acts violate the right to housing. Indeed, from all these acts, it is understood that the victims could not live in peace regardless of whether they were under a roof or not.
It follows that Article 16 of the Maputo Protocol was violated On the violation of Article 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol

Article 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol obliges all States Parties to take all appropriate measures to promote women's access to and control over productive resources such as land and to guarantee their right to property. This article protects one of the aspects of the right to sustainable development of women in Africa. It aims notably at the promotion of women's economic rights and independence.

In particular, States must put in place legislation and administrative practices so that women enjoy on an equal footing the same rights as men over economic resources, notably equal access to ownership of land and other property, to credit, to inheritance, to natural resources and to new appropriate techniques. In other words, this provision invites States to contribute to facilitating the independent development of women and, consequently, to enabling their economic potential. They must, in particular, make available to them the productive resources necessary for their economic fulfilment.

In the present case, the Commission observes that quite a lot of property belonging to the victims was destroyed. These notably include houses and numerous other effects they contained. The testimonies show notably that thefts, extortions, destruction of shops, theft of money, telephones... characterized the attacks perpetrated by the soldiers. The Commission considers that all these effects constitute productive resources for the victims and concludes that the Respondent State was not in a position to protect them.
It follows that Article 19(c) of the Maputo Protocol was violated
The Complainants allege the violation of Articles 16 of the Charter and of Article 14(1) of the Maputo Protocol.

Article 16 of the Charter provides as follows: "1. Every individual shall have the right to enjoy the best attainable state of physical and mental health. 2. States Parties to the present Charter shall take the necessary measures to protect the health of their people and to ensure that they receive medical attention when they are sick."

In the case of Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and INTERIGHTS v. Egypt, the Commission noted that the right to health functions directly or indirectly as a precondition to all the other human rights recognized by the African Charter. This was also emphasized in the Communication Purohit and Moore v. The Gambia where the Commission indicated that the enjoyment of the right to health as widely understood is vital to all aspects of a person's life and well-being, and is crucial to the realization of all the other fundamental human rights and freedoms. According to the Commission, this right includes the right to health facilities, access to goods and services which must be guaranteed to all, without discrimination of any kind.

The Commission also indicated in its Principles and Guidelines on the Implementation of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights that the right to health also includes the right to be free from unjustified interference, including, among others, the right not to be subjected to torture and other forms of ill-treatment. What is more, in the same principles and guidelines, the Commission indicated that one of the minimum core obligations of the right to health is to prevent violence against women and mitigate its impact on the physical and mental health of survivors.

In this case, as already explained above, the Complainants were subjected to torture and other inhuman and degrading treatment. In this sense, the Commission considers that this constitutes an unjustified interference with the right to health within the meaning of Article 16 of the Charter. In particular, the Commission observes that the gang rapes perpetrated by the FRDC against the victims in the presence of their husbands and children left them with indelible physical and moral after-effects. The Commission notes that, moreover, the Respondent State did nothing to prevent them or to mitigate their impact on their physical or mental health. Yet, as indicated by the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in its general comment No. 14, a State fails in its obligation to protect the right to health when it "fails to take all necessary measures to safeguard persons within their jurisdiction from infringements of the right to health by third parties."
It follows that Article 16 of the African Charter was violated. On the alleged violation of Article 14(1) of the Maputo Protocol

Article 14(1) provides as follows: "States Parties shall ensure that the right to health of women, including sexual and reproductive health is respected and promoted". This provision protects women's rights to sexual and reproductive health. The Maputo Protocol gives details as to the content of these rights by stipulating that these rights include: "a) the right to control their fertility; b) the right to decide whether to have children, the number of children and the spacing of children; c) the right to choose any method of contraception; d) the right to self-protection and to be protected against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV/AIDS; e) the right to be informed on one's health status and on the health status of one's partner, particularly if affected with sexually transmitted infections, including HIV/AIDS, in accordance with internationally recognized standards and best practices; f) the right to family planning education".

The Commission considers that States have an obligation to ensure that all the aspects described above are respected. In particular, States must ensure that laws, policies, administrative procedures and practices, as well as socio-cultural norms and attitudes that impede access to family planning/contraception or the right of women to exercise control over fertility are avoided. The Commission considers that all these elements infringe the woman's right to life, to non-discrimination and to health.

As for the right to self-protection and to be protected against HIV and sexually transmitted infections, it recalls the general obligation of the State to create a favourable legal and social environment enabling women to be in a position to freely and fully realize their right to protect themselves and to be protected. The right to be informed of the health status of one's partner is also crucial. The Commission considers that it "enables women to make informed decisions about their own health, in particular where they could be exposed to serious risks of infection".

In the present case, the Commission observes that although the Complainants assert that some of the victims were infected with HIV/AIDS following the violence they faced, they do not give any supporting documents.
It follows that Article 14.1 of the Maputo Protocol was not violated

The Complainants allege the violation of Article 1 of the Charter which provides that: "The Member States of the Organization of African Unity parties to the present Charter shall recognize the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in this Charter and shall undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them". This provision means purely and simply that States must give effect to the provisions of the Charter. In the present case, the Complainants consider that by ratifying the African Charter, the DRC undertook to ensure respect for the rights protected by this Charter by developing the necessary measures to prevent their violation, and by remedying it in case of violation. They also consider that by violating provisions of the Charter, the DRC also violated Article 1 of the Charter.

As emerges from its well-established jurisprudence, the Commission observes that indeed, the violation of a provision of the Charter implies a violation of Article 1 of the Charter. Thus, a violation of any provision of the Charter automatically constitutes a violation of Article 1 of the Charter insofar as it evidences the failure of the State Party to adopt adequate measures to give effect to the provisions of the African Charter.
Consequently, having already found a violation of the provisions of the Charter, the Commission concludes that Article 1 of the Charter was also violated.

The Complainants request a number of various reparations. The African Charter does not provide a specific provision on reparations in case of found violations of the rights enshrined therein. However, the right to reparations for violation of human rights obligations being a fundamental principle of international law, the Commission considers that it goes without saying that any harm must be repaired even in the absence of a legal provision. This was, moreover, recalled by the Permanent Court of International Justice in the following terms: "it is a principle of international law that the breach of an engagement involves an obligation to make reparation in an adequate form. Reparation therefore is the indispensable complement of a failure to apply a convention and there is no necessity for this to be stated in the convention itself."

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has also concluded that any violation of the rights enshrined in the Charter gives rise to a right to reparation. This is so, for example, in the case of Jean-Marie Atangana Mebara v. Republic of Cameroon, where the Commission indicated that reparation may take various forms depending on the rights violated and the circumstances of the case, ranging from administrative, legislative and judicial actions to monetary compensation.

In the present case, the Complainants make a series of requests for reparation. The Commission proposes to analyze them one by one. a. On the declaration of the violation of certain provisions of the Charter and the Maputo Protocol

The Complainants implore the Commission to declare that the Democratic Republic of the Congo violated Articles 1, 5, 6, 7, 14 and 16 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights and Articles 3(1), 4(1), 8(a) and (e), 14(1), 16, and 19(c) of the Protocol to the African Charter on the Rights of Women in Africa.

As already developed, the Commission found the violations of the provisions of the Charter indicated above and of certain other provisions of the Maputo Protocol. It follows that the Commission is justified in making a declaration. b. On the recommendation that the Respondent State prosecute the perpetrators and enforce the decision of the High Military Court

The Complainants request the Commission to recommend that the DRC prosecute and punish the perpetrators of the violations within six months from the notification of the decision on the merits, and ensure the immediate enforcement of the judgment of the High Military Court once rendered. They also request that this enforcement be carried out without prejudice to subsequent recommendations issued by the African Commission.

The Commission wishes to recall that one of the obligations of States to ensure the implementation of human rights is the "obligation to protect". Under this obligation, States are required to ensure that the enjoyment by every person, without discrimination, of all human rights is protected against abuses by third parties. Such protection must be achieved not only by the introduction of laws and measures aimed at protecting human rights as emerges from Article 1 of the Charter, but also by the establishment of affordable and accessible remedial procedures in case of abuse of these rights.

As the Commission has already stressed in the Communication, Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights & INTERIGHTS v. Egypt, States must above all "put in place normative systems and institutions to maintain a justice system that offers remedies for violations and imposes sanctions on offenders". Thus, in this respect, States must ensure that the persons responsible for any violation are held accountable through administrative, administrative, disciplinary or judicial sanctions, as appropriate or as needed. In this sense, it follows that the Complainants' request is well founded.

The Commission shares the view of the Complainants who wish it to request the Respondent State to enforce the decision of the High Military Court once rendered, without prejudice to the recommendations issued by the African Commission. Indeed, the Commission the commission not being a criminal court to punish the perpetrators of offences, it is the responsibility of States to criminalize them and to ensure that all the sanctions imposed on them are enforced. Moreover, it is the Commission's practice to recommend that the calculation of damages resulting from human rights violations at the end of a communication be made by national courts. The recommendation to have a decision enforced would be in line with this practice.
