In its request for provisional measures addressed to the Respondent State, the Commission requested that the Respondent State take the necessary measures to ensure that no member of the immediate or extended family of the First victim and no witness who might be involved in the present case has his or her rights called into question as a result of the submission of the case to the Commission. The Commission particularly requested that the authorities of Burundi take measures to ensure that State agents involved in the case or their sympathisers do not directly or indirectly undertake reprisals against the family of the victim and the witnesses who might be involved.

In its response to the request for provisional measures, the Respondent State indicated that "the witnesses as well as the members of the family of the victim are protected like other citizens, otherwise they would already have lodged a complaint against those who attempted to threaten them". The State adds that so far, no incident related to this Communication has yet been recorded and that this results from the security measures taken by the various State authorities to preserve peace and security throughout the national territory. The Respondent State further affirmed that it is always ready to cooperate with the Commission in the event of possible threats against the authors of the communication, the witnesses or the family of the victim.

The Complainants reacted to the Respondent State's response by transmitting a note in which they consider that the note submitted by the State mentions no particular protective measure in favour of the family of the victim as compared to other citizens and that yet specific protective measures are necessary as set out in the initial request and noted by the Commission. However, the Complainants provide no further information on threats that would have occurred as a result of the complaint pending before the Commission.

When seized of the Communication, the Commission had noted that, in view of the information provided at that stage, it was not in a position to assess whether the An organ of theAfrican Union The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights31 Bijilo Annex Layout Kombo North DistrictWest Coast Region Gambia Phone: (220) 230 4361 Fax: (220) 441 95 02 Email: ao-banjul@afrika-union.org allegations of serious or massive human rights violations were sufficiently substantiated or not.
Moreover, as the Complainant has addressed specific requests to the Commission, it must respond to them, which makes the request for transfer subsidiary.

The Complainants maintain that the Communication must be declared admissible on the ground that it fulfils all the requirements of Article 56 of the African Charter. In their argumentation, the emphasis is placed on the requirement laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter, which could be disputed by the State.

The Complainants maintain that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies must not stand in the way of the admissibility of the present Communication. They invoke 3 arguments in support of their position; they indeed maintain that local remedies have been unduly prolonged, that they have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory and that it is dangerous to use them.

As regards the first argument relating to the undue prolongation of remedies, the Complainants in their brief on admissibility submit that the infringement of the right to life, particularly extrajudicial execution, constitutes a serious violation of human rights and that therefore the State must automatically conduct an investigation, even in the absence of a complaint. In this case, the headless body of the victim was found on 3 July 2012 and on the same day the administrative and judicial authorities went to the site to record the facts. A judicial file was opened. However, the complainants report that despite the horror of the situation, more than 21 months have elapsed without an impartial, prompt and diligent investigation being conducted. Moreover, in other cases, sometimes even more complex, particular speed marked the investigation and judgment. For the Complainants, the slowness observed in the case that is the subject of the present Communication is particularly worrying and symptomatic of the authorities' lack of will to acknowledge responsibility. Consequently, the inaction of the national authorities cannot prevent the seizure of the African Commission, all the more so as no remedy is available at the domestic level.

Concerning the second argument, namely that local remedies have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory. The Complainants submit that numerous NGOs with APRODH at the forefront mobilised on behalf of the family of the victim as soon as the facts occurred, in order to denounce his execution and obtain the opening of a prompt and effective investigation with a view to prosecuting the alleged perpetrators. According to the information transmitted by the authorities, a judicial file had been opened and an investigation was under way at the Prosecutor's Office in June 2013. However, the reference number of the file was not transmitted and the conclusions of this alleged investigation were not communicated, either to the family or to the mobilised NGOs. The Complainants also submit that they attempted to join the Rwembe trial as civil party and were refused by the authorities.

Moreover, it appears that no investigative act was conducted by the judicial authorities and no member of the family was ever heard on the case, or called in connection with the investigation of the file. The existence of an autopsy report is not established either.

For the Complainants, the fact that the Burundian authorities were fully aware of the occurrence of this crime and that it was their responsibility to take the necessary measures to shed light on the facts. However, in view of the passivity of the authorities, the Complainants therefore consider that local remedies were activated and proved ineffective and unsatisfactory.

On the third argument, according to which it is dangerous to use local remedies. The Complainants maintain that the various threats to which the victim was subjected before his death, and which had forced him to take refuge in hiding. Moreover, before his execution, Mr Jean-Claude NDimumahoro and his family were victims of harassment by State agents or SNR agents. In addition, it appears that State agents had been involved in his abduction and execution, which legitimately exacerbated the family's fears. Then, after the discovery of the victim's body, whose decapitated head was never found, surveillance of the family continued, to the point that the victim's wife had to move away for her protection and that of her children, because imbonerakure prowled permanently around the house and threatened anyone who wished to accompany the family in its mourning. In view of all these elements, it appears that the family's fears are well founded and that it is dangerous for them to seek justice at the local level.

The Respondent State maintains that the Communication must be declared inadmissible for failure to comply with the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

The Respondent State justifies its position by maintaining that the facts of which the Commission is seized still fall within the jurisdiction of the Burundian courts because a criminal file is open at the Gitega Public Prosecutor's Office under number RMP 41547 and the Gitega High Court heard the case under file number RPC 547 and that the NGO coalition submitting this Communication is aware of this state of affairs.

In its brief on admissibility, the Respondent State indicates that points 105 to 183 of the Complainants' submissions on admissibility must not be taken into account, for the simple reason that the file relating to this crime is following its course before a competent Burundian court. And consequently it requests that the Communication be declared inadmissible because local remedies have not been exhausted. It therefore requests the Commission to invite the authors to follow the procedure initiated before the body seized in accordance with the laws and regulations in force in Burundi.

The Complainants' additional observations are found both in their brief in response on admissibility and in their note relating to the implementation of the provisional measures. In these additional observations, the Complainants indicated that the Respondent State gives no indication as to the different stages of the investigation which it considers to be under way and also provides no evidence of the summonses issued or of the efforts undertaken to obtain the appearance of the witnesses and families of the victim in conditions of safety. The Complainants consider that the State in fact provides no new substantial element.
Article 56 of the African Charter prescribes seven (7) requirements that must be cumulatively fulfilled for a Communication to be declared admissible by the Commission.

In the present case, only one of the requirements, namely that provided for in Article 56(5) of the African Charter, is contested by the parties. After thorough examination of the file, the Commission is itself satisfied that the six (6) other requirements provided for in Articles 56(1), (2), (3), (4), (6) and (7) are fulfilled.

Indeed, the authors of the Communication have indicated their identity; the Communication concerns alleged violations of the African Charter that were allegedly committed in 2012, that is, well after the entry into force of the African Charter in Burundi. The Communication contains no disparaging or insulting terms towards the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union; the information communicated by the Complainants in the Communication derives among other things from reports of recognised bodies in Burundi and internationally. Moreover, it does not emerge from the file that the present case has already been settled in accordance with either the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity (currently the Constitutive Act of the African Union), or the provisions of the African Charter. As regards the requirement laid down in Article 56(6), in its Communication Tsatsu Tsikata v. Republic of Ghana, the Commission has already noted the link between Article 56(5) and Article 56(6); it therefore intends to give reasons for its position on this point after the analysis of Article 56(5).

Concerning Article 56(5) of the African Charter, which is contested by the parties, it provides that, to be admissible, Communications must "be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious to the Commission that the procedure of achieving these remedies would be unduly prolonged".

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has developed exceptions to the rule of exhaustion of local remedies. In its decision on Communication 147/95-149/96 Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission indeed indicated that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies cannot apply if the remedies in question are not available, effective or satisfactory. The Commission has also established that if the complainant cannot go before a court of his country because he fears for his life or for that of members of his family, the remedies are considered non-existent for him.

In this case, the Complainants submit that no information has been transmitted on the investigative acts conducted and the results of the investigation; assuming that it was conducted, neither to the family nor to the NGOs that followed up the case. They therefore consider that one (1) year and five (5) months after the occurrence of the facts (3 July 2012), these remain unpunished and that the procedure is unduly prolonged. The Respondent State indicated that a criminal file is open at the Gitega Public Prosecutor's Office under number RMP 41547 and that the Gitega High Court heard the case under file number RPC 547. Consequently, what now matters for the Commission is to analyse the procedure initiated by the Respondent State, in view of the arguments on admissibility put forward by the Complainant and in light of the responses and arguments provided by the Respondent State and of the latter's obligations.

The promptness of the procedure for establishing responsibility, beginning with the investigation, is undoubtedly a key factor. The Commission notes that one (1) year and five (5) months seems a long period for an investigation that is not yet closed. However, it is not so much the prolongation in itself that is in question, but it is the normal or abnormal nature of the prolongation of the local remedies initiated that must be examined. In this regard, the Commission has already stressed in its decision on Communication 293/04 - Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Zimbabwe, the need to take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the reasons put forward to justify the prolongation of the remedies in order to determine whether the prolongation is normal or abnormal. The Commission will therefore examine, in light of the applicable legal instruments, the facts and the circumstances of the case, whether the remedies in question have been prolonged in a normal or abnormal manner.

The Commission notes, on the one hand, that the Respondent State has not responded to the Complainants' allegation that in certain more complex cases, the competent authorities conducted the prosecution and judgment with speed.

From the Respondent State's arguments listed above, it appears that the non-conclusion or slowness (notably of the investigation which it says is under way) is linked to the failure of the members of the victim's family and the witnesses to appear and testify at the Prosecutor's Office. In its response concerning the implementation of the provisional measures, the State had affirmed that "the case had been heavily publicised but the witnesses do not come forward to give their statements". However, the Complainants have maintained since their initial submissions that no information on the investigative acts conducted, nor the results of the investigation, was communicated to the members of the family. Moreover, as the State has not clearly indicated having issued summonses, this may suggest that no summons was received either by the members of the family or by the other persons concerned and may imply a manifest will on the part of the State not to pursue the case.

Faced with this disagreement between the parties on the materiality of the summonses issued, the Commission must first rule on the question of the burden of proof. The burden of proof lies in principle on the one who accuses or makes the allegation, therefore on the Complainants. However, as the International Court of Justice (ICJ) stressed in the case Ahmadou Sadio Diallo (Republic of Guinea v. Republic of the Congo), it would be wrong to consider this principle, inspired by the adage onus probandi incumbit actori, as an absolute rule. The Commission agrees with the ICJ: ...it cannot as a general rule be demanded of an applicant that he prove the negative facts which he asserts. A public authority is generally able to demonstrate that it has followed the appropriate procedures and applied the guarantees required by law - if such was the case - by producing documentary evidence of the actions that have been carried out.

The Commission notes in this regard that the Respondent State has not placed on file material proof of the summonses issued. In the present case, the Complainants allege a negative fact (the absence of summons) the contrary proof of which should logically be in the possession of the Respondent State. Indeed, if summonses were in fact issued, it was for the Respondent State to provide the documents attesting to the existence of these summonses and their notification to the parties. The Respondent State, although aware of the Complainants' allegation concerning the absence of summons, has placed no proof on file.

In any event, the Commission notes the fact that the Public Prosecutor's Office, by virtue of the prerogatives linked to the exercise of public prosecution, must in principle have the necessary means to compel the appearance of any person whose hearing is necessary in the context of the examination of a file. According to the United Nations Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extra-Legal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions, the investigative authority must have the power to oblige persons allegedly involved in cases of executions to appear and testify, including witnesses. In the same vein, the Commission notes that Law No. 1/10 of 03 April 2013 revising the Code of Criminal Procedure in Burundi provides in its Articles 79, 82, 83, 335 and 336 a list of diligent actions (warrant to bring, referral before the competent judge, summons to appear) that the Public Prosecutor's Office may implement to bring summoned persons to appear. The Respondent State has not, however, indicated what diligent actions were implemented in accordance with its obligations to hear the witnesses for the prosecution and for the defence in this case. The publicising of a case, as the State indicates, cannot replace these legal means.

In view of the nature of the alleged violations, which requires a prompt investigation in order to establish responsibility, and in the absence of sufficient justification by the Respondent State to explain the slowness of the investigation into the death of the victim since July 2012 and the lack of communications concerning the actions undertaken and the results of the investigation, at least the initial results, it is demonstrated that the State has not taken all the measures to deal with this case with all the required speed, which in this case constitutes an undue prolongation of the remedies.

The Complainants argue the State's lack of will to establish responsibility for the crime in the present case and the existing dysfunction within the judicial apparatus. The Respondent State did not respond specifically to these allegations. The Commission has, in its jurisprudence, indicated that a remedy that has no chance of success does not constitute an effective remedy and that a remedy is satisfactory when it is capable of giving satisfaction to the Complainant. The Commission finds the prolonged nature of the remedies in the present case; it also notes the attempts by the Respondent State to discourage all persons who had tried to move the investigation forward. Although having stressed that it had opened an investigation into the case of the victim, the State has provided no elements to contradict the Complainants' statements as to its lack of will to do justice.

As to the dysfunction on which the Complainants rely, the Commission notes that it emerges even from the Complainants' allegations that Burundian justice has functioned fully in other cases and that the Complainants do not describe sufficiently how the supposed dysfunction is an obstacle in the present case.

In sum, the Commission concludes that the allegation that the State lacks the will to establish responsibility may be admissible in view of the arguments provided by the Complainants and the absence of contrary proof on the part of the respondent. As regards the dysfunction of the entire judicial apparatus of Burundi, the Commission finds that it cannot be established in view of the elements provided by the Complainants.

The Complainants argue that no investigative act was in reality conducted by the judicial authorities since no information was communicated on this and that the family of the victim was never contacted or heard in the context of the investigation. The Commission considers that the Respondent State was well aware of the Complainants' allegations and that, if it alleges the contrary, it should have provided proof that summonses were actually sent. In the absence of evidence showing the minimum actions undertaken, notably the effectiveness of the summonses, the Commission considers that there is thereby an ineffectiveness of local remedies, notably of the investigative or inquiry acts conducted.

The complainants submit that it is dangerous for the family to seek justice from Burundian justice, particularly following the thinly veiled threats received from members of the ruling party who sometimes addressed the victim's grandfather directly; asking him to warn his grandson of the risks incurred if he continued to be active in the FNL party. Moreover, after the death of the victim, imbonakure prevented all persons wishing to accompany the family in mourning from approaching the victim's house; this pressure and insecurity led the widow to change her residence for fear for her life and that of her children. Finally, even before his death the victim had been forced to live in hiding because of increasingly pressing death threats against him.

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has already stressed the fact that when remedies prove dangerous for the Complainant, it would not be reasonable to ask him to exhaust them. In case 147/95-149/96 Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission indicated that: "The existence of a local remedy must be sufficiently certain, not only in theory but also in practice, failing which it will be neither available nor effective. Consequently, if the complainant cannot turn to the courts of his country because he fears for his life or for that of members of his family, local remedies are considered non-existent for him".

Furthermore, the Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extra-Legal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions provide that: complainants, witnesses, those conducting the investigation and their families shall be protected from violence, threats of violence or any other form of intimidation. Those potentially implicated in extra-legal, arbitrary or summary executions shall be removed from any position of control or power, whether direct or indirect, over complainants, witnesses and their families, as well as those conducting investigations.

Moreover, in its decision on Communication Kazeem Aminu v. Nigeria, where the victim was obliged to live in hiding to escape persecution by the security services, the Commission decided to exempt him from the exhaustion of local remedies.

From all the foregoing, it emerges that the question that arises is whether the risks mentioned are legitimate or well founded. To that end, it is appropriate to take into account in the analysis the nature of the alleged violations, the profile of the alleged perpetrators and the context surrounding the case in order to assess whether or not the risks incurred by the Complainants if they brought legal action are well founded.

On the nature of the alleged violations, the Commission notes their serious character. The need has already been stressed, in the case of allegations of serious crimes such as torture and homicide, to ensure protection capable of providing victims or their relatives with the necessary guarantees to bring legal action. In the present case, the facts reported by the Complainants concerning the case of the victim allege serious violations, notably infringement of the right to life.

Next, during his lifetime the victim was the subject of threats from representatives of the Burundian national police and the intelligence services and also from the imbonerakure who are alleged to have committed serious abuses. Subsequently, the family of the victim was subjected to harassment by State agents, namely SNR agents and the police. It is therefore evident that Burundian State institutions are implicated.

As to the context, the facts reported show that the growing pressure and the increasingly marked threats against the victim before his execution legitimately created an environment of terror in his family that contributed to sustaining a feeling of fear. As a reminder, the body of Mr Jean-Claude Ndimumahoro was found decapitated and the head was never found. Moreover, according to a testimony he was allegedly tortured before his execution. From these facts it appears that the use of local remedies may prove dangerous for the family of the victim.

The Complainants also report that there is no legal and judicial framework for the protection of victims and witnesses in Burundi, this information being supported by the concluding observations of the Committee against Torture in 2007 following the examination of Burundi's report. The Respondent State in its brief on admissibility makes no mention of the existence of a legal and institutional framework for the protection of victims and witnesses in Burundi nor of the effectiveness of such a framework if it existed. In its note on the provisional measures, the State vaguely indicated that the families of victims are protected like other citizens without further arguments on this point. This statement supports the allegation of absence of particular protection in the case of certain serious crimes and this is such as to terrify victims and witnesses of atrocious crimes.

Finally, as regards Article 56(6) of the African Charter which prescribes that the Communication must "be submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted" or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter", it should be stressed again that in this case, the parties agree that local remedies have not been exhausted. Having already established that the remedies are being unduly prolonged and not being able to identify in the Respondent State's code of criminal procedure the time limit for the investigation of such a file, all the more so as the State does not give the list of investigative acts performed and does not clearly indicate at what stage of the investigations the file is, it is for the Commission to count the time limit for its seizure from the moment when the Complainants should reasonably have become aware of the undue prolongation of local remedies.

The Complainants indicate that despite the existence of a judicial file opened on behalf of the victim, at the time of submission of the Communication they were not aware of the file number and that according to the authorities, the investigation was still under way. However, they have had access to none of the investigative acts and no member of the family was ever heard on the case or called in connection with the investigation of the file. Moreover, the existence or not of an autopsy report has not been established either.

In its submissions on admissibility the Respondent State has provided no elements contradicting or justifying this, merely indicating that a judicial file in the name of the victim with number RMP No. 41547 existed at the Gitega Public Prosecutor's Office.

Unlike the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and the American Convention on Human Rights which set a specific time limit for the submission of communications: six months, the African Charter provides only that communications must be submitted "within a reasonable period" which is not defined. The Commission therefore deals with each case on its merits to determine a reasonable period.

Although in the case Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Republic of Sudan the Commission declared that the expiry of two years and five months or twenty-nine months without any reason or justification was considered unreasonable. The Commission had also noted that "when a complainant has a valid and compelling reason for not submitting his complaint to the Commission, the latter has a responsibility, in the interest of fairness and justice, to give the Complainant an opportunity to be heard."

In the present case, the Respondent State itself acknowledges that the case is still pending before the courts; the Complainants seized the Commission on 09 June 2014 for, among other reasons, the undue prolongation of the procedure, notably an investigation that has lasted for more than a year without any results. The Commission therefore considers that the time within which it was seized is reasonable.
The Commission therefore declared the communication admissible.

The complainant alleges that Mr Jean Claude Ndimumahoro (the victim) suffered an attempted assassination, preceded by a violation of his rights to liberty, dignity, physical integrity, as well as to freedom of opinion, expression and association, precisely because of his membership of an opposition political party, in this case the FNL.

He alleges more than 130 extrajudicial executions, the vast majority of them targeting Hutu FNL activists or former combatants. As proof, he cites the report of the United Nations Secretary-General submitted to the United Nations Security Council and documents of Human Right Watch (HRW) and Crises Group. He also cites a 2012 HRW report, which indicates that "demobilised FNL combatants are also being forced to join the SNR and the Imbonerakure, on pain of being killed, in order to recruit into the SNR men who can easily identify former and current FNL members. Many of these members went into hiding after the threats".
To support his position, the complainant cites the Commission's jurisprudence in the various communications.

The complainant, citing the Commission's jurisprudence, argues that the right to life implies not only its protection by the State, notably by taking measures to prevent extrajudicial executions, but also the obligation to have investigations opened by independent authorities with sufficient resources.

He affirms that it follows from the Commission's jurisprudence that an execution is considered extrajudicial if it is carried out by a State agent or with his consent, followed by an arbitrary procedure (inappropriate, unfair, unpredictable or unlawful) or an absence of procedure.

He affirms that in the case of the victim, he was decapitated and his head was not found, but that the rest of his body was abandoned on 3 July 2012 in Bugarama (Muranvya). He affirms that all this happened when the victim went to a meeting with his long-time friend, also a former FNL member who had become a police officer and one of the bodyguards of the Deputy Police Commissioner of Gitega. He affirms that when they arrived at the place, he was forcibly taken by four (4) police officers into a Toyota Hilux vehicle with tinted windows, a vehicle identified as belonging to the Administrator of Gitega.

According to the witnesses indicated by the applicant, the victim was detained in the SNR cells before being decapitated. The complainant reinforces this version with the testimony of Zacharie Ngenzedbuhoro who, in the context of the case of Mr An Organ of the The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights31 Bijilo Annex Law Court, Kono, North District,West Coast Region, GambiaPhone: (220) 230 4360 Fax: (220) 441 06 04Email: au-humanrights@au.int Nurweze, Deputy Provincial Commissioner of the internal security police of Gitega, confirmed that the victim was in the hands of the authorities of the Respondent State before he was found dead, because they were detained together between 23 and 28 June 2012.

The complainant further indicates evidence of the involvement of the authorities in the death of the victim, the pressure and threats he suffered before his death, referring to the depositions of witnesses. On this basis, the complainant considers that the killing of the victim by State agents, followed by the absence of a proper procedure on the part of the competent authorities, confirm that the victim was arbitrarily executed, which constitutes, according to the Commission's jurisprudence cited above, a violation of Article 4 of the Charter.

The complainant maintains that the detention of the victim by the authorities of the Respondent State and his incommunicado detention, before being decapitated and his body left in the street for several days before being found, constitute a violation of his right to dignity and to legal personality. To that end, he cites the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee. For the complainant, the human essence of the victim was denied.

The complainant alleges that during the trial of Mr Nurweze, the Deputy Provincial Commissioner of the internal security police of Gitega, Mr Zacharie Ngenzedbuhoro, stated that he and the victim had been tortured, that is, that they had been undressed and beaten; they had slept naked on the cold cemented floor; food was served to them on the floor for them to eat; they had no contact with their family or any idea of the fate that awaited them, which, for the complainant and according to the jurisprudence of the Commission and of the Committee against Torture, constitutes a violation of Article 5 of the Charter in respect of the victim and his relatives because of the suffering and anguish that this situation caused them.

The applicant alleges the violation of the positive obligations of the Respondent State under Article 5 of the Charter for having failed to take measures to avoid what happened to the victim, namely "to create a transparent, independent and effective judicial system", to conduct effective investigations and to punish those responsible. In the case of the victim, the complainant alleges that although an investigation was opened, it was not effective since no autopsy was performed, the family of the victim was never heard and no measure of reparation was granted.

The complainant maintains that the detention of the victim before his decapitation and the abandonment of his body in the street constitutes a violation of his right to liberty An Organe de The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights31 Bijilo Annex Layout, Kombo North District,West Coast Region Gambia Phone: (220) 230 4361 Fax: (220) 441 05 04 Email: au-bijilo@africa-union.org and security, in the form of arbitrary detention, in violation of Article 6 of the Charter. He affirms that the Commission has declared that this is a right whose violation endangers the exercise of other rights, such as the right to family, the right to privacy, the right to freedom of assembly, association and expression and the right to freedom of movement.

The complainant mentions situations which the Commission and other bodies have already indicated constituted violations of the right to liberty and security, namely detentions not authorised by security and law enforcement forces, that is, arbitrary arrests, detentionsincomunicado, detentions without charge and without presentation to the judicial authorities.

The applicant alleges that, although the State Party opened a judicial investigation to identify and hold the perpetrators responsible, as well as to compensate for the damage caused to the victim, despite the appeal of the international community, this investigation has not produced the expected results. The complainant cited the Commission's jurisprudence which confirms the right of every person to have access to justice, exercised by competent bodies in accordance with the law, and that this provision will therefore be violated whenever the authorities impede it. Thus, the complainant alleges that the right of the victim and his family to access justice was violated.
On the other hand, the complainant alleges that the failure of Burundian justice, demonstrated by the exhaustion of local remedies, constitutes a violation of the victim's right of access to justice.

The complainant affirms that the victim was persecuted and killed because of his political activity as a member of the FNL, which constitutes a violation of his right to freedom of opinion and expression, a human right which the Commission has held to be fundamental for the personal development and political consciousness of the individual, and vital for his participation in the political affairs of his country.

The complainant cites cases where the Commission considered that the right to freedom of opinion and expression had been violated, namely that there is no clause derogating from the right to freedom of opinion and expression even where there is a serious and imminent danger to the security of the State; that the reference to laws and regulations is aimed at the provisions of international law and that where the restriction of rights is possible, it must be minimal and not compromise the guaranteed rights; that the detention of opponents constitutes a complete restriction of freedom of expression, as does the persecution of persons for their membership of a political party.

The Complainant cites the Commission's jurisprudence in cases where it considers that freedom of association is articulated around the idea of the prohibition of State interference in the free constitution of associations, and held that the prohibition of gatherings of persons for political purposes, the formation of political parties, as well as the detention or persecution of individuals because of their membership of an opposition movement, constituted a violation of freedom of association. In this case, the complainant considers that the detention and subsequent decapitation of the victim were due to his membership of the FNL, which, in his view, constitutes a violation of his right of association under Article 10(1) of the Charter.

The complainant, citing the Commission, alleges that the right of every person to take part in the conduct of public affairs of his country includes the right to vote and to be elected in transparent and periodic elections, which is also a right inherent in citizenship and participation in political activities. Consequently, the complainant considers that the detention and subsequent decapitation of the victim because of his membership of a political party prevented him from taking part in the conduct of the political affairs of his country through his party, in violation of Article 13(1) of the Charter.

The complainant, citing the Commission's jurisprudence, affirms that arbitrary detention and incommunicado confinement constitute a violation of the right to family since the person is separated from his family. He also cites the decision of the United Nations Human Rights Committee which considers that the death of his wife following ill-treatment inflicted by State agents constitutes a violation of the right to family, provided for in Article 23 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Consequently, the complainant considers that in the present case, the detention and subsequent decapitation of the victim led to his separation from his family and therefore to a violation of his right to family provided for in Article 18(1) of the Charter.

The complainant, citing the Commission's jurisprudence, maintains that the Respondent State violated Article 1 of the Charter by not taking all the An Organ of the The African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights31 Bijilo Annex Layout Kombo North DistrictWest Coast Region GambiaPhone: (220) 230 4361 Fax: (220) 447 05 04Email: au-banjul@afrika-union.orghttps://achpr.org.int/ appropriate measures to prevent the violations committed against the victim, including his death, as well as by not opening an effective investigation aimed at identifying and holding accountable the perpetrators of the detention and decapitation of the victim.

The complainant requests the Commission to find the alleged violations and to order the State concerned to: i) open a thorough and effective investigation into the detention and decapitation of the victim and into the other violations committed against him, by independent and impartial judicial bodies, in order to identify and hold the perpetrators criminally responsible; ii) grant appropriate reparations to the beneficiaries of the victim, including payment of monetary compensation for the material and moral damage suffered, as well as measures of restitution, psychological, social and economic rehabilitation, satisfaction (apologies and firm condemnation of the violations committed and publication of the Commission's decision) and non-repetition, with a view to ensuring political pluralism in the latter case; iii) urgently adopt legislation aimed at protecting victims and witnesses, notably in the context of judicial proceedings, in order to guarantee unhindered access to the courts.

The Commission notes that the complainant alleges that Mr Jean Claude Ndimumahoro (victim) was killed by law enforcement forces and that his head was cut off and separated from the rest of his body and abandoned in the street where he was found, after having been tortured and having been subjected to a number of inhuman treatments, not to mention the persecutions and death threats he had suffered previously.

The Commission notes that the applicant's observations and the respective allegations of violation of the victim's rights indicate that the central question of the case is whether the decapitation was preceded by torture or inhuman treatment and various threats, as well as by the absence of an official and thorough investigation. Consequently, the Commission will examine the alleged violations in the following order: Articles 4, 5, 6, 7 and 26, 9, 18(1) and 1 of the Charter.

The Commission further notes that while the question of the absence of an official and thorough investigation is raised by the complainant in relation to the violation of Article 5 of the Charter, it will be examined separately because the obligation to open an effective investigation is linked to the whole case.

Article 4 of the Charter provides that "Human beings are inviolable. Every human being shall be entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of this right".

The Commission notes that the complainant affirms that the victim was killed and that his head was cut off and hidden in an unknown place by law enforcement agents of the Respondent State, which, according to the complainant, amounts to an extrajudicial execution since the competent authorities did not open an official investigation.

The Commission notes that the Charter does not define arbitrary execution and does not mention the concept of extrajudicial execution either. Nevertheless, in its General Comment No. 3, the Commission considers that the deprivation of life is arbitrary if it is not authorised by international law or by the most favourable domestic provisions. This includes compliance with the criteria of appropriateness, justice, predictability, reasonableness, necessity and proportionality, or again if the deprivation of life does not respect the procedural or substantive guarantees provided for by the Charter.

The Commission notes that before Comment No. 3, it had already commented on the question in Article 19 v. The State of Eritrea, where it used the definition of the Human Rights Committee according to which The term "arbitrary" must not be equated solely with something "against the law", but must be interpreted more broadly to include elements of inappropriateness, injustice, lack of predictability and due process of law... pre-trial detention in the sense that detention must be not only lawful but also reasonable in all the circumstances... as well as pre-trial detention must also be necessary in all the circumstances.

The Commission notes that in the case Forum of Conscience v. Sierra Leone, the Commission specifically stated that "any violation of this right without due process amounts to an arbitrary deprivation of life". For its part, the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (African Court), drawing on the jurisprudence of the Commission, the United Nations Human Rights Committee and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, held that whether or not the deprivation of life is arbitrary must be assessed on the basis of three criteria: whether the deprivation is provided for by law; whether it is applied by a competent court; and whether it followed due process. It follows that if these three criteria are not met, the deprivation of life would be arbitrary

As regards extrajudicial executions, it should be recalled that in the case Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum v. Zimbabwe, the Commission, drawing on the United Nations Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extra-Legal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions, as well as on its manual, considered that extrajudicial executions are those carried out by State agents or by third parties in violation of the right to life.

For the reasons mentioned above, the Commission notes that arbitrary deprivation of life occurs in the context of an unfair judicial procedure and that extrajudicial execution takes place outside the framework of a judicial procedure. In both cases, there is an unlawful deprivation of life under Article 4 of the Charter and, consequently, an obligation to take appropriate measures to remedy the said violation.

In the present case, the question is whether there was a deprivation of the right to life in the form of an extrajudicial execution and whether measures were taken to ensure that the perpetrators answer for their acts and that the relatives of the victim obtain reparation. To that end, the Commission will examine (i) whether the deprivation of the right to life was committed by State agents or whether it was tolerated or consented to by State agents.

The Commission stresses that there is no doubt about the death of the victim, as this fact was not contested by the Respondent State when it submitted its observations on the admissibility of the communication. On the contrary, it acknowledged that the investigations into the circumstances of the victim's death were still ongoing and that, consequently, the submission of the case to the Commission was premature. On this basis, it remains to be determined whether the victim was killed by the agents of the Respondent State as the complainant claims.

The Commission notes that the applicant presents as evidence the testimony of the victim's grandmother (annex 2) which confirms that on the day of his disappearance, he was going to the station in the company of his friend, whom the applicant claims to be one of the guards of the Deputy Police Commissioner of Gitega. This version of the facts is confirmed by the victim's wife (annex 3).

The Commission notes that the testimony of the president of the Burundian Association for the Protection of Human Rights and Detained Persons (APRODH) (annex 4) is particularly important. It indicates that in addition to having recovered the decapitated body and handed it over to the morgue of Muramvya hospital, the association asked in vain the administrator of the zone where the body was found to assume his responsibilities. On the other hand, APRODH conducted investigations which made it possible to obtain information from anonymous witnesses confirming that the victim was arrested at the Kamenge station, Bujumbura, by Commissioner Michel Rwembe (Rwembe), aboard a Hilux vehicle of the Administrator of Gitega, Mr Valentim Nahimana. APRODH specifies that one of the persons in the SNR cells, Mr Zacarie NGENZEBUHORO, confirmed having shared his cell with the victim and that he had also been arrested by the same Rwembe. Another person held in the SNR cells, also arrested by Rwembe, Mrs Constance Kabiri, confirmed having shared her cell with the victim (Annex 5).

The Commission also notes the testimony of one of the chiefs of Songa hill, who states that he held office from 2000 to 2005 and was re-elected in 2010, in which he declares having informed Rwembe that a dangerous thief was in the area. Accompanied by Rwembe and his agents, they went to capture the thief who was in the house of another man (identified in the file). When they arrived at his house, they were unable to capture the thief and Rwembe ordered his agents to kill the owner of the house in which the thief was supposed to be, which they did. The chief of Songa hill stated that he opposed the execution of the gentleman who was sheltering the thief, and Rwembe ordered his agents to kill him, which did not happen because he managed to escape. However, he received threats from Rwembe until he reported the matter to APRODH, and the threats then ceased.

The Commission notes that with the testimonies mentioned above and the general description of the circumstances of the victim's detention and subsequent decapitation, in particular the testimonies of the persons who shared the SNR cells with the victim, the burden of proof is transferred to the Respondent State, which would have the responsibility to rebut the complainant's allegations. In the case Amnesty International v. Sudan, the Commission, invoking its long practice, stated that in cases of human rights violations, the burden of proof lies with the government (see ACHPR/59/91, ACHPR/60/91, ACHPR/64/91, ACHPR/87/93 and ACHPR/101/93). If the government does not provide evidence to contradict an allegation of human rights violation made against it, the Commission will consider it proven, or at least likely or plausible.

The Commission notes that in its observations on admissibility, the Respondent State does not deny any of the facts presented in the complaint, but essentially limits itself to saying that the investigation is ongoing and that the Commission should therefore declare the complaint inadmissible.

The Commission notes that the applicant's observations are sufficiently clear on the circumstances of the victim's detention, involving the authorities of the Respondent State in the person of Commissioner Rwembe and his agents. In light of the evidence submitted, and in the absence of contrary elements on the part of the Respondent State, the Commission is convinced that the victim was arrested and placed in detention by the authorities of the Respondent State. As he was not released before his body appeared decapitated, the Commission concludes that the decapitation is attributable to the Respondent State. From the foregoing, the Commission concludes that there was an arbitrary and extrajudicial execution of the victim by decapitation, one of the most serious forms of violation of the right to life provided for in Article 4 of the Charter.

Article 5 of the Charter states that: Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited.

The Commission notes that this provision of the Charter aims to protect the dignity of the human person. Indeed, the dignity of the human person will be fully respected only if individuals are able to fully enjoy and exercise all the rights inherent in the human person as set out in the Charter and in other applicable human rights instruments. Consequently, when a person is limited in the enjoyment or exercise of his rights, this ultimately affects, in one way or another, his dignity. Thus, the prohibitions provided for in Article 5 of the Charter aim to preserve the hard core of dignity.

The Commission notes that the question that arises here is whether the core of Article 5 of the Charter has been violated, as the complainant claims. In the case El-Sharkawi v. Egypt, the Commission held that in order to determine whether the alleged abuses, conditions of detention and incommunicado detention of the victim were committed in violation of Article 5, the Commission must first determine whether the alleged acts constitute acts of torture and other ill-treatment and, if so, whether there is sufficient evidence to support these allegations.

In the case El-Sharkawi v. Egypt, the Commission invoked its jurisprudence and the Robben Island Guidelines for the Prohibition and Prevention of Torture in Africa, to adopt the definition of torture contained in Article 1 of the United Nations Convention against Torture, according to which "torture" means any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for such purposes as obtaining from him or a third person information or a confession, punishing him for an act he or a third person has committed or is suspected of having committed, or intimidating or coercing him or a third person, or for any reason based on discrimination of any kind, when such pain or suffering is inflicted by or at the instigation of or with the consent or acquiescence of a public official or other person acting in an official capacity.

In the same decision, the Commission considered that this definition of torture contains four (4) cumulative elements, namely: i) the mental or physical suffering must be severe; ii) the act or omission must be intentionally inflicted; iii) the commission of this act or omission must have a specific purpose; iv) and the act or omission must be inflicted by a public official or with his express or tacit consent.

In the present case, the conditions of detention, the lack of communication with the family, the physical violence, the throwing of food on the ground for the victim to eat, and the fact that the victim was decapitated, indicate the severity of the suffering inflicted; there is also no doubt that these acts were carried out intentionally, by State agents, for a specific purpose, namely to pressure the victim to denounce other FNL members, change party or abandon his activities within the party. If these four elements are present, we must conclude that the victim was tortured.
For the reasons mentioned above, the Commission finds a violation of Article 5 of the Charter.

Article 6 of the Charter states that: Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained.

The Commission notes that this provision of the Charter clearly prohibits detentions that were not carried out in accordance with the law. The Commission's Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa set out the obligations of States with regard to the right to liberty and security, including the prohibition of arbitrary detention, the obligation to detain only when the conditions strictly prescribed by law are met, on the order of the competent authorities and in accordance with their decision and for the purposes determined by law, and the obligation to open effective investigations in order to identify the perpetrators, hold them accountable and provide reparation to the victims.

The above-mentioned Article protects two (2) fundamental rights, namely freedom of action and movement and personal security. The first right has several aspects that can be summarised in two: the aspect that includes the right not to be detained or imprisoned by public authorities, except for reasons and under conditions prescribed by law; and the aspect that includes the right not to have one's liberty restricted or to be confined in a certain space, without reasons and under conditions prescribed by law.

As regards personal security, it implies that citizens and all those who have chosen Africa to live in must be able to do so in safety and peacefully, free from threats and attacks emanating from public authorities or private individuals.

Any restriction on these two (2) rights must comply with what is previously established in a given legal norm. These rights are mentioned in the Charter in a simplistic manner and without mentioning the guarantees enjoyed by prisoners (detainees and convicts), which explains why certain underdeveloped penal systems or those less concerned with these aspects contained in most Constitutions of African countries do not sufficiently protect individuals whose liberty is limited, in particular detentions considered arbitrary (unlawful/irregular and indefinite). This is what happened in this case.

The Commission recalls that in the case Constitutional Rights Project/Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, it had observed that "where individuals are detained without charge, [...] this constitutes an arbitrary deprivation of their liberty and thus a violation of Article 6".

In the present case, the detention of the victim that preceded his decapitation also took place outside the legal framework, since there is no trace of a competent authority having ordered his detention. It is for this reason that the Commission considered his execution as extrajudicial. It must therefore be concluded that the victim's rights to liberty and security, as provided for in Article 6 of the Charter, were violated even before his decapitation.

Article 7 of the Charter provides that: 1. Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts of violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force; (b) The right to be presumed innocent until proved guilty by a competent court or tribunal; (c) The right to defence, including the right to be defended by counsel of his choice; (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal. 2. No one may be condemned for an act or omission which did not constitute a legally punishable offence at the time it was committed. No penalty may be inflicted for an offence for which no provision was made at the time it was committed. Punishment is personal and can be imposed only on the offender.

For its part, Article 26 of the Charter provides that: States parties to the present Charter shall have the duty to guarantee the independence of the Courts and shall allow the establishment and improvement of appropriate national institutions entrusted with the promotion and protection of the rights and freedoms guaranteed by the present Charter.

The Commission notes that Article 7 concerns the procedural component of the right to a fair trial and that Article 26 concerns its institutional aspect, that is, the existence of courts whose independence must be guaranteed by States parties.

The Commission considers that in the context of the present case, the question of access to justice must be analysed in correlation with the Respondent State's obligation to open an effective investigation after learning of the decapitation of the victim. However, the Commission had already concluded that the Respondent State had not complied with its obligation to open an effective investigation after learning of the decapitation of the victim, notably by not allowing the effective participation of the victim's relatives in the proceedings as civil party. Indeed, it is unnecessary for the Commission to revisit this question under Article 7 since it has already been examined under Articles 4 and 5 of the Charter and the conclusions of that examination are also applicable in this case. The Commission considers, however, that a particular aspect concerning access to justice arises at the time when the victim was detained without anyone knowing where he was. Between 23 June 2012, the date of his arrest, and 3 July 2012, the date on which his body appeared decapitated, the victim was objectively prevented by the authorities holding him incommunicado from accessing justice to assert his rights, namely to challenge his arbitrary detention, which could have saved his life.

Under the Commission's Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, the victim has the right to be informed, at the time of his arrest, of the reasons for his detention, of his right to have recourse to a lawyer and to be examined by a doctor, as well as of his right to communicate with his family or friends.

The Commission is particularly strict as regards access to justice. For example, in the cases El-Sharkawi v. Egypt and Constitutional Rights Project and Civil Liberties Organisation v. Nigeria, the Commission held that the mere detention of persons without trial or charge constitutes a violation of the right of access to justice. In the present case, the situation is more serious because the victim was detained without his relatives knowing where he was, and outside of criminal proceedings, so that the possibility of accessing justice to protect himself against arbitrary detention was nil, and the relatives could do nothing on behalf of the victim.

As regards the alleged violation of Article 26 of the Charter, the Commission considers that the complainant has not presented evidence demonstrating the lack of independence of the judiciary in his particular case. On the other hand, for the victim, the question of the independence of the judiciary did not arise since he was unable to seize the courts to challenge his detention. Consequently, the Commission finds a violation of Article 7(1)(a), insofar as the victim was detained without knowing where he was and, on the other hand, a non-violation of Article 26, because the question of the independence of the courts does not arise, the victim never having brought the case before the courts.
Article 9(2) of the Charter provides that Every individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the law.
Article 10(1) of the Charter states that "Every individual shall have the right to free association provided that he abides by the law."

Article 13(1) of the Charter states that "Every citizen shall have the right to participate freely in the government of his country, either directly or through freely chosen representatives in accordance with the provisions of the law."

The Commission notes that the three (3) Articles of the Charter are linked. The first concerns the right of every person to have opinions and to disseminate them. The second concerns freedom of association and the third participation in the public affairs of the country. In other words, in a democratic society governed by law, freedom of expression is guaranteed and can be exercised individually or within an association, notably of a political nature. By contrast, participation in the political affairs of the country is essentially through membership of a political party.

The Commission notes that, as indicated in the Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information (Declaration of Principles), freedom of expression is fundamental in a democratic society, in particular for the purposes of the direct and indirect participation of citizens in the public affairs of their country through political associations.

In this case, the victim was arrested and decapitated because of his membership of a political party, in this case the FNL, and his opposition to the government. By joining the FNL, the victim was exercising his right to be part of a political association opposed to the government and to exercise his political freedoms through that party, while taking part in the conduct of the public affairs of his country through that party.

The Commission recognises that these three (3) rights are not absolute. However, as regards an arrest followed by a decapitation in the conditions already seen in the examination of the allegations of violation of Articles 4, 5 and 6 of the Charter, the Commission is of the view that there is no question of examining a possible justification of restrictions on Articles 9(2), 10(1) and 13(1) of the Charter.

The Commission finds that not only did the Respondent State not take the measures it should have taken to ensure the victim an optimal exercise of his rights, but it allowed its agents to detain and decapitate him for having exercised his rights. Consequently, the Commission finds that the violation of Articles 9(2), 20(1) and 13(1) of the Charter is flagrant and no longer needs to be demonstrated.
Article 18(1) of the Charter provides that The family shall be the natural unit and basis of society. It shall be protected by the State which shall take care of its physical health and moral.

The Commission finds that the idea of forming a family is inseparable from cohabitation, from being together, from sharing the same family home, except in the case of compelling reasons or if the couple itself decides otherwise. In the event of separation for compelling reasons, contact with the family must be maintained. It is no coincidence that the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa provide for the right of detainees to maintain contact with their family. This provision also aims to enable the detainee to remain in contact with his family.

The Commission's interpretation of this provision reaffirms that it imposes on the State a positive obligation with regard to the family. The State has the obligation to help the family satisfy its needs and interests and to protect it against abuses of all kinds perpetrated by its own leaders and organs and by third parties.

The State also has the negative obligation to refrain from violating the rights and interests of the family. Thus, in its action and in order to comply with the provisions of Article 18(1) and (2), the State must take measures taking into account the interests of the family, the right to family life and the safeguarding of its unity.

In this case, the situation is even more serious since the victim's relatives, during his detention, had no idea where he was and how they could obtain news of him in order to exercise their right to visit him. The worst occurred when his body was found decapitated and abandoned in the street. The Respondent State, which should have taken measures to protect the family as it has the duty to do under Article 18(1) of the Charter, allowed its agents to carry out acts that infringed this right in its most serious form, namely the extrajudicial execution of one of its members.
