De surcroît, l'Etat défendeur soutient que le plaignant aurait dû attendre de faire appel ou se pourvoir en cassation avant de saisir la Commission sans indiquer à quel moment le plaignant obtiendrait même une décision qui pourrait servir de base pour un éventuel appel ou pourvoi en cassation.

Il est difficile pour un plaignant dans ces circonstances de savoir quand est-ce qu'il faut se décider à saisir une instance régionale telle que la Commission. La Commission est consciente qu'un retard anormal dans l'administration de la justice équivaut à un déni de justice ; en l'espèce, les assertions de l'Etat défendeur ne donnent pas de garanti quant aux chances que l'affaire sera traitée de manière prompte, au contraire, cela laisse croire que le traitement de l'affaire pourrait durer indéfiniment.

Au regard de ce qui précède, il ne serait pas judicieux de renvoyer le plaignant devant les tribunaux nationaux surtout qu'il y a un risque que le plaignant attende encore plusieurs années sans suite de la procédure interne engagée. Dans l'intérêt de la justice, la Commission ne saurait dans un tel cas considérer que le délai de saisine est déraisonnable.
Au vu de ce qui précède, la Commission africaine déclare la présente Communication recevable.

Le Plaignant allègue la violation de l'article 7 (1) (d) qui dispose que « toute personne a droit à ce que sa cause soit entendue plus particulièrement en son aspect relatif au droit d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable par une juridiction impartiale ». Il affirme que les circonstances de la présente cause font apparaître d'une part, une absence de délai raisonnable puisque, selon lui, certaines affaires le concernant ne sont pas toujours tranchées et, d'autre part, les juridictions saisies ne sont pas impartiales.

Pour ce qui concerne la violation du droit d'être jugée dans un délai raisonnable, le Plaignant soutient son allégation en se basant sur une résolution de la Commission sur le droit au recours et à un procès équitable, et une jurisprudence de la Commission développée dans la communication Article 19 c. Erythrée pour indiquer que les circonstances du Plaignant ou de la victime doivent être prises en compte et que la complexité des faits ne peut justifier le non-respect du délai raisonnable.

Quant au soutien à son allégation sur la violation du droit d'être jugé par une juridiction impartiale, le Plaignant évoque les Directives et principes sur le droit à un procès équitable de la commission qui précisent le sens du droit d'être jugé par une juridiction impartiale. Sur base de ces directives et principes, le Plaignant relève le critère pour de la détermination de la violation de ce droit à savoir le fait que le juge puisse avoir une opinion préconçue risquant de peser lourdement sur sa décision ou qu'il soit susceptible de consulter une autorité supérieure avant de rendre sa décision.

Le Plaignant réitère qu'il lui a semblé que les juges étaient liés avec les plus hautes instances de pouvoir exécutifs et avaient une opinion préconçue de la cause à son détriment. Pour soutenir cette allégation, il relève le fait qu'il attend toujours le délibéré concernant l'opposition qu'il a formulé le 10 avril 2006 devant le Président du Tribunal de Libreville et auprès du Conservateur foncier pour empêcher l'enregistrement de l'acquisition frauduleuse des terrains indivis litigieux. Il ajoute qu'il demeure sans aucune nouvelle sur la plainte pénale dont il a saisi un juge d'instruction en 2008 et sur l'appel interjeté par Me NFONE contre une condamnation civile du requérant du 04 février 2009. Le requérant rappelle que, par ailleurs, cette condamnation en première instance ignore les preuves que les ventes litigieuses étaient nulles. Il fait également savoir que la magistrate qui a pris cette décision habitait une des parcelles litigieuses

L'Etat défendeur demande à la Commission de rejeter le moyen tiré de l'absence de suite donnée à la procédure du Plaignant devant le juge en faisant valoir que ce prolongement de procédure ne peut nullement être imputable à l'institution judiciaire. Il affirme que le Juge d'instruction du deuxième Cabinet a reçu la déposition du Plaignant le 02 juillet 2008 mais que pour l'année judiciaire qui a suivi (2008-2009), le Conseil supérieur de la Magistrature a désigné un nouveau juge d'instruction qui a été affecté dans ce Cabinet. Il ajoute que, malheureusement, ce dernier s'est rendu compte de l'existence des liens familiaux entre lui et les parties (C'est à dire tous les héritiers Migolet) et s'est dessaisi du dossier par un ordonnance de dessaisissement du 30 janvier 2009 en application de l'article 79 du code de Procédure Pénale.

L'Etat défendeur ajoute enfin que jusqu'au 18 février 2009, le dernier juge n'a pas pu notifier au plaignant ce dessaisissement pour deux raisons principales notamment le manque d'adresse précise du plaignant et des autres héritiers, et le manque de suivi de son dossier. Selon l'Etat défendeur, le Plaignant n'a pas pu suivre la procédure d'autant qu'il ne peut produire aucune lettre de relance avec accusé de réception du Cabinet du juge d'instruction étant donné qu'il n'avait ni constitué un avocat, ni élu un domicile auprès d'un cabinet d'avocat qui aurait pu servir d'adresse pour la notification des informations relevant de son dossier d'instruction.

En se basant sur la jurisprudence de la Commission selon laquelle il faut prendre en considération les circonstances de l'affaire et les raisons justifiant le prolongement des recours pour déterminer si ce prolongement est normal ou anormal, l'Etat défendeur demande, enfin, à la Commission de considérer que le prolongement de cette procédure est justifié. Sur le moyen tiré de l'absence de suite donnée à la procédure du Plaignant devant le juge civil a) Sur la requête du 20 mars 2006 (reçue le 27/03/06) et portant opposition à la vente effectuée par Madame RELONGOUE Lydie

Tout en relevant l'absence d'un accusé de réception et du numéro d'enregistrement, l'Etat défendeur fait valoir que le Plaignant n'a jamais déposé de requête en opposition à la vente au greffe. Selon lui, l'opposition dont fait valoir le Plaignant a un cachet qui ne comporte ni le sceau de la République gabonaise, ni l'indication de la date et le numéro d'enregistrement, ni du greffe ayant reçu la requête comme l'exige l'article 409 du Code de procédure civile. Il réitère, en conséquence, que le droit du Plaignant au procès équitable n'a pas été violé sous cet aspect d'autant qu'il n'a jamais exercé son droit d'estre en justice. b) Sur la requête reçue au greffe civile le 10/04/06 sous le numéro 395/05/06

Tout en affirmant avoir bien réceptionné et enregistré au Greffe du Tribunal de Grande Instance de Libreville cette requête en référé du Plaignant portant sur la rétractation et la mise en conservation des sommes indûment perçues, l'Etat défendeur s'interroge sur la participation dans le déroulement de l'instance. Il souligne, en effet, que le Plaignant n'a pas rapporté la preuve du retour d'assignation au Greffe par lui-même ou par l'huissier qu'il a mandaté à cette fin pour que son dossier soit enrôlé. Il insiste que, finalement, aucune décision ne pouvait être rendue des lors que le juge n'avait pas été saisi. Selon l'Etat défendeur, le Plaignant n'a pas suivi ses dossiers.

Quant à l'allégation du Plaignant selon laquelle les magistrats « ont organisé une cabale contre lui », l'Etat défendeur se demande comment on pourrait justifier que dans une autre instance introduite par le Plaignant dans la même période, le Tribunal a fait droit à sa demande d'expertise.
Dans ses observations de réplique, le plaignant estime que les arguments de l'Etat défendeur ne sont pas fondés.

Le Plaignant allègue que le moyen de l'Etat défendeur selon lequel le prolongement de la procédure serait dû à l'absence d'adresse et d'une négligence du requérant à suivre la procédure ne tient pas. Selon lui, une absence de diligence d'un justiciable est sanctionnée, soit par la radiation de l'affaire, soit par la péremption de l'instance et le Gouvernement n'a pas pu fournir une copie d'un de ces actes.

Le Plaignant insiste, par ailleurs, qu'il existe des formalités obligatoires que doit contenir toute plainte, en particulier les formalités d'identification et d'adresse. Il réitère que pour cette raison, sa plainte comprenait bel et bien son identification telle qu'exigée. Il ajoute que, d'autre part, un juge d'instruction, de par la loi, dispose de toutes les formes de communication et des moyens officiels (Police et Gendarmerie) pour donner suite à une procédure.

Sur le moyen de l'Etat défendeur selon lequel le cachet de la requête du 20 mars 2006 ne comporte ni sceau, ni indication de la date et du numéro d'enregistrement, ni du greffe ayant reçu cette requête, le Plaignant réplique que « le Président du Tribunal peut être joint de deux manières : directement par son secrétariat particulier, comme fut le cas de cette lettre ; ou indirectement par le Greffe civil ». Selon lui, cette requête ne devrait pas comprendre de numéro d'enregistrement ou d'accusé de réception par le Greffe civil car il n'en était ni le destinataire ni le réceptionnaire. Il réitère que cela ne déroge aucunement à la régularité et à la validité de la procédure. De la requête reçue au greffe civile le 10 avril 2006 sous le numéro 395/05/ 06

Le Plaignant déclare ne pas comprendre l'argumentaire de l'Etat défendeur d'une possible absence de retour d'assignation car selon lui, si la requête a été enregistrée, c'est que l'assignation a été enrôlée sinon il n'y aurait pas eu l'enregistrement de la requête. De surcroît, il dit qu'il lui est difficile de comprendre comment l'Etat s'interrogerait sur l'enrôlement de l'assignation. Selon lui, si pour les besoins de raisonnement il était admis que l'assignation n'avait pas été enrôlée, l'Etat défendeur ne s'interrogerait pas sur ce fait, plutôt il le proclamerait avec des preuves à l'appui puisqu'en tant qu'Etat, il dispose de tous les moyens pour savoir ce qui se passe dans ses tribunaux.

L'article 7 (1) (d) protège le droit à un procès équitable en ces termes : Toute personne a droit à ce que sa cause soit entendue. Ce droit comprend : [...] d) le droit d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable par une juridiction impartiale. Dans le cas sous analyse, le requérant estime que ce droit a été violée sous deux aspects, celui de l'absence de délai raisonnable et celui d'une absence d'impartialité des juridictions saisies. La commission se propose d'analyser chacun de ces deux aspects par rapport aux circonstances de la cause afin de pouvoir déterminer s'il y a eu violation du droit à un procès équitable.

La notion de droit d'être jugé dans un délai raisonnable fait appel à la compréhension de la notion de « délai raisonnable ». Malheureusement, la Charte n'en donne pas la définition. En l'absence de cette définition dans la Charte, la Commission relève d'abord que cette expression contient une juxtaposition de deux termes : celui de « délai » et celui de « raisonnable ». Le premier se réfère à un intervalle de temps pendant lequel se produit une action ; et dans le cadre d'une instance judiciaire, un intervalle de temps dans lequel se produit un procès, un jugement. Quant au second terme, l'adjectif « raisonnable », il peut être défini comme étant ce qui est logique et satisfaisant. Il en résulte que le vocable « délai raisonnable » tel que voulu par la Charte fait référence à un intervalle de temps qui n'est ni étonnamment long, ni abusivement court. En d'autres termes, la Charte veut que la durée du procès soit d'une durée acceptable ou qui n'est pas excessivement longue.

Ceci dit, la question qui se pose est celle de savoir comment déterminer la durée maximale de ce délai. En d'autres termes, quelle est la durée d'un délai raisonnable ? Comme la Commission l'a déjà indiqué dans sa jurisprudence, la question relative à ce qui est raisonnable ne peut être exprimée en termes de délai global qui s'applique à tous les cas, mais elle doit plutôt dépendre des circonstances. Cette question a été développée par la Cour Européenne des Droits de l'homme qui a établi les critères pour apprécier le caractère de délai raisonnable en l'occurrence la complexité de l'affaire, le comportement du requérant, le comportement des autorités judiciaires et l'enjeu du litige.

Dans son Observation Générale no 32, le Comité des droits de l'homme des Nations Unies a, lui aussi, insisté sur l'importance de la rapidité de la procédure comme garantie au procès équitable. Dans son commentaire, ce Comité est revenu sur les éléments d'appréciation du délai raisonnable dans un procès civil. Selon lui, les retards qui ne justifient ni la complexité de l'affaire ni la conduite des parties portent atteinte au principe du procès équitable consacré par le Pacte relatif aux relatifs aux droits civils et politiques.

Dans son Observation Générale sur l'article 14 du Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques, le Comité des droits de l'homme a indiqué que l'impartialité s'analyse sous deux aspects en termes suivants : « Premièrement, les juges ne doivent pas laisser des partis pris ou des préjugés personnels influencer leur jugement ni nourrir d'idées préconçues au sujet de l'affaire dont ils sont saisis, ni agir de manière à favoriser indûment les intérêts de l'une des parties au détriment de l'autre. Deuxièmement, le tribunal doit aussi donner une impression d'impartialité à un observateur raisonnable. Ainsi, un procès sérieusement entaché par la participation d'un juge qui, selon le droit interne, aurait dû être écarté, ne peut pas normalement être considéré comme un procès impartial. » Ainsi, selon le Comité des droits de l'homme, l'impartialité concerne aussi bien les juges que le tribunal en général.

C'est dans ce même ordre d'idées que la Cour Européenne des Droits de l'Homme a souligné que l'impartialité doit s'apprécier selon deux manières : selon une démarche subjective et une démarche objective. Alors que la première tient compte de la « conviction personnelle et du comportement de tel juge, c'est-à-dire du point de savoir si celui-ci a fait preuve de parti pris ou préjugé personnel dans tel cas », la seconde consiste à déterminer si, « abstraction faite du comportement de ses membres, le tribunal offrait, notamment à travers sa composition, des garanties suffisantes pour exclure tout doute légitime quant à son impartialité ».

Dans l'affaire Denisov c. Ukraine, cette même Cour a relevé que l'impartialité se définit par l'absence de préjugé ou de parti pris. L'impartialité du Tribunal est une garantie fondamentale. En effet, l'accès du tribunal n'aurait aucun sens si ce dernier n'est pas impartial. Par ailleurs, l'impartialité du Tribunal constitue une réflexion même de la démocratie, les deux notions étant consubstantielles. L'impartialité des juges est la condition fondamentale de la confiance que les tribunaux doivent s'inspirer dans une société démocratique. Il incombe aux Etats parties de la Charte d'agencer leur système judiciaire de manière à lui permettre de répondre aux exigences de l'impartialité voulues par les dispositions de l'article 7 (1) (d).

Il résulte des arguments du Plaignant que, selon lui, l'absence du délai raisonnable serait dû à une absence d'impartialité des juridictions qu'il a saisies. La Commission relève que le Plaignant n'a pas apporté de preuves ou d'éléments suffisants pour en déduire que les juges étaient liés personnellement avec les hautes instances du Pouvoir exécutif avec une opinion préconçue de sa cause comme le pressent le plaignant. En effet, ce dernier ne se borne qu'à donner des exemples de requêtes pour lequel il a longuement attendu leur délibéré. C'est cette longue attente de délibéré qui crée en lui une présomption que les juges avaient des idées préconçues. Aux yeux de la Commission, ceci ne suffit pas pour conclure l'absence d'impartialité. En particulier, non seulement le Plaignant n'établit pas l'existence d'opinions préconçues chez les juges, mais également il ne définit pas le lien de causalité entre les délais déraisonnables et un comportement particulier des juges. La Commission se propose plutôt d'analyser ces exemples au cas par cas pour déterminer si leurs délais ne sont pas raisonnables au sens de l'article 7 (1) (d) de la Charte pour enfin établir les causes de ces délais s'il y a lieu.

Dans le cas sous analyse, l'Etat défendeur soutient que le prolongement de la procédure serait dû principalement à l'absence d'adresse et d'une négligence du requérant à suivre la procédure. Comme la Commission l'a ci-haut indiquée, le comportement du plaignant peut diminuer, voire exclure, la responsabilité étatique. Il revient alors à la commission d'analyser la portée des faits imputables au plaignant quant à leur impact sur le délai du procès susmentionné. Effet, l'Etat défendeur soutient que tous les magistrats d'instructions qui se sont succédé dans cette affaire n'ont pas abouti à l'instruction pour défaut d'adresse du Plaignant.

La Commission conçoit mal qu'une instance judiciaire aurait reçu une plainte qui ne comporte aucune adresse du Plaignant. Effet, le minimum d'éléments qu'une instance judiciaire doit considérer pour enregistrer une plainte est l'identification des parties qui comprend leur adresse. Une instance judiciaire qui ignorerait de retenir l'adresse des parties lors de l'enregistrement de la plainte s'exposerait au risque de violer le droit aux procès équitable. En fait, à défaut d'une adresse, il lui serait difficile de garantir le droit au procès équitable quant à son exigence selon laquelle les parties doivent être informées sur les éléments du procès et les différentes étapes de la procédure.

Les Etats partie à la Charte ont l'obligation de garantir ce droit en mettant en place des mesures législatives nécessaires pour donner effet aux différents aspects du droit à ce que sa cause soit entendue. En d'autres termes, les Etats doivent s'assurer que tous les obstacles au bon déroulement du procès sont contournés. En particulier, comme l'a indiqué la commission dans les Directives et Principes sur le Droit à un procès équitable et à l'assistance judiciaire en Afrique, les Etats doivent veiller à ce que l'accès aux services judiciaires ne soit pas entravé, entre autres, par l'absence d'assistance pour comprendre les procédures et accomplir les formalités. L'administration de la justice doit être organisée de sorte à permettre au tribunal de contacter les justiciables chaque fois que de besoin.

Quant à l'argument de l'Etat défendeur selon lequel le Plaignant n'aurait pas constitué un avocat ou un Cabinet d'Avocats qui aurait pu servir d'adresse, la Commission considère qu'il n'est pas pertinent. En effet, la Commission est de l'avis du Plaignant qu'il serait contraire au droit à toute personne d'avoir accès à un Tribunal d'exiger aux justiciables d'avoir un avocat. Ceci rendrait plutôt la justice inaccessible et sélective car elle coûterait chère.

De tout ce qui précède, la Commission conclut que les retards de procédure ne sont pas dus au fait du plaignant, mais plutôt à l'organisation judiciaire gabonaise qui n'a pas pu mettre en place un système juridique garantissant le droit à l'information. Il en résulte que l'Etat défendeur a violé l'article 7 (1) (d) de la Charte sous cet aspect. Sur le moyen tiré de l'absence de suite donnée à la procédure devant le juge civile a. Sur la requête du 20 mars 2006 (reçue le 27/03/06) et portant opposition à la vente effectuée par Madame RELONGOUE Lydie

Sur le moyen de défense de l'Etat défendeur selon lequel le Plaignant n'a pas déposé de plainte en opposition à la vente pour motif que cette opposition ne contient ni le sceau de la République gabonaise, ni l'indication de date et de numéro d'enregistrement du greffe ayant reçu la requête, la Commission relève que le point de discorde est celui de savoir si la saisine a été régulière ou pas. En d'autres termes, il s'agit de savoir si, selon la procédure civile gabonaise, la saisine du Tribunal se fait au Secrétariat particulier du Président du Tribunal ou au Greffe du Tribunal. Bien que le Plaignant soutienne que les deux sont possibles, il n'en donne pas de base légale. Il aurait surtout soutenu son affirmation par l'indication des dispositions du Code Civil gabonais qui le prévoient.

En l'absence d'une telle justification, la Commission n'a d'autres choix que de décider sur base des éléments procurés par les parties. Une analyse approfondie des éléments à la disposition de la commission soumis par les parties fait apparaître que les requêtes introduites par le requérant sont de deux catégories.

La première catégorie est composée des correspondances qu'il a adressées au Tribunal en tant qu'institution. Il s'agit notamment de la requête en référé portant sur la rétractation et la mise en conservation des sommes indûment perçues introduites au Tribunal de Libreville par le requérant le 10 avril 2006. Cette requête a un numéro d'enregistrement et le timbre de son accusé de réception porte l'emblème de la République et la mention « Le Greffier Civil ».

La deuxième catégorie est composée de correspondances adressées au Président du Tribunal pour solliciter son intervention afin qu'il puisse prendre des mesures en sa qualité de fonctionnaire en chef du Tribunal en charge des questions administratives. Il en est ainsi, par exemple, pour la requête datée du 5 avril 2006 (reçue le 6 avril 2006) par laquelle le plaignant sollicitait l'intervention du Président du Tribunal pour accéder aux actes de la vente frauduleuse et pour la correspondance du Plaignant au Président du Tribunal de Libreville du 31 mai 2019 (reçue le 06 juin 2019) pour dénoncer l'entrave de la justice, la partialité et la collusion du Tribunal de Libreville. Ces requêtes ont des caractéristiques en commun. Elles ne comportent pas de numéro d'enregistrement et les timbres d'accusé de leur réception révèlent que ces dernières portent une mention « Secrétariat du Président ».

La Requête introduite par le plaignant le 20 mars 2006 (reçue le 27 mars 2006) pour faire opposition à la vente effectuée par Madame RELONGUE Lydie rentre dans cette catégorie. Le timbre de son accusé de réception comporte, elle aussi, la mention « Secrétariat du Président ».

Il résulte des précédentes observations que la requête à laquelle le plaignant fait référence n'était pas adressée au Tribunal en tant qu'institution judiciaire mais plutôt à son Président pour solliciter son intervention ou sa diligence en sa qualité de fonctionnaire en chef du Tribunal en charge des questions administratives. Ainsi, comme l'affirme, d'ailleurs, le Plaignant dans son mémoire en réplique, le greffe civil n'en était pas le destinataire ; l'objectif principal du Plaignant était plutôt de joindre le Président du Tribunal. Dans ces circonstances, la Commission est de l'avis de l'Etat défendeur que le Tribunal n'a pas été régulièrement saisi.

Le greffe civil ne pouvait pas enregistrer une affaire à laquelle elle n'avait pas été saisie comme l'exige le Code civile gabonais en son article 409 qui précise que : « L'original de la requête, accompagnée d'autant de copies que de défenseurs est remis ou adressé au greffe de la juridiction compétente qui l'enregistre immédiatement et inscrit sur l'original la date et le numéro d'enregistrement. Seule la date de l'enregistrement fait foi de la date de la requête qui est interruptive de prescription, si elle est suivie d'une assignation »

En l'absence de saisine régulière, l'absence du délai raisonnable ne peut pas être imputable à l'institution judiciaire. Comme déjà indiqué, en matière civile, le délai raisonnable peut être subordonné à la diligence des intéressés. Sous cet aspect, la Commission conclut qu'il n'y a pas eu violation du délai raisonnable b. Sur la requête reçue au greffe civile le 10/04/06 sous le numéro 395/05/06
Par rapport à cette requête, la commission trouve que les parties ne s'entendent pas sur la définition de l'enrôlement d'une affaire aux yeux de la procédure civile gabonaise.

L'Etat défendeur affirme n'avoir pas enrôlé l'affaire car selon lui, le Plaignant n'a pas rapporté la preuve de retour d'assignation du greffe qu'il a mandaté comme l'exige l'article 425 du code civil gabonais qui dispose comme suit : « Le Tribunal est saisi par la Comparution volontaire des parties, soit par le dépôt au greffe de l'assignation ». La Commission rappelle qu'il n'est pas de sa compétence d'interpréter la législation des Etats. Il s'agit d'une responsabilité des autorités nationales, et notamment des Cours et Tribunaux nationaux qui ont la compétence d'interpréter la législation interne. Le rôle de la Commission se limite à vérifier la compatibilité avec la Charte des effets de pareille interprétation.

Néanmoins, la Commission observe que, bien que le Plaignant affirme que la victime a retourné l'assignation au Greffe Civil le 23 août 2006, il n'en donne pas de pièce justificative. En l'absence de cette preuve, la Commission n'a d'autres choix que de constater que la victime ne s'est pas conformée aux exigences du Code Civil gabonais et, est de l'avis de l'Etat défendeur selon laquelle comme il n'y a pas eu de retour d'assignation, le tribunal n'a pas été régulièrement saisi. Il en résulte que sous cet aspect, l'article 7 (1) (d) n'a pas été violé.
De toutes ces observations, la Commission conclut que l'Etat défendeur a violé l'article 7(1) (d) sous un seul aspect La Commission,Pour ces motifs,

Dit que la République Gabonaise a violé l'article 7 (1) (d) de la Charte. En conséquence, La commission demande à la République Gabonaise : i. De prendre les mesures adéquates en vue de rétablir le Plaignant dans la pleine jouissance de ses droits. ii. D'accorder à la victime des dommages et intérêts pour le préjudice causé par les violations constatées. iii. De lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre- vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée par la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples lors de sa 70 Session Ordinaire tenue virtuellement du 23 Février 2022 au 9 Mars 2022

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat), received on 14 August 2015, a Communication submitted by Counsel Christophe Meyer (the Complainant), in the name and on behalf of Mr. Blaise Jean Joseph Migolet (the victim) against the Gabonese Republic (Gabon or Respondent State).
The Complainant informs that the victim is an heir of the late Jean-Stanislus Migolet who disappeared on 6 July 1987, bequeathing his estate to three (3) wives and their children.

The Complainant reports that some co-owners in undivided ownership manoeuvred in order to be able to sell the property belonging to the undivided estate with the aim of appropriating all the succession rights.
The Complainant reports in effect that some co-owners resorted to fraudulent practices to sell plots without the victim's knowledge with the "probable" complicity of a notary and even of a judge.

The Complainant cites the example of an order referenced No. 87/2005-2006 of 13 March 2006 which allowed the sale of an undivided property at the office of Notary Lydie Relongoue Bevigna. The Complainant reports that the victim filed an objection to the said order before the President of the Court and with the Land Registrar to oppose the registration of the acquisition, which he considers fraudulent, of the undivided lands but that, until today, the victim is still awaiting the deliberation. He adds that the victim also lodged a criminal complaint in 2008 by seizing an examining magistrate but that no follow-up was given to this action. The Complainant stresses that the victim's remedies against these fraudulent practices were invariably rejected.

Furthermore, the Complainant informs that another dispute pitted the victim against Mr. Diawara Madikandja. He reports in effect that on 14 October 2007, after the victim understood the influence of Mr. Diawara Madikandja on the judicial setbacks that he allegedly suffered, the victim decided to evict him from the building which the latter had leased from him and, according to the Complainant, was subletting in violation of the contractual clauses.
The Complainant reports that following the eviction of Mr. Diawara Madikandja, the latter seized the judge for interim relief who sentenced the victim to a penalty payment of 5,000,000 CFA francs.

He adds that the co-owners to whom the victim had objected organized a "cabal" against him, accusing him of theft and destruction of the immovable and movable property of Mr. Diawara Madikandja. The Complainant indicates that a complaint was lodged to that effect, that the victim was heard at the Nkembo Police Station for these facts but that none of the exculpatory elements was taken into account and that the supposed witnesses of the theft were not heard.

The Complainant reports that despite the investigation being solely for the prosecution and the absence of the constituent elements of the offence, the victim was prosecuted before the criminal courts and was finally acquitted on 04 February 2009. The Complainant adds that the civil courts, on the other hand, convicted the victim and that the presiding judge refused to take into consideration all the elements at issue. He further stresses that the judge in question herself lives on one of the disputed plots.

The Complainant affirms having exhausted all available and useful local remedies and requests the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) to assess the time taken to seize it according to the particularity of the case and to deduce from it that there is a good and compelling reason on the part of the victim that explains the time taken to address the present Communication to the Commission.
The Complainant indicates that the complaint has not been submitted to another international body for the settlement of disputes or of similar competence.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 7, notably Article 7(1)(d) of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).
The Complainant requests that a violation of the victim's right to a fair trial be recognized with regard to the facts he alleges.
The Secretariat received the Communication on 14 August 2015 and acknowledged receipt on 27 August 2015.

Pursuant to Rules 93(2)(j) and 93(4) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure, the Secretariat invited the Complainant to indicate whether the complaint transmitted to the Secretariat has been submitted to another international body for the settlement of disputes or of similar competence in accordance with Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

By letter dated 28 August 2015, the Complainant indicated to the Secretariat that the complaint has not been submitted to another international body for the settlement of disputes or of similar competence. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 10 September 2015.

On 15 October 2015, the Secretariat requested the Complainant to clarify whether the complaint is submitted under Articles 48 and 49 of the African Charter as appears from the cover page of the Communication or under Article 55 of the African Charter as appears from the content of the Communication. By letter of 16 October 2015, the Complainant transmitted his response to the Commission, indicating that it was an error and that the Communication is submitted on the basis of Article 55 of the African Charter. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt by letter dated 30 October 2015.
At its 57th Ordinary Session held from 04 to 18 November 2015 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission seized itself of the Communication.

By letter of 30 November 2015, the Secretariat informed the Complainant of the decision on seizure and invited him to submit his observations on admissibility within a period of two months in accordance with Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure. By Note Verbale dated the same day, the Secretariat transmitted the decision on seizure and the Communication to the Respondent State.

On 14 January 2016 (by email) and 04 February 2016 (by post), the Complainant transmitted his observations on the admissibility of the Communication and the Commission acknowledged receipt on 9 February 2016. On 15 February 2016, the Secretariat sent the Complainant's observations to the Respondent State and requested it to transmit its written brief on the admissibility of the Communication within a period of two months from notification.

On 23 February 2016, the Secretariat received an email from a Legal Adviser at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Respondent State, alleging not to have received the documents annexed to the Complainant's brief on admissibility.

By email of 4 March 2016, the Secretariat sent the required annexes back to the legal adviser of the Respondent State and indicated that these had already been transmitted via D.H.L to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Francophonie and Regional Integration of the Gabonese Republic.

On 30 March 2016, the Secretariat received an email from the Legal Adviser, transmitting a Note Verbale from the Respondent State dated 30 March 2016 requesting an additional period of one month to submit its brief on the admissibility of the Communication. The same request reached the Secretariat later by post on 16 June 2016.
On 12 April 2016, the Secretariat received the Respondent State's observations on the admissibility of the Communication.

By Note Verbale of 18 April 2016, the Secretariat acknowledged receipt of the Respondent State's observations on the admissibility of the Communication and noted the fact that the Secretariat received the Respondent State's observations before having had time to respond to the request for extension of the time limit set for the submission of the said observations. By letter dated the same day, the Secretariat transmitted the Respondent State's observations to the Complainant and invited him to submit his additional observations, if any, within a period of one month.

On 03 May 2016, by Note Verbale and letter, the Secretariat informed the Respondent State and the Complainant that the Commission decided at its 58th Ordinary Session held from 6 to 20 April 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia, to defer its decision on admissibility pending any additional observations from the Complainant on the admissibility of the Communication.

On 04 May 2016, the Complainant transmitted his additional observations on admissibility. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt by letter of 13 May 2016 but requested the Complainant to provide a clarification. Indeed, the Complainant's submissions refer to application No. 395/05/06 of 10 April 2006 as an annexed document but this reference did not appear on any of the documents actually annexed.
On 30 May 2016, the Complainant transmitted application No. 395/05/06 of 10 April 2006.
On 6 September 2016, the Secretariat transmitted to the Respondent State, for information, the Complainant's additional observations on the Respondent State's brief.

By Notes Verbales and letters of 23 November 2016, 13 April 2017 and 5 June 2017, the Secretariat informed the parties that the Commission decided respectively at its 59th Ordinary Session, 21st Extraordinary Session and 60th Ordinary Session, to defer its decision on the admissibility of the Communication to a later Session.

At its 22nd Extraordinary Session held in Dakar, Senegal from 29 July to 7 August 2017 the Commission declared the Communication admissible and invited the Complainant to transmit to it his observations on the merits within a period of sixty (60) days from the date of notification of the decision on admissibility in accordance with the provisions of Rule 108(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

By letter and Note Verbale of 8 December 2017, the Secretariat transmitted the decision on admissibility to the parties and invited the Complainant to transmit to it his observations on the merits within a period of 60 days from receipt.
By a letter of 18 December 2017, the Complainant transmitted to the Secretariat of the Commission his observations on the merits.
The Complainant's arguments focus on the temporal and territorial jurisdiction of the Commission and on the admissibility requirements laid down in Article 56(5) and (6) of the African Charter.

The Complainant maintains that the Commission has jurisdiction ratione loci and temporis to hear cases against States that have ratified the African Charter, that Gabon has ratified it since 20 February 1986 and that the alleged violations postdate the said ratification.

With regard to the Complainant's arguments relating to Article 56(5) of the African Charter on the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant maintains that the remedies are unduly prolonged. In support of this allegation, he maintains that the objection that the victim filed against order No. 87/2005-2006 of 13 March 2006 has been under deliberation for 9 years and that the criminal complaint that the victim lodged in 2008 has still not been dealt with.

With regard to the arguments relating to the requirement that communications must be submitted within a reasonable time from the exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant maintains that on this subject, the Commission makes its analysis on a case-by-case basis. He supports this assertion by citing as an example the Commission's decision in communication 310/05 Darfur Relief and Documentation Center v. Republic of Sudan (paras 74 to 77) in which, according to him, the Commission declared that a period of two years and five months or twenty-nine months without any reason was not reasonable. He then maintains that on the occasion of its decision in Communication 305/05 Article 19 and others v. Zimbabwe (para 92), the Commission indicated that "when a complainant has a valid and compelling reason for not submitting his complaint to the Commission, the latter has the responsibility, in the interest of fairness and justice, to grant the complainant an opportunity to be heard".

The Complainant, on the basis of these arguments, requests the Commission to consider that there is a "good and compelling" reason on the part of the victim that explains the time taken to submit the Communication and accordingly, to consider that the time taken to submit the complaint is reasonable.
The Respondent State maintains that the Communication must be declared inadmissible. In support of this position, the Respondent State raises three objections of inadmissibility.

First, the Respondent State maintains that the Complainant's Communication contains disparaging language towards the Gabonese State and its institutions and therefore does not comply with the requirement laid down in Article 56(3) of the African Charter that the Communication must not contain disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the African Union. The Respondent State denounces in particular the following assertion of the Complainant: "on several occasions, it seemed to him that these judges were in reality personally linked with the highest authorities of the executive power and had a preconceived opinion of his case".

It maintains that these assertions without evidence discredit the institutions of the Gabonese Republic, call into question the independence of the judicial authority and the credibility of the institutions. It further maintains that this offends the principle of the separation of powers and that of the independence of the judiciary and denies Gabonese judges all competence and all objectivity. The Respondent State cites as an example the Commission's decision on Communication 65/92 Ligue Camerounaise des Droits de l'Homme v. Cameroon in which the Commission is said to have considered that the language is insulting because of the use of terms such as "regime of torture" and "government of barbarism".
Furthermore, for the Respondent State, local remedies have not been exhausted and it subdivides this ground into two arguments.

In the first place, the Respondent State maintains that the Complainant does not provide proof concerning the information that the victim lodged an objection against an order No. 87/2005-2006 of 13 March 2006 before the President of the Court. It asserts that the Complainant produces in support neither the impugned order nor the objection lodged against it. For the Respondent State, the Complainant should have attached a copy of the said application bearing the stamp of the Registry of the Court, the date of receipt and the number assigned. In the second place, the Respondent State maintains that the complaint lodged by the Complainant in 2008 before the examining magistrate is still under investigation; it attaches a letter from the examining magistrate attesting to this status of the file. The Respondent State further asserts that in criminal matters, the duration of a case depends on its complexity and that no provision of the Gabonese Code of Criminal Procedure fixes its time limit, that it may extend over several years as long as the sought truth has not sufficiently manifested itself to the judge who pursues his investigations without it being possible to consider that the procedure "is unduly prolonged".

Finally, the Respondent State maintains that the time within which the Communication was submitted is not reasonable. In the Respondent State's view, the Complainant did not wait for the Gabonese judge to rule on his case, which could have opened the way for him to other domestic proceedings such as appeal and cassation in case of an unfavourable decision. The Respondent State therefore considers that, local remedies not having been exhausted, the reasonable time giving him the right to seize the Commission could not have begun to run.
In his additional observations, the Complainant considers that the Respondent State's objections of inadmissibility are ill-founded.

With regard to the objection that the communication contains disparaging and insulting language directed against the Respondent State and its institutions, the Complainant maintains that what is prohibited by the African Charter is the use of insulting or disparaging "terms" and that the sentence in question contains none, that it is made up of deliberately neutral and purely descriptive words used for the simple and legitimate purpose of specifying the content of the grievance. For the Complainant, no term used has a pejorative character and therefore cannot be of a disparaging or insulting nature. The Complainant stresses that the Respondent State does not challenge any particular term that would be disparaging or insulting but the entirety of the sentence in question cited as shocking by its implications and that this is different from the prescription of the Charter.

As for the allegation that the Communication should be declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant argues that the very confirmation by the Respondent State of the fact that the case relating to the criminal complaint lodged by the victim in 2008 is still under investigation is of a nature to support the fact that the local remedy procedure is unduly prolonged. Citing Communication 251/2002 Lawyers for Human Rights vs. Swaziland, 11 May 2005 (2005), para 27, the Complainant maintains that compliance with the exhaustion of local remedies is not a requirement where the continuation of the violations is such that a judicial remedy to this violation seems unlikely. In addition the Complainant transmitted a copy of application No. 395/05/06 of 10 April 2006 (bearing the stamp of the registrar of the Court of First Instance, a date and a number) and a copy of the letter of the Land Registry 416/MEFBP/CPFH/ of 12 May 2006 relating to the objection to the sale.

Finally, with regard to the objection that the Communication is not submitted within a reasonable time, the Complainant maintains that the Respondent State's arguments in support of this objection refer to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies and not that of submission within a reasonable time. He reaffirms the fact that the Commission decides on the reasonable time on a case-by-case basis and that it considers that if the complainant has a valid and compelling reason for not submitting his complaint to the Commission's examination, the latter has the responsibility in the interest of fairness and justice to grant the complainant an opportunity to be heard. On this basis, the Complainant requests the Commission to consider that there is a "good and compelling" reason that explains the time taken to address the present communication and consequently, not to declare the Communication inadmissible on the ground that the time of submission is not reasonable.

Article 56 of the African Charter prescribes the following seven (7) requirements which must be cumulatively fulfilled for a Communication to be declared admissible by the Commission: 1. Indicate their authors even if the latter request anonymity; 2. Are compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter; 3. Are not written in disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or to the Organization of African Unity; 4. Are not based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; 5. Are sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; 6. Are submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter; 7. Do not deal with cases which have been settled by these States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter.
In the present case, three of the requirements, notably those provided for in Article 56(3), (5) and (6) of the African Charter, are contested by the parties.

After thorough examination of the file, the Commission is itself satisfied that the four (4) other requirements provided for in Articles 56(1), (2), (4), and (7) are fulfilled. Indeed, the author of the Communication has indicated his identity; the Communication concerns alleged violations of the African Charter which are said to have been committed well after the entry into force of the African Charter in the Gabonese Republic. The information communicated by the Complainant does not derive from information disseminated solely through the mass media. Moreover, it does not emerge from the file that the present case has already been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or of the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the provisions of the African Charter.
As for the three requirements that are the subject of disagreement between the parties, it is appropriate to analyze them successively.

For the Respondent State, by asserting that according to the victim, "on several occasions, it seemed to him that these judges were in reality personally linked with the highest authorities of the executive power and had a preconceived opinion of his case", the Complainant discredits the institutions of the Gabonese Republic, calls into question the independence of the judicial authority from the judicial power, the credibility of the institutions, offends the principle of the separation of powers and that of the independence of the judiciary and denies Gabonese judges all competence and all objectivity. For the Complainant, the State does not challenge a particular term but a whole sentence whereas Article 56(3) speaks of "terms". He further maintains that there is no disparaging or insulting term used in the sentence in question and that the State fails to challenge a particular term but the entirety of the sentence whereas Article 56(3) refers to "terms" and not to a sentence.

As to whether Article 56(3) also applies to sentences that would be disparaging or insulting in nature, the Commission does not agree with the Complainant's strict interpretation of Article 56(3). Indeed, the objective pursued by this requirement is to avoid insulting or disparaging remarks. A sentence may not contain a particularly disparaging or insulting term but constitute as a whole a statement of a nature to insult or to disparage the State concerned, its institutions or the African Union. The word "terms" must here be interpreted broadly. Moreover, in its analysis of the requirement laid down in Article 56(3), the Commission uses many times the words "remark" or "language" that would be insulting or disparaging and not necessarily disparaging or insulting "terms".

It is therefore now appropriate to see whether the sentence in question constitutes a remark of a disparaging or insulting nature. The Commission makes this examination on a case-by-case basis but over time, it has drawn out in its jurisprudence a few criteria that guide its assessment.

Indeed, in its decision on Communication 284/03 Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights v. Zimbabwe, the Commission stated that: In determining whether a particular remark is disparaging or insulting and whether it has tarnished the integrity of the Judiciary or another State institution, the Commission must verify whether the said remark or the said language aims to unlawfully or intentionally violate the dignity, reputation or integrity of a judicial officer or body and whether it is used in a calculated manner to pollute the mind of the public or of any reasonable person in order to discredit and weaken public confidence in that institution. The language must aim to undermine the integrity and status of the institution and to discredit it.
It emerges from this jurisprudence that the unlawful character, the intention and the purpose are the determining criteria for analyzing whether language is disparaging or insulting.

The Commission notes that the sentence in question occurs in the context of the Complainant's arguments aimed at supporting his allegation of the violation of the victim's right to a fair trial. Indeed, one of the positions maintained by the Complainant in the Communication is that the fact that the judge may have a preconceived opinion likely to weigh heavily on the decision is a determining factor in the assessment of the right to be tried by an impartial court and he cites the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa as the basis of this position.

It is clear to the Commission that it is to support the allegation of violation of the right to a fair trial that the Complainant indicated that "on several occasions, it seemed to him that these judges were in reality personally linked with the highest authorities of the executive power and had a preconceived opinion of his case". The Commission recalls that Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter sets out the right to be tried by an impartial court as part of the right to have one's cause heard. The Commission notes that the Complainant is fully entitled to seize the Commission and to express himself to present his arguments on the alleged violation of this right (he is therefore acting legitimately).

Furthermore, on reading the complaint, the Commission notes that it is only with the aim of proving the violation of his right to be tried by an impartial court that the Complainant cited the incriminated sentence (thus with the intention of supporting his position on his right that was allegedly violated). The Commission is aware that allegations of human rights violations may by their nature give a negative reflection of the State and its institutions. In this case, the sentence in question is intrinsically linked to the Complainant's main allegation concerning the violation of Article 7(1)(d).

From the point of view of the very substance of the sentence, after analysis of each of the words taken in isolation and of the whole sentence placed in the context of the complaint, the Commission finds that the purpose of this sentence is neither to damage the reputation or integrity of an official or of the judicial body nor to corrupt the public mind, slander or undermine confidence and integrity. The Commission would like to note that the expressions "torturous regimes" or "governmental barbarisms" used in Communication 65/92 Ligue Camerounaise des Droits de l'Homme v. Cameroon cited by the Respondent State are not similar to the expressions used by the Complainant in the present sentence in question. Moreover, the Complainant does not state categorically but indicates that it "seemed" to the victim, thus implying that this might not be the case.

In view of the foregoing, the Commission considers that the incriminated sentence does not constitute a disparaging or insulting remark but is used for the sole purpose of supporting the allegation of violation of the victim's right to a fair trial; the objection of inadmissibility based on the language used is therefore rejected.
Concerning this objection, the Respondent State articulates its ground of inadmissibility around two arguments.

First, it maintains that the Complainant does not provide proof concerning the information that the victim lodged an objection against an order No. 87/2005-2006 of 13 March 2006. It maintains that the Complainant produces in support neither the impugned order nor the objection lodged against it. The Commission notes that since his initial submissions, the Complainant attached a copy of the order in question. In his reply brief to the Respondent State's observations on admissibility, the Complainant transmitted a copy of the application in objection that he allegedly made against the said order. The Secretariat sent back for information the said observations and the attached documents to the Respondent State which did not inform the Commission that it was challenging the authenticity of the documents whose existence is doubted in its observations. The Commission therefore sees no reason not to take into consideration the fact that the said order did indeed exist and that an objection against it was made.

The subsequent question is why, since the objection made in April 2006, no follow-up has been given to the victim's application. On this subject, the Complainant precisely alleges that the domestic procedure was unduly prolonged. In its jurisprudence, the Commission has already established the principle that the assessment of the normal or abnormal character of a domestic procedure is made on a case-by-case basis.

However, for the purpose of determining the normal or abnormal nature of the prolongation of a procedure, the Commission has already stressed in its decision on Communication 293/04 Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa / Zimbabwe, the need to take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the reasons justifying the prolongation of the remedies in order to determine whether the prolongation is normal or abnormal.

In the present case, it is a case concerning the right to property, notably land law, in which nothing in the reported facts reveals any particular complexity. In the parties' submissions, nothing in the context in Gabon shows the existence of circumstances of a nature to prevent the hearing of such a case, more precisely, of a nature to prevent a judicial follow-up from being given to the objection made by the victim. Furthermore, the Respondent State contented itself with casting doubt on the order and the objection in question but did not give any reason that would justify the fact that this case has been pending for at least nine (9) years before the Gabonese judicial authority. On this point, the Commission concludes that the procedure is unduly prolonged because nothing in the circumstances surrounding the case justifies the time taken and no reason is advanced to justify the time taken to deal with it domestically.

With regard to the second argument supporting the Respondent State's objection of inadmissibility, the latter maintains that the complaint lodged by the Complainant in 2008 before the judge is still under investigation, that there is no time limit provided by the Code of Criminal Procedure for such an investigation and that in criminal matters, the duration of the investigation depends on the complexity of the case.

In seeking whether the procedure is unduly long or not, the Commission will again make its analysis in light of the circumstances surrounding the case and the reasons advanced by the Respondent State to justify the time taken for the procedure.

The Commission notes that the Respondent State submitted in its observations on admissibility, a letter from the examining magistrate of the Court of Major Jurisdiction (Tribunal de Grande Instance) of Libreville of April 2016, indicating that the case is still under investigation but without giving the reason or reasons that justify why, for seven (7) years, the file has still been at this stage. In criminal matters, there are steps that can evidence the diligence shown by the court seized, for example summonses, the hearing of witnesses, the issuing of a summons to appear. However, no reason is advanced by the Respondent State to justify why since 2008, the case is still at the investigation stage. It is true that the search for the truth may take the examining magistrate quite a lot of time depending on the case but it is for the State to prove the necessity of taking so much time or at the very least, to indicate the investigative acts undertaken. Furthermore, from the content of the documents submitted by the parties, the Commission detects no element in the context surrounding the case that would be of a nature to justify such a file being pending since 2008.

From the analysis of the two arguments supporting the objection of inadmissibility raised by the Respondent State, the Commission concludes that the exception to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies prescribed in Article 56(5) of the African Charter is applicable in this case because of the undue prolongation of the domestic procedure.

With regard to Article 56(6) of the African Charter, the Complainant prays the Commission to consider that there is a good reason that justifies his seizure in 2015 and that the time of submission is therefore reasonable.

In contrast, for the Respondent State, the Complainant should have waited for the Gabonese judge to rule on the victim's case and from there, in case of an unfavourable decision he could have appealed or lodged an appeal in cassation. For the Respondent State, the Complainant not having exhausted local remedies, the reasonable time giving the right to seize the Commission could not have begun to run.

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has already indicated that the assessment of the reasonableness of the time is made on a case-by-case basis. Thus, if for example in its decisions on the admissibility of Communications 305/05, Article 19 & others v. Zimbabwe and 310/05: Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Sudan, the Commission respectively considered that seizing it within a period of two years and of two years and five months was not reasonable, this does not mean that in other cases where the complainant took as much or more time, the time would automatically be considered unreasonable by the Commission.

In the present case, it is the undue prolongation of local remedies that has been established. The question is therefore, in such circumstances, from what moment the Complainant should have become aware of the undue prolongation and submitted his Communication as the Commission indicated in its decision on Communication 322/06 Tsatsu Tsikata v. Republic of Ghana.

However, in the present Communication, such a starting point is difficult to establish. Indeed, it emerges from the file that despite several follow-up efforts, the victim could not be informed of the period at which his file would actually be dealt with. Moreover, the Respondent State asserts that the duration of the investigation of a case depends on its complexity and that no provision of the Gabonese Code of Criminal Procedure fixes its time limit, that it "may extend over several years, as long as the sought truth has not sufficiently manifested itself to the judge, who pursues his investigations ...". The Respondent State asserts this without saying how the present case is complex. Moreover, the Respondent State maintains that the Complainant should have waited to appeal or lodge an appeal in cassation before seizing the Commission without indicating when the Complainant would even obtain a decision that could serve as a basis for a possible appeal or appeal in cassation.

It is difficult for a complainant in these circumstances to know when to decide to seize a regional body such as the Commission. The Commission is aware that an undue delay in the administration of justice amounts to a denial of justice; in this case, the Respondent State's assertions give no guarantee as to the chances that the case will be dealt with promptly, on the contrary, they lead one to believe that the handling of the case could last indefinitely.

In view of the foregoing, it would not be judicious to refer the Complainant back to the national courts especially as there is a risk that the Complainant would wait several more years without follow-up to the domestic procedure initiated. In the interest of justice, the Commission cannot in such a case consider that the time for seizure is unreasonable.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission declares the present Communication admissible.

The Complainant alleges the violation of Article 7(1)(d) which provides that "every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard, more particularly in its aspect relating to the right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court". He asserts that the circumstances of the present case show, on the one hand, an absence of reasonable time since, according to him, certain cases concerning him have still not been decided and, on the other hand, that the courts seized are not impartial.

As regards the violation of the right to be tried within a reasonable time, the Complainant supports his allegation by relying on a resolution of the Commission on the right to recourse and fair trial, and a jurisprudence of the Commission developed in the communication Article 19 v. Eritrea to indicate that the circumstances of the Complainant or the victim must be taken into account and that the complexity of the facts cannot justify non-compliance with the reasonable time.

As to the support for his allegation on the violation of the right to be tried by an impartial court, the Complainant invokes the Commission's Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial which specify the meaning of the right to be tried by an impartial court. On the basis of these principles and guidelines, the Complainant notes the criterion for determining the violation of this right, namely the fact that the judge may have a preconceived opinion likely to weigh heavily on his decision or that he is likely to consult a higher authority before rendering his decision.

The Complainant reiterates that it seemed to him that the judges were linked with the highest authorities of the executive power and had a preconceived opinion of the case to his detriment. To support this allegation, he notes the fact that he is still awaiting the deliberation concerning the objection he made on 10 April 2006 before the President of the Court of Libreville and with the Land Registrar to prevent the registration of the fraudulent acquisition of the disputed undivided lands. He adds that he remains without any news of the criminal complaint he lodged with an examining magistrate in 2008 and of the appeal lodged by Counsel NFONE against a civil conviction of the applicant of 04 February 2009. The applicant recalls that, moreover, this conviction at first instance ignores the evidence that the disputed sales were null and void. He also makes it known that the judge who took this decision lived on one of the disputed plots

The Respondent State requests the Commission to reject the ground based on the absence of follow-up given to the Complainant's proceedings before the judge by arguing that this prolongation of the procedure cannot in any way be attributed to the judicial institution. It asserts that the Examining Magistrate of the second Chambers received the Complainant's deposition on 02 July 2008 but that for the following judicial year (2008-2009), the Higher Council of the Judiciary appointed a new examining magistrate who was assigned to this Chambers. It adds that, unfortunately, the latter became aware of the existence of family ties between himself and the parties (that is, all the Migolet heirs) and withdrew from the case by an order of withdrawal of 30 January 2009 in application of Article 79 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The Respondent State finally adds that until 18 February 2009, the last judge was unable to notify the Complainant of this withdrawal for two main reasons, notably the lack of a precise address of the Complainant and of the other heirs, and the lack of follow-up of his file. According to the Respondent State, the Complainant was unable to follow the procedure especially as he cannot produce any reminder letter with acknowledgment of receipt from the Chambers of the examining magistrate given that he had neither retained a lawyer, nor elected domicile with a law firm which could have served as an address for the notification of information relating to his investigation file.

Relying on the Commission's jurisprudence according to which it is necessary to take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the reasons justifying the prolongation of remedies in order to determine whether this prolongation is normal or abnormal, the Respondent State finally requests the Commission to consider that the prolongation of this procedure is justified. On the ground based on the absence of follow-up given to the Complainant's proceedings before the civil judge a) On the application of 20 March 2006 (received on 27/03/06) and concerning an objection to the sale carried out by Madame RELONGOUE Lydie

While noting the absence of an acknowledgment of receipt and of the registration number, the Respondent State argues that the Complainant never filed an application in objection to the sale with the registry. According to it, the objection relied on by the Complainant bears a stamp that includes neither the seal of the Gabonese Republic, nor the indication of the date and the registration number, nor of the registry that received the application as required by Article 409 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It reiterates, consequently, that the Complainant's right to a fair trial was not violated in this respect especially as he never exercised his right to bring proceedings (droit d'estre en justice). b) On the application received at the civil registry on 10/04/06 under number 395/05/06

While asserting that it did receive and register at the Registry of the Court of Major Jurisdiction of Libreville this application for interim relief by the Complainant concerning the retraction and the safekeeping of the sums unduly received, the Respondent State questions the participation in the conduct of the proceedings. It stresses, indeed, that the Complainant did not provide proof of the return of the summons to the Registry by himself or by the bailiff he mandated for this purpose so that his case would be entered on the roll. It insists that, ultimately, no decision could be rendered since the judge had not been seized. According to the Respondent State, the Complainant did not follow up his files.

As to the Complainant's allegation that the magistrates "organized a cabal against him", the Respondent State wonders how one could justify that in another proceeding brought by the Complainant in the same period, the Court granted his request for expert appraisal.
In his reply observations, the Complainant considers that the Respondent State's arguments are not well founded.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State's ground that the prolongation of the procedure would be due to the absence of an address and to negligence of the applicant in following the procedure does not hold. According to him, a litigant's lack of diligence is sanctioned either by striking the case off the list or by the lapse of the proceedings and the Government was unable to provide a copy of any of these acts.

The Complainant insists, moreover, that there are mandatory formalities that every complaint must contain, in particular the formalities of identification and address. He reiterates that for this reason, his complaint did indeed include his identification as required. He adds that, on the other hand, an examining magistrate, by law, has at his disposal all forms of communication and official means (Police and Gendarmerie) to follow up on a procedure.

On the Respondent State's ground that the stamp on the application of 20 March 2006 bears neither seal, nor indication of the date and the registration number, nor of the registry that received this application, the Complainant replies that "the President of the Court can be reached in two ways: directly through his private secretariat, as was the case with this letter; or indirectly through the Civil Registry". According to him, this application should not include a registration number or an acknowledgment of receipt by the Civil Registry because it was neither the addressee nor the recipient. He reiterates that this in no way detracts from the regularity and validity of the procedure. On the application received at the civil registry on 10 April 2006 under number 395/05/ 06

The Complainant states that he does not understand the Respondent State's argument of a possible absence of return of the summons because according to him, if the application was registered, it is because the summons was entered on the roll otherwise the application would not have been registered. Moreover, he says it is difficult for him to understand how the State would question the entering of the summons on the roll. According to him, if for the sake of argument it were admitted that the summons had not been entered on the roll, the Respondent State would not question this fact, rather it would proclaim it with supporting evidence since as a State, it has all the means to know what happens in its courts.

Article 7(1)(d) protects the right to a fair trial in these terms: Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: [...] (d) The right to be tried within a reasonable time by an impartial court or tribunal. In the case under analysis, the applicant considers that this right was violated in two respects, that of the absence of reasonable time and that of an absence of impartiality of the courts seized. The Commission proposes to analyze each of these two aspects in relation to the circumstances of the case in order to be able to determine whether there was a violation of the right to a fair trial.

The notion of the right to be tried within a reasonable time calls for an understanding of the notion of "reasonable time". Unfortunately, the Charter does not give its definition. In the absence of this definition in the Charter, the Commission first notes that this expression contains a juxtaposition of two terms: that of "time" and that of "reasonable". The first refers to an interval of time during which an action occurs; and in the context of judicial proceedings, an interval of time in which a trial, a judgment takes place. As for the second term, the adjective "reasonable", it can be defined as what is logical and satisfactory. It follows that the term "reasonable time" as intended by the Charter refers to an interval of time that is neither surprisingly long nor abusively short. In other words, the Charter wants the duration of the trial to be of an acceptable length or not excessively long.

That said, the question that arises is how to determine the maximum length of this time. In other words, what is the length of a reasonable time? As the Commission has already indicated in its jurisprudence, the question of what is reasonable cannot be expressed in terms of an overall time limit that applies to all cases, but must rather depend on the circumstances. This question was developed by the European Court of Human Rights which established the criteria for assessing the reasonableness of time, namely the complexity of the case, the conduct of the applicant, the conduct of the judicial authorities and what is at stake in the dispute.

In its General Comment No. 32, the United Nations Human Rights Committee also stressed the importance of the speed of proceedings as a guarantee of a fair trial. In its commentary, this Committee returned to the elements for assessing the reasonable time in a civil trial. According to it, delays that are justified neither by the complexity of the case nor by the conduct of the parties undermine the principle of a fair trial enshrined in the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

In its General Comment on Article 14 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the Human Rights Committee indicated that impartiality is analyzed in two aspects in the following terms: "First, judges must not allow their judgement to be influenced by personal bias or prejudice, nor harbour preconceptions about the particular case before them, nor act in ways that improperly promote the interests of one of the parties to the detriment of the other. Second, the tribunal must also appear to a reasonable observer to be impartial. For instance, a trial substantially affected by the participation of a judge who, under domestic statutes, should have been disqualified cannot normally be considered to be impartial." Thus, according to the Human Rights Committee, impartiality concerns both the judges and the tribunal in general.

It is along these same lines that the European Court of Human Rights has stressed that impartiality must be assessed in two ways: according to a subjective approach and an objective approach. Whereas the first takes into account the "personal conviction and the behaviour of a particular judge, that is, whether the judge held any personal prejudice or bias in a given case", the second consists in determining whether, "quite apart from the judge's personal conduct, the tribunal itself and, among other aspects, its composition, offered sufficient guarantees to exclude any legitimate doubt in respect of its impartiality".

In the case of Denisov v. Ukraine, this same Court noted that impartiality is defined by the absence of prejudice or bias. The impartiality of the Tribunal is a fundamental guarantee. Indeed, access to the tribunal would have no meaning if the latter is not impartial. Moreover, the impartiality of the Tribunal constitutes a very reflection of democracy, the two notions being consubstantial. The impartiality of judges is the fundamental condition of the confidence which courts must inspire in a democratic society. It is incumbent on the States Parties to the Charter to arrange their judicial system in such a way as to enable it to meet the requirements of impartiality intended by the provisions of Article 7(1)(d).

It emerges from the Complainant's arguments that, according to him, the absence of reasonable time would be due to an absence of impartiality of the courts he seized. The Commission notes that the Complainant has not provided sufficient evidence or elements to deduce that the judges were personally linked with the high authorities of the Executive Power with a preconceived opinion of his case as the complainant senses. Indeed, the latter merely gives examples of applications for which he waited a long time for their deliberation. It is this long wait for deliberation that creates in him a presumption that the judges had preconceived ideas. In the eyes of the Commission, this is not sufficient to conclude the absence of impartiality. In particular, not only does the Complainant not establish the existence of preconceived opinions among the judges, but he also does not define the causal link between the unreasonable delays and a particular behaviour of the judges. The Commission rather proposes to analyze these examples on a case-by-case basis to determine whether their delays are not reasonable within the meaning of Article 7(1)(d) of the Charter in order finally to establish the causes of these delays if any.

In the case under analysis, the Respondent State maintains that the prolongation of the procedure would be due mainly to the absence of an address and to negligence of the applicant in following the procedure. As the Commission indicated above, the conduct of the complainant may diminish, or even exclude, State responsibility. It is then for the Commission to analyze the scope of the facts attributable to the complainant as to their impact on the time of the aforementioned trial. Indeed, the Respondent State maintains that all the investigating magistrates who succeeded one another in this case did not complete the investigation for lack of an address of the Complainant.

The Commission finds it hard to conceive that a judicial body would have received a complaint that contains no address of the Complainant. Indeed, the minimum elements that a judicial body must consider in order to register a complaint is the identification of the parties which includes their address. A judicial body that failed to retain the address of the parties upon registration of the complaint would expose itself to the risk of violating the right to a fair trial. In fact, in the absence of an address, it would be difficult for it to guarantee the right to a fair trial as to its requirement that the parties must be informed of the elements of the trial and the different stages of the procedure.

The States Parties to the Charter have the obligation to guarantee this right by putting in place the legislative measures necessary to give effect to the various aspects of the right to have one's cause heard. In other words, States must ensure that all obstacles to the proper conduct of the trial are circumvented. In particular, as the Commission indicated in the Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, States must ensure that access to judicial services is not impeded, among other things, by the absence of assistance to understand the procedures and complete the formalities. The administration of justice must be organized so as to enable the court to contact litigants whenever necessary.

As for the Respondent State's argument that the Complainant had not retained a lawyer or a Law Firm which could have served as an address, the Commission considers that it is not relevant. Indeed, the Commission shares the Complainant's view that it would be contrary to the right of every person to have access to a Court to require litigants to have a lawyer. This would rather make justice inaccessible and selective because it would be expensive.
