République Démocratique du Congo que pour être qualifiés de torture, les actes perpétrés doivent non seulement être des peines ou souffrances sévères, mais surtout causées par ou à l'instigation d'une autorité publique, avec le but de punir ou d'obtenir une information ou un aveu, lesdites peines ou souffrances pouvant être physiques ou mentales.

Par ailleurs, le Comité des droits de l'homme a constamment reconnu dans sa jurisprudence que « l'angoisse et la détresse que la disparition [...] a causées à toute sa famille proche » est constitutive d'une violation de l'article 7 du Pacte sur les droits civils et politiques à l'endroit des proches de la victime. Dans Chitay Nech et al.C/Guatemala, la Cour interaméricaine a également estimé que la souffrance, l'angoisse des proches de la victime d'une violation grave des droits de l'homme emporte violation de leur droit à l'intégrité.

En l'espèce les Plaignants soumettent que M. Jackson Ndikuriyo a été victime d'une exécution extrajudiciaire le 25 aout 2010 ce qui représente une atteinte irrémédiable à sa vie et son intégrité physique et psychologique. De plus sa dépouille a été abandonnée sur place durant toute une nuit et n'a pas été remise à sa famille pour qu'elle puisse l'enterrer dignement ; niant ainsi son essence humaine ce qui implique une violation de sa personnalité juridique. Ils ajoutent que la famille de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo et la victime collatérale des 2actes de tortures et d'intimidations subis par ce dernier. En effet, les multiples intimidations ayant conduit la victime à se réfugier dans la clandestinité ont causé une angoisse et une crainte pour sa famille qui s'inquiétait pour la sécurité de la victime mais aussi pour sa propre sécurité car redoutant d'éventuelles représailles de la part des personnes qui en avaient après M. Jackson Ndikuriyo. Enfin la mort brutale de la victime a créé une détresse émotionnelle ayant un impact négatif sur les membres de sa famille

A l'analyse des faits, Il est clairement établi que les menaces de mort de plus en plus pressante à son endroit, ainsi que les divers actes de harcèlement et d'intimidations ont généré une détresse émotionnelle qui ont poussé la victime à vivre dans la clandestinité car craignant pour sa vie. Dans International PEN, Constitutional Rights Project, Civil Liberties Organisation and Interights (on behalf of Ken Saro-Wiwa Jnr.) / Nigeria, la Commission a considéré que l'article 5 interdit non seulement la torture, mais aussi les traitements cruels, inhumains ou dégradants. Cela comprend non seulement les actes qui causent de graves souffrances physiques ou psychologiques, mais aussi ceux qui humilient l'individu ou le force à agir contre sa volonté ou sa conscience.

Il ne peut être valablement soutenu que vivre dans la clandestinité est un choix que l'on fait de gaieté de cœur et il ne peut en aucun cas être considéré que cet état de fait n'a aucune incidence sur la condition physique et psychologique de la personne qui en fait l'expérience. En effet, la peur et l'angoisse induites par les actes d'intimidations peuvent être considérées comme une torture mentale.

Par ailleurs, lorsque l'on considère les menaces à peine voilées, proférées par les autorités à l'endroit de la famille de la victime, notamment par le Directeur Général de la Police qui avait déclaré à la radio que le corps ne serait pas rendu à la famille et que la victime « n'avait eu que ce qu'elle méritait », couplé au refus d'autoriser la famille d'organiser un enterrement décent à la victime, le constat de traitement inhumain et dégradant à l'égard de la victime et sa famille est difficilement contestable.

Dans son Observation générale n° 4 concernant le droit à la réparation pour les victimes de torture et autres peines ou traitements cruels, inhumains ou dégradants, la Commission précise qu'une personne est considérée comme une victime indépendamment du fait que l'auteur de la violation soit ou non identifié, arrêté, poursuivi ou condamné et quels que soient les liens de parenté entre l'auteur et la victime. Le terme « victime » s'entend également des membres de la famille proche ou des personnes à charge de la victime directe et des personnes qui, en intervenant pour venir en aide à une victime ou pour empêcher qu'elle ne devienne victime, ont subi un préjudice.

S'agissant de la dignité de la personne humaine ce n'est pas seulement un droit fondamental en soi, mais il constitue la base même des droits fondamentaux. C'est au vu de l'importance capitale qu'elle revêt que le Préambule de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme de 1948 débute en ces termes «considérant que la reconnaissance de la dignité inhérente à tous les membres de la famille humaine et de leurs droits égaux et inaliénables constitue le fondement de la liberté, de la justice et de la paix dans le monde ». Ceci suppose donc que tout acte susceptible de nuire à la dignité humaine constitue une violation des droits fondamentaux de la personne humaine, ainsi le harcèlement moral, la discrimination, la diffamation, la dénonciation calomnieuse, les injures peuvent être considérées comme étant des actes qui portent atteinte à la dignité de la personne humaine.

Or l'anonymat, l'absence de sépulture ou l'impossibilité d'accéder au lieu d'inhumation pour la famille, posent la question de l'accompagnement des morts. En Afrique, particulièrement, enterrer son mort c'est l'honorer, cela fait partie des rites les plus importants de la vie et le respect des morts et de l'ordre du sacré. Denier le droit d'enterrer dignement un proche, c'est comme renier l'essence humaine et dénigrer la valeur de ce dernier et ce qu'il représente pour sa famille. Ceci peut également constituer une insulte et une souffrance morale pour la famille.

En refusant de rendre le corps du défunt à sa famille à dessein, les représentants de l'Etat ont violé le respect à la dignité humaine qui dans la culture africaine s'applique également aux morts. Par ailleurs, le caractère volontaire de cet acte démontre la détermination manifeste des représentants de l'Etat de blesser la famille et porter atteinte à son honneur et à celle du défunt, sachant l'importance que les rites d'enterrement et de deuil occupent dans nos sociétés africaines.

De ce qui précède, il est clairement établi que des actes de torture morale ont été perpétrés à l'encontre de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo et de sa famille. Il apparaît également qu'une violation manifeste de la dignité inhérente à chaque être humain a été commise. La Commission considère donc que l'Etat défendeur a failli à ses obligations en vertu de l'article 5 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples et constate la violation de cet article.

L'article 6 de la Charte africaine dispose que « tout individu a droit à la liberté et à la sécurité de sa personne. Nul ne peut être privé de sa liberté sauf pour des motifs et dans des conditions préalablement déterminées par la loi ; en particulier nul ne peut être arrêté ou détenu arbitrairement ».

La Commission a établi dans Sudan Human Rights Organisation & Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) c. Sudan que la liberté individuelle est une condition fondamentale dont chacun peut généralement jouir. En être privé est un fait qui semble avoir un effet direct et indésirable sur la jouissance de plusieurs autres droits, y compris le droit à la vie et à une famille.

En l'espèce la violation de l'article 6 porte principalement sur l'incapacité de l'Etat à assurer la sécurité de la personne de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo, qui a subi plusieurs atteintes à sa liberté et sa sécurité, et fait l'objet d'intenses menaces par des agents de l'Etat, qui l'ont contraint à vivre dans la clandestinité car craignant pour sa vie. Il a également fait l'objet de deux arrestations l'une en 2009 et la seconde en 2010 qui s'est soldée par son décès. Les circonstances précédemment citées, ont entraîné peur et angoisse couplée à une insécurité physique et psychique, à l'endroit de la victime, causant indubitablement une violation à son droit à la sécurité de sa personne.

L'incapacité de l'Etat à protéger la victime alors qu'elle était sous sa protection peut constituer une circonstance aggravante car ayant conduit à une situation irrémédiable c'est-à-dire la mort de la victime. Ceci est d'autant plus criant lorsque l'on constate que M. Jackson Ndikuriyo a été la seule victime de la supposée embuscade.

En effet, l'Etat est le premier garant de la sécurité des personnes sous sa responsabilité, particulièrement lorsque ces personnes ne peuvent pas assurer leur propre protection. La Commission l'a d'ailleurs bien établie dans Zimbabwe Human Rights NGO Forum c. Zimbabwe, lorsqu'elle a conclu qu'un acte imputable à un tiers peut bien induire la responsabilité de l'Etat lorsque ce dernier n'a pu prévenir la survenance de la violation (...).

Ainsi, en n'agissant pas conformément au principe de précaution qui exige de prendre toutes les mesures nécessaires pour assurer la protection de la victime qui était déjà vulnérable, l'Etat s'est rendu complice sinon responsable des actes de restrictions de la liberté de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo ainsi que des atteintes à son intégrité physique ayant résulté à sa mort.

Les Lignes directrices sur les conditions d'arrestation, de garde à vue et de détention provisoire en Afrique (Lignes directrices de Luanda) définissent le terme « arrestation » comme l'acte qui consiste à appréhender une personne du chef d'une prétendue infraction, ou du fait d'une autorité compétente pour arrêter et détenir une personne telle que la loi l'y autorise. Elles précisent en outre que tout individu a droit à la liberté et à la sécurité de sa personne. La détention doit toujours être une mesure exceptionnelle de dernier recours. Nul ne peut être l'objet d'arrestations ou de détentions arbitraires ou illégales.

Dans son Observation générale n° 35 sur l'article 9 (Liberté et sécurité de la personne) du Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques, le Comité des droits de l'homme a établi que la sécurité de la personne vise la protection contre les atteintes corporelles et psychologiques, ou l'intégrité corporelle et mentale. Il a également estimé que la privation de liberté représente une restriction plus sévère à la circulation (...).

Si dans Abdel Hadi, Ali Radi & Autres c. République du Soudan, la Commission a reconnu que la privation de liberté est l'une des formes légitimes de contrôle de l'État sur les personnes relevant de sa juridiction. Elle a cependant précisé que, toute arrestation ou détention devait être effectuée conformément à la procédure établie par le droit interne, faute de quoi une telle arrestation serait considérée comme arbitraire. Dans le cas de la première arrestation de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo aucune inculpation n'a été faite à son encontre, cet état de fait a fragiliser ce dernier et les intimidations qui ont suivi l'ont forcé à entrer en clandestinité en car craignant pour sa vie. Il peut donc être conclu que cette arrestation était arbitraire.
Par conséquent, la Commission constate que l'Etat violé les principes de l'article 6.

L'article 7(1) (a) de la Charte africaine dispose que « toute personne a droit à ce que sa cause soit entendue. Ce droit comprend, le droit de saisir les juridictions nationales compétentes de tout acte violant les droits fondamentaux qui lui sont reconnus et garantis par les conventions, les lois, règlements et coutumes en vigueur (...) »

L'article 26 quant à lui fait obligation aux Etats de « garantir l'indépendance des Tribunaux et de permettre l'établissement et le perfectionnement d'institutions nationales appropriées chargées de la promotion et de la protection des droits et libertés garantis par la Charte. »

Comme souligner par les Plaintants dans leurs soumissions, la violation des articles 7(1) (a) et 26 de la Charte africaine peut être constatée dans des situations où l'impartialité des tribunaux n'est pas garantie notamment en raison de la nomination des juges par les autorités gouvernementales et politiques.

Par ailleurs l'analyse de sa jurisprudence fournit des exemples d'obstacles pouvant empêcher l'accès des victimes aux tribunaux et/ou la partialité des tribunaux. Nonobstant cet état de fait, il revient à la Commission d'établir à lumière des faits et arguments qui lui sont soumis si dans le cas d'espèce la même conclusion peut s'appliquer.
La Commission va dans un premier temps procéder à l'analyse des faits pour déterminer s'il y a eu violation de l'article 7 (1) (a) et ensuite se pencher sur la violation alléguée de l'article 26.

Concernant la violation de l'article 7(1) (a) ; le droit de voir sa cause entendue suppose que les mesures nécessaires à la résolution du préjudice subit soient concrètement mises en œuvre en vue de rétablir la victime dans son droit. Dans le cas d'espèce, hormis l'ouverture d'un dossier par le Ministère public suite à l'arrestation de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo en 2009, aucune autre action n'a été menée. Force est de conclure que la cause n'a pas été entendue malgré les démarches initiées. Les arguments des Plaintants soumis à cet égard en soutien de la recevabilité de la présente communication le démontre clairement.

Ensuite, sur la base de la jurisprudence établie par le Comité contre la torture des Nations Unies, l'Etat a l'obligation d'enquêter dans des cas de graves violations des droits de l'homme telle que la torture. Par ailleurs, dans son observation générale sur le droit à la vie, la Commission recommande aux États d'adopter des mesures aussi bien pour prévenir les privations arbitraires de la vie que de mener des enquêtes rapides, impartiales, approfondies et transparentes sur toute privation de ce type ayant pu se produire, en amenant les responsables à répondre de leurs actes (...). De ce fait une violation avérée du droit à la vie, devrait pouvoir faire l'objet de la même obligation et partant la diligence de la justice prévaloir. Cette diligence pourrait se traduire par une protection adéquate donnée à la victime et la célérité de l'enquête sur les causes de son décès, mais surtout dans la recherche des responsables de son exécution extrajudiciaire pour laquelle aucune poursuite n'a été entamée.

Dans l'affaire Association of Victims of Post Electoral Violence et Interights c. Cameroun, la Commission met un accent particulier sur l'obligation de l'Etat de « mener des investigations » et de « prendre des mesures conséquentes » pour empêcher la violation mais également y remédier. L'obligation d'enquêter et de poursuivre est réitérée dans Sudan Human Rights Organisation et Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) c. Soudan, où la Commission a conclu que l'absence d'enquête dans les cas d'exécutions arbitraires et extrajudiciaires équivaut à une violation du droit à la vie.

En l'espèce, les Plaintants ont soumis que l'Avocat de la victime Me Nyamoya a été arrêté pour avoir dénoncer les faits survenus à la victime, et que les policiers qui comme la victime, revendiquaient activement leurs droits ont également été mis en prison. Par ailleurs toute personne s'intéressant de près ou de loin à cette affaire a fait l'objet de menace, c'est le cas notamment du Président de l'APRODH qui a reçu des menaces directes du Ministre de l'intérieur lui défendant de continuer à parler du dossier de la victime. Il est donc clairement établie que tout a été mis en œuvre pour que la cause de la victime ne soit pas entendue.
Suite à l'analyse des arguments des Plaintants à l'aune de la jurisprudence établie, la Commission conclut à une violation des dispositions de l'article 7(1) (a) de la Charte

Concernant la violation alléguée de l'article 26, relatif à l'exigence d'indépendance des tribunaux il convient de l'analyser en combinaison avec l'article 7(1) (d), qui se rapporte au principe d'impartialité prévue à l'article 7 1(d) de la Charte africaine, même si ce dernier n'a guère été évoqué par les Plaintants, la Commission estime qu'il est nécessaire de l'associer à l'analyse présente. Ainsi, si parfois on désigne la nécessaire impartialité du juge sous le vocable « indépendance », L'impartialité se rapproche beaucoup plus de l'indépendance personnelle du magistrat par opposition à l'indépendance collective de la magistrature. L'indépendance se ramène à un « statut » et l'impartialité à un « état d'esprit ».

Dans ses Directives et principes sur le droit à un procès équitable et à l'assistance judiciaire en Afrique, la Commission va dans le même sens en indiquant que la garantie d'un procès équitable, suppose l'existence d'une instance juridictionnelle indépendante et impartiale.Ceci suppose que l'indépendance des instances juridictionnelles et celles des juges doit être garantie par la constitution et les lois du pays et créée par la loi pour rendre des décisions au sujet de questions respectée de tous ; gouvernement, institutions et autorités. Par ailleurs, les magistrats se doivent de régler les affaires dont ils sont saisis sans restrictions et sans être l'objet d'influences, incitations, pressions, menaces ou interventions indues, directes ou indirectes, de la part de qui que ce soit ou pour quelque raison que ce soit, pour en garantir son impartialité.

En l'espèce, les Plaintants font valoir que des nombreux cas de violations flagrantes des droits de l'homme impliquant des agents de l'Etat y compris des actes de tortures ou des atteintes à la vie, ne font pas l'objet d'un suivi rigoureux de la part de la justice et dans les rares cas ayant abouti, les peines ou les dédommagement des victimes sont insignifiants au vu des préjudices subis.Ils ont également évoqué l'absence d'indépendance du système judiciaire vis-à-vis du pouvoir exécutif, ce qui représente un obstacle majeur à la lutte contre l'impunité.

Si dans sa décision Organisation Mondiale Contre la Torture et Ligue de la Zone Afrique pour la Défense des Droits des Enfants et Elèves (pour le compte de Céline) c. République Démocratique du Congo, la Commission avait estimé que le seul défaut d'efficacité des procédures concernées ne peuvent suffire à établir le manque d'indépendance des tribunaux qui suppose nécessairement des éléments d'interférence extérieure, particulièrement en l'absence de preuves soutenant cette allégation, dans le cas présent, les conclusions des Etats généraux de la justice burundaise tenues du 5 au 9 aout 2013 ont mis en exergue, la nécessité de reformer le système pour en assurer son indépendance, notamment vis-à-vis de l'exécutif, sujet de préoccupation central durant les discussions.

S'agissant de l'impunité généralisée au Burundi notamment sur les questions d'exécutions extrajudiciaire, la Commission d'enquête des Nations Unies sur le Burundi a dans son rapport de 2017 a relevé de longs délais dans les procédures judiciaires, l'organisation de certains procès sensibles dans l'enceinte de prisons, avec un effet dissuasif sur la présence d'observateurs, ainsi que des procès expéditifs en application de la procédure de « flagrance». Elle a également souligné le manque d'indépendance du système judiciaire observé de longue date au Burundi a aggravé l'impunité régnant dans le pays. Les cas d'impunité au Burundi, particulièrement en ce qui concerne les exécutions extrajudiciaires ont été rapportées par plusieurs rapports d'ONG internationales y compris par les Nations Unies
Sur cette base l'indépendance de la justice peut donc être questionnée. La Commission est donc d'avis qu'il y a violation de l'article 26 de la Charte.

Sur la base des dispositions de l'article 9(2) de la Charte africaine dispose que, « toute personne a le droit d'exprimer et de diffuser ses opinions dans le cadre des lois et règlements ». Les Plaintants soumettent que la liberté d'opinion, a été définie par la Commission comme « un droit humain fondamental, essentiel au développement personnel d'un individu et à sa conscience politique » et vitale » pour sa participation effective à la conduite des affaires publiques de son pays ». Ainsi, elle est érigée en fondement inhérent à toute société démocratique. Ils ajoutent que la Commission a rappelé à cet égard que l'exercice légitime des droits de l'homme ne pose aucun problème pour un Etat démocratique régi par la primauté du droit »
Ils soutiennent également que la protection de la liberté d'opinion politique à travers l'article 9 de la Charte africaine a été confirmée par la jurisprudence de la Commission africaine.

Le Principe n°2 portant sur la non-ingérence dans la Liberté d'opinion des Principes généraux contenue dans la Déclaration de Principes sur la Liberté d'Expression et l'Accès à l'Information en Afrique de 2019, dispose que La liberté d'opinion, notamment le droit de se forger et de changer toute sorte d'opinion, à tout moment et pour quelque raison que ce soit, est un droit humain fondamental et inaliénable et un élément indispensable à l'exercice de la liberté d'expression. Les États n'interfèrent pas dans la liberté d'opinion de quiconque.

Dans la précédente Déclaration sur la Liberté d'Expression en Afrique de 2002 de la Commission, il est expressément demandé aux Etats de s'assurer que les lois relatives à la diffamation ne permettent pas de punir des personnes pour des déclarations exactes, des opinions ou des déclarations concernant des personnalités très connues qu'il était raisonnable de faire dans les circonstances et que les personnalités publiques doivent tolérer beaucoup plus de critiques.

Dans son Observation Général n°34 de l'article 19 du Pacte international relatif aux droits civils et politiques sur la liberté d'opinion et liberté d'expression. Le Comité sur les droits de l'homme à considérer qu'ériger en infraction pénale le fait d'avoir une opinion est incompatible avec le paragraphe 1 de l'article 19. Le harcèlement, l'intimidation ou la stigmatisation, y compris l'arrestation, la détention, le jugement ou l'emprisonnement, en raison des opinions que la personne peut professer constitue une violation du paragraphe 1 de l'article 19.
L'Observation indique également que toute forme de tentative de coercion visant à obtenir de quelqu'un qu'il ait ou qu'il n'ait pas une opinion est interdite.

De ce fait la détention du policier Jackson Ndikuriyo sans inculpation en décembre 2009 après qu'il ait publiquement soutenu que la corruption sévit au sein de la Police, ainsi que les intimidations et harcèlement dont il a fait l'objet y compris son exécution extrajudiciaire, peuvent raisonnablement être considérés comme étant les conséquences de l'exercice de sa liberté d'expression.

En effet comme soumis par les Plaintants, les intimidations et autres menaces à l'encontre de la victime n'avaient pour unique but que de faire taire M. Jackson Ndikuriyo. Or s'il est admis que le droit d'avoir une opinion et de l'exprimé est garanti par la Charte africaine, restreindre l'exercice de ce droit par quelques moyens que ce soit peut-être raisonnable considérée comme une violation de l'article 9(2) de ladite Charte.
En conclusion de l'analyse des faits et des divers textes juridiques pertinents sur la question, la Commission considère qu'il y a eu violation de l'article 9(2).

Les Plaintants soumettent que les droits de la famille de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo ont été violés, du fait de son exécution extrajudiciaire mais également des faits de tortures, actes d'intimidations et de harcèlements dont il a fait l'objet.

L'article 18(1) de la Charte africaine consacre la famille comme étant l'élément naturel et la base de la société et par conséquent elle doit être protégée par l'Etat qui veille à sa santé physique et morale.

La Commission a clairement énoncé que la séparation des membres d'une famille constitue une violation au droit contenu à l'article 18(1), elle a également rappelé que l'Etat a une obligation positive à l'égard de la famille, qu'il se doit d'assister dans la satisfaction de ses besoins et de ses intérêts et de protéger cette même institution des abus de toute sorte par ses propres agents et organes et par des parties tierces. Dans l'exercice de ses obligations positives, l'État exerce une obligation négative qui est celle d'empêcher la survenance de tout acte visant à violer les droits ainsi consacrés.

La Déclaration des principes fondamentaux de justice relatifs aux victimes de la criminalité et aux victimes d'abus de pouvoir, adoptée par l'Assemblée générale dans sa résolution 40/34 du 29 novembre 1985, considère comme "victimes" des personnes qui, individuellement ou collectivement, ont subi un préjudice, notamment une atteinte à leur intégrité physique ou mentale, une souffrance morale, une perte matérielle, ou une atteinte grave à leurs droits fondamentaux, en raison d'actes ou d'omissions qui enfreignent les lois pénales en vigueur dans un Etat Membre. Il peut s'agir de la famille proche ou des personnes à la charge de la victime directe.

Au-delà des dispositions contenues dans la Charte africaine il est unanimement accepté que la famille constitue le socle de la société, particulièrement en Afrique où elle revêt un caractère sacré. Ainsi, assurer la protection de la famille c'est préserver l'équilibre de la nation. Il est donc primordial de s'assurer que cette protection se fasse selon les normes établies.

Dans le cas d'espèce, la famille de M. Jackson Ndikuriyo a souffert des actes de torture morale, traitement inhumains et dégradants, des intimidations et du harcèlement subi par la victime qui l'ont également affectée. Ensuite, elle a subi l'angoisse et la détresse émotionnelle causée par son décès. A cela s'ajoute les inquiétudes pour sa sécurité physique mais aussi économique avec la mort de la victime qui subvenait aux besoins de la famille. De plus, ses enfants se sont retrouvés orphelins, privé de l'un de leurs parents. Ceci peut constituer une violation de l'article 18(3) de la Charte africaine des droits et du bien-être de l'enfant africain, qui dispose qu'aucun enfant ne peut être privé de son entretien en raison du statut marital de ses parents. La mère de ses enfants étant désormais veuve, l'entretien et l'avenir de ces derniers est désormais incertain avec la perte de celui qui assurait la sécurité financière.

Il convient maintenant d'analyser si l'Etat a failli ou non à son obligation positive envers la famille. L'obligation positive suppose le respect d'une obligation négative par l'Etat qui consiste à s'assurer qu'il n'y a pas de violation des droits et des intérêts de la famille. La sécurité, physique et morale de la famille implique la protection des droits sociaux économiques pour sa réalisation. Le décès de la victime a brisé l'unité de la famille que l'Etat se doit de protéger en vertu des dispositions de l'article 18(1) de la Charte.

Au vu de ce qui précède il ne fait aucun doute que l'Etat n'a pas été capable de protéger la vie de la victime causant une perte irrémissible pour sa famille mais a également brisé l'unité de celle-ci. La Commission constate donc la violation effective de l'article 18(1) par l'Etat défendeur.

L'article 1 de la Charte africaine impose aux Etats parties à la Charte africaine de reconnaître les droits qui y sont garantis et d'adopter des mesures législatives et autres pour donner effet à ces droits, devoirs et libertés.

La jurisprudence de la Commission a établi que toute violation de l'une des dispositions de la Charte africaine, entraîne automatiquement la violation de l'article 1 En d'autres termes, si un Etat partie n'assure pas le respect des droits contenus dans la Charte africaine, cela constitue une violation de la Charte africaine.

À cet égard, et après avoir constaté que l'État défendeur a violé plusieurs articles de la Charte africaine, à savoir les articles 2, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) (a) lu conjointement avec 26, 9(2) et 18(1), la Commission conclut que l'État défendeur a violé l'article 1 de la Charte africaine.

En outre, cette responsabilité est automatiquement engagée dès qu'il est conclu à la violation d'un droit protégé par la Charte. Au vu de tout ce qui précède, la Commission conclut à une violation des dispositions de l'article 1. La Commission,Par ces motifs,
Dit que la République du Burundi a violé les dispositions des articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) (a) lu conjointement avec 26, 9(2) et 18(1) de la Charte.

En conséquence : i. Demande à la République du Burundi de mener une enquête approfondie par le biais des organes judiciaires indépendantes sur l'exécution de la victime et les autres violations subies ; ii. De mettre en place des mécanismes pour lutter contre l'impunité généralisée en matière d'exécution extrajudiciaire et d'atteintes au droit à la vie ; iii. Demande en outre à la République du Burundi d'accorder aux ayants droits de la Victime une réparation adéquate et suffisante ainsi que l'assistance médicale et psychologique nécessaire, s'il y a toujours lieu ; iv. S'assurer de la pleine application de la Loi n°1/04 du 27 juin 2016 portant protection des victimes, des témoins et d'autres personnes en situation de risque ; v. Demande à la République du Burundi d'adopter toutes les mesures nécessaires pour que de tels faits ne se reproduisent pas et s'assurer que la loi sur les partis politiques respecte les principes démocratiques et le pluralisme politique ; vi. Demande enfin à la République du Burundi de lui rapporter par écrit, dans les cent quatre-vingt jours (180) jours de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée lors de la 72 Session ordinaire privée de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples tenue virtuellement du 19 juillet au 2 août 2022

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received on 9 June 2014 a Communication submitted by the Association of Christians for the Abolition of Torture (ACAT-Burundi), the Association for the Protection of Human Rights and Detained Persons (APRODH), the Forum for Conscience and Development (FOCODE), the Forum for the Strengthening of Civil Society (FORSC) and Track International(TRIAL) hereinafter referred to as "the Complainants" on behalf of the late Jackson Ndikuriyo hereinafter referred to as the "victim" and his family hereinafter referred to as the "victim's family".

The Complaint was submitted against the Republic of Burundi (hereinafter referred to as Respondent State or Burundi), a State that ratified the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) on 28 July 1989.

The Complainants indicate that the victim, Jackson Ndikuriyo, was a Burundian citizen, born in 1985, that he was married and the father of three children. The Complainants add that he was a police officer at the Citiboke brigade in Burundi, that he had been placed in detention without charge in December 2009 after publicly maintaining that corruption was rife within the Police.

They report that after his release in January 2010, the victim continued to demand from his superiors the payment of the allowances that had been promised to them and that this insistence was at the origin of his dismissal in August 2010. They report that, considering that he had been the victim of wrongful dismissal, the victim had recourse to the services of a lawyer to assert his rights.

The Complainants report that since his dismissal, the victim continually faced acts of intimidation and threats including death threats to the point that he had been forced to live in hiding. They further inform that the victim had confided to his lawyer, Maître Nyamoya, that the acts of intimidation were orchestrated by the then Deputy Director General of the police.

The Complainants report that on 26 August 2010, while the victim was going to the town centre in the company of Mr Sévérin Misago to meet a friend, they were arrested, bound and violently beaten with sticks by police officers. They specify that the police officers then informed Commissioner Mr Rémegie Nzeyimana who went to the place of the arrest and took the victim and Mr Sévérin Misago on board.

The Complainants continue by indicating that Mr Sévérin Misago was taken to the police station whereas the victim was held in the Commissioner's vehicle in the company of other police officers; they report that Mr Sévérin Misago heard gunshots some time after having been taken to the police station and that he then saw a police officer with the victim's shoes.

The Complainants report that the day after his arrest, the victim's body was found not far from the Police Station. They explain that the Commissioner in a public statement asserted that it was during an ambush set against the police that the victim accidentally met his death.

The Complainants explain that the victim's family went to the place where the body was but turned back at the sight of the many police officers and Imbonerakure (youths who, according to the Complainants, are affiliated with the majority party CNDD-FDD and are accused of having committed numerous abuses) who were guarding the body. The victim's family later attempted on various occasions to recover the body without success. According to the Complainants, the Director General of the Police Fabien Ndayishimye had declared that the body would not be handed over to the family; the latter later learned that the victim's body had been buried.

The Complainants maintain that in cases of serious human rights violations such as torture or extrajudicial executions, the State must automatically conduct an investigation, and that it is not necessary for a complaint in due form to be filed to set justice in motion. They maintain that in any event, in the present case, the threats hanging over those who tried to claim justice render remedies inaccessible. The Complainants report that the Commission of Inquiry set up on the initiative of the Prosecutor General of the Republic indicates that an investigation has been opened and that a judicial file would be opened without further details.

The Complainants insist on the fact that the presence of the Imbonerakure around the victim's body and the refusal of the authorities to hand the body over to the family plunged the latter into terror. They allege that this terror intensified with the detention of Maître Nyamoya which occurred, according to them, because he publicly accused certain police officers of being involved in the victim's death. They also cite, to justify the family's fears, the imprisonment of police officers who, like the victim, were actively claiming their rights and the threats, notably those of the Minister of the Interior against the President of APRODH, forbidding him to continue to speak about the victim's case.

The Complainants specify that there is no legal and institutional framework in Burundi for the protection of victims and witnesses of human rights violations, that the State should be requested to take provisional measures to avoid reprisals against the victim's family and the witnesses during the period of examination of the case by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission).

The Complainants allege that the victim's case is not isolated, that several cases of serious violations are recorded in Burundi including extrajudicial executions, arbitrary detentions and torture. They base their allegations mainly on reports of the United Nations Office in Burundi and other organisations which date for the most part from 2010, 2011 and 2012 and on recommendations made to Burundi during the universal periodic review in 2013. They maintain that, for the most part, the cases have remained unpunished.
The Complainants state that the matter has not been submitted to another international body of dispute settlement or of similar competence. The Complaint:
The Complainants allege the violation of the following articles of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) 1, 4, 5, 6, 7.1 a, 9.2, 18.1 and 26. The Request:

The Complainants request the Commission to: a. Grant provisional measures to the victim's family and the witnesses; b. Consider the transfer of the Communication to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Court) pursuant to Rule 118.3 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure; c. Declare the Communication admissible; d. Find that the facts show a violation by the Respondent State with regard to the victim of the following articles of the African Charter: 4, 5, 6, 9.2 read together with Article 1 and of Articles 5, 7.1.a, 18.1 and 26 read together with Article 1 with regard to the Second victim; e. Order Burundi, in application of Articles 7.1. a and 26 of the African Charter, to conduct a prompt, thorough and effective investigation into the execution of the victim and the other violations suffered, by independent and impartial judicial bodies for the purpose of instituting criminal proceedings against the perpetrators and punishing them. Require Burundi to immediately suspend administratively the alleged perpetrators pending the institution of proceedings; f. Order Burundi to offer appropriate reparation to the victim's beneficiaries. Require Burundi to provide guarantees of non-repetition in particular through public apologies addressed to the victim's relatives and a strong message condemning such acts and their impunity; g. Request Burundi to urgently adopt legislation aimed at protecting victims and witnesses, notably in the case of judicial proceedings, in order to effectively guarantee the right of access to courts; h. Request Burundi to adopt all necessary measures so that such acts do not recur and to ensure political pluralism; i. Request Burundi to publish the Commission's findings; j. Order Burundi to report, within a period of 3 months, on the action it will have taken on the conclusions of the Commission.
The Complaint reached the Secretariat of the African Commission on 09 June 2014. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt thereof on 13 June 2014.

During its 16th Extraordinary Session held in Kigali from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Rwanda, the African Commission examined the Communication and decided to seize itself of it. The Commission also requested the taking of provisional measures by the Respondent State but rejected the request for referral of the case to the Court.

By letter dated 12 August 2014, the Secretariat informed the Complainants and the Respondent State of the seizure of the Communication and at the same time sent a copy of the Communication to the Respondent State and invited the Complainants to submit their arguments on admissibility within a period of two (02) months from notification.
On 16 October 2014, the Complainants transmitted a correspondence to the Secretariat, inviting the Commission to refer to their arguments on admissibility contained in their initial submissions.

On 28 October 2014, the Secretariat sent back to the Respondent State copies of the Complainants' initial submissions and invited it to refer to the Complainants' arguments on admissibility and to transmit its own within a period of two (02) months from notification.

On 24 March 2015, the Respondent State received a letter from the Secretariat informing it that during its 17th Extraordinary Session held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 19 to 28 February 2015, the African Commission examined the Communication and decided to grant it an additional period of 30 calendar days from notification to transmit its observations on admissibility.

On 18 May 2015, the African Commission sent to the Respondent State two Notes Verbales, informing it respectively that during its 56th Ordinary Session, the Commission decided to defer its decision on the admissibility of the Communication owing to time constraints.

On 1 June 2015, the Secretariat received a report from Burundi on the implementation of the provisional measures; the Secretariat transmitted it to the Complainants on 04 June 2015 and the latter transmitted a note relating thereto on 02 July 2015.

On 22 June 2015, the Secretariat received Burundi's observations on the admissibility of the Communication; the Secretariat acknowledged receipt thereof by Note Verbale of 24 June 2015. On the same date, the Secretariat moreover transmitted Burundi's observations to the Complainants who responded to them by letter of 08 July 2015.

On 13 August 2015, the Secretariat informed the parties that the Commission decided during its 18th Extraordinary Session held from 29 July to 07 August 2015 in Nairobi, Kenya, to defer its decision on the admissibility of the Communication to its 57th Ordinary Session in order to take into account all the documents transmitted by the parties on admissibility.
On 2 November 2015, the Respondent State again transmitted a copy of its observations on admissibility which had already been transmitted on 22 June 2015.

By Letter and Note Verbale of 1 December 2015, the Secretariat informed the parties that during its 57th Ordinary Session, held from 04 to 18 November 2015 in Banjul, in the Islamic Republic of The Gambia, the Commission decided to defer the examination of the Communication to a later Session.

By letter and Note Verbale of 04 March 2016, the Secretariat informed the parties that during its 19th Extraordinary Session held from 16 to 25 February 2016 in Banjul, in the Islamic Republic of The Gambia, the Commission decided to defer its decision on admissibility to a later Session.

By letter of 27 June 2016, the Secretariat informed the parties that during its 20th Extraordinary Session held from 09 to 18 June 2016 in Banjul, in the Islamic Republic of The Gambia, the Commission decided to defer its decision on admissibility to a later Session.

During its 22nd Extraordinary Session held from 29 July to 7 August 2017, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declared the communication admissible and informed the parties in accordance with the provisions of Rule 108 of its Rules of Procedure. Provisional measures:

In its request for provisional measures addressed to the Respondent State, the Commission requested that the Respondent State take the necessary measures to ensure that no member of the immediate or extended family of the First victim and no witness who might be involved in the present case have their rights called into question as a result of the submission of the case before the Commission. The Commission particularly requested that the authorities of Burundi take measures to ensure that the State agents involved in the case or their sympathisers do not undertake, directly or indirectly, reprisals against the victim's family and the witnesses who might be involved.

In its response to the request for provisional measures, the Respondent State indicated that "the witnesses as well as the members of the victim's family are protected like other citizens otherwise they would already have lodged a complaint against those who would try to threaten them". The State adds that so far, no incident related to this Communication has yet been recorded and that this results from the security measures taken by the various State authorities to preserve peace and security throughout the national territory. The Respondent State further affirmed that it is always ready to cooperate with the Commission in the event of possible threats against the authors of the communication, the witnesses or the victim's family.

The Complainants reacted to the Respondent State's response by transmitting a note in which they consider that the note submitted by the State mentions no particular protection measure in favour of the victim's family compared to other citizens and that yet, specific protection measures are necessary as was set out in the initial request and found by the Commission. However, the Complainants provide no further information on threats that would have occurred as a result of the complaint pending before the Commission.

It should be noted that, when the complainant was invited to present observations on admissibility, he invoked the brief that he had transmitted to the Commission at the seizure stage and in which he had requested that the case be submitted to the Court. In its examination as to the seizure of the Communication, the Commission decided not to refer the case to the Court. It should however be observed that, even after having requested this referral, the complainant continued the procedure by formulating other requests concerning the merits of the case.

In light of the foregoing, the Commission is of the view that the request for referral to the Court is subsidiary, given that the other requests presented and which deal with the subject matter of the Communication were directly addressed to the Commission, which must rule on them. Also, the Commission considers that it is in no way bound by the request to seize the Court. The Complainants' arguments on admissibility:

The Complainants maintain that the Communication must be declared admissible on the ground that it fulfils all the conditions required by Article 56 of the African Charter. In their argumentation, emphasis is placed on the condition laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter, which could be disputed by the State.

The Complainants maintain that the condition of exhaustion of local remedies should not stand in the way of the admissibility of the present Communication. They invoke 3 grounds in support of their position; they indeed maintain that local remedies have been unduly prolonged, that they have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory and that it is dangerous to use them.

As regards the first ground relating to the undue prolongation of remedies. The Complainants in their brief on admissibility submit that the violation of the right to life, particularly extrajudicial execution, constitutes a serious violation of human rights and that consequently, the State must automatically conduct an investigation, even in the absence of a complaint. However, despite the setting up of a Commission of Inquiry on cases of judicial execution and torture including that of the victim, the Burundian authorities have remained passive and lack the will to establish responsibility in this case. They indicate that in the present case, the facts date from 26 August 2010 and that three years and seven months (3 years and 7 months) later, they remain unpunished; that this state of affairs "it clearly appears that no effective, diligent and prompt investigation has been opened and conducted on the facts, despite their gravity" of the Respondent State because, according to them, in other cases sometimes even more complex, particular speed has marked the investigation and the trial.

Concerning the second ground, namely that local remedies have proved ineffective and unsatisfactory. The Complainants submit that many NGOs mobilised on behalf of the victim's family from the occurrence of the facts, in order to denounce his execution and obtain the opening of a prompt and effective investigation with a view to prosecuting the alleged perpetrators. A group of NGOs including APRODH, FORSC, OAG, Ligue Iteka and OLUCOME met in October 2010 with the Minister of the Interior Mr Edouard Nduzimna in order to once again demand the opening of an investigation into the incriminated facts. The Embassy of the United States in Burundi also questioned the Burundian government on the multiplication of cases of politically motivated executions including the case of the victim. The Complainants also maintain that, despite the report of the Commission of Inquiry, which indicates that the case of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo would have been the subject of an investigation, and that it would be under pre-trial investigation at the Prosecutor General's Office of the Republic, no reference number of the opened file had been mentioned and no detail concerning this case had been given. More precisely, the Complainants state that no information on the investigative acts carried out, or the results of the investigation assuming it was opened and conducted, was ever communicated either to the family or to the NGOs that followed this case. The Complainants therefore conclude that no effective, prompt and impartial investigation was ever opened and conducted by the Burundian authorities.

On the third ground, according to which it is dangerous to use local remedies, the Complainants maintain that the various threats to which the victim was subjected before his death, and which had forced him to take refuge in hiding, the fact that the victim was arrested by the police and killed while he was in their hands, the refusal of the police officers to hand the victim's body over to the family, so that it could have a dignified burial, "as he had got what he deserved", the arrest of his Lawyer Me Nyamoya for having denounced the facts that happened to the victim, the imprisonment of police officers who, like the victim, were actively claiming their rights and the threats including those of the Minister of the Interior against the President of APRODH forbidding him to continue to speak about the victim's case sufficiently demonstrate that the family's fears are well founded and that it is dangerous for it to seek to obtain justice. The Respondent State's arguments on admissibility:

The Respondent State maintains that the Communication must be declared inadmissible for failure to comply with the condition of exhaustion of local remedies required by Article 56 (5) of the African Charter.

The Respondent State justifies its position by maintaining that the facts of which the Commission is seized still fall within the jurisdiction of the Burundian courts because a criminal file is duly registered at the Prosecutor General's Office of the Republic under number RMPG 618/HG/CA/MN/MA and the case is still under investigation.

In addition to the information transmitted in its brief on admissibility, its report on the implementation of the provisional measures also contains arguments relating to admissibility which should be considered for the proper administration of justice. The Respondent State indicates therein that a Commission on extrajudicial executions and acts of torture was created to analyse this file and summonses had been addressed to witnesses for the prosecution and for the defence but so far nobody had appeared. The Respondent State further indicates that the judicial authorities did everything to publicise these cases in order to encourage the witnesses and families of the victims to come forward to give their statements but that this was in vain. Moreover, the State also maintains that the witnesses and families as well as all persons concerned by this case benefit from the same protection as any citizens in Burundi. Additional submissions of the Complainants

The additional observations of the Complainants are found both in their reply brief on admissibility and in their note on the implementation of the provisional measures. In these additional observations, the Complainants indicated that the Respondent State gives no indication as to the different stages of the investigation which it considers to be ongoing and neither does it provide evidence of the summonses made or of the efforts undertaken to obtain the appearance of the witnesses and the victim's family in conditions of security. The Complainants consider that the State in fact provides no new substantial element. Analysis of the Commission on admissibility:
Article 56 of the African Charter prescribes seven (7) conditions that must be cumulatively met for a Communication to be declared admissible by the Commission.

In the present case, only one of the conditions, namely that provided for in Article 56 (5) of the African Charter, is contested by the parties. After thorough examination of the file, the Commission is itself satisfied that the six(6) other conditions provided for in Articles 56 (1), (2), (3), (4) (6) and (7) are met.

Indeed, the authors of the Communication have indicated their identity; the Communication concerns alleged violations of the African Charter that were allegedly committed in 2011, that is to say well after the entry into force of the African Charter in Burundi. The Communication contains no disparaging or insulting terms against the Respondent State, its institutions or the African Union; the information communicated by the Complainants in the Communication derives among others from reports of recognised bodies in Burundi and at the international level. Moreover, it does not emerge from the file that the present case has already been settled in accordance with either the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or of the Charter of the Organisation of African Unity (currently the Constitutive Act of the African Union) or the provisions of the African Charter. As regards the condition laid down in Article 56 (6), in its Communication Tsatsu Tsikata v. Republic of Ghana, the Commission already noted the link between Article 56 (5) and Article 56(6); it therefore intends to give reasons for its position on this point after the analysis of Article 56 (5).

Concerning Article 56 (5) of the African Charter, which is contested by the parties, it provides that, to be admissible, Communications must "be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious to the Commission that the procedure of achieving these remedies would be unduly prolonged".

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has developed exceptions to the rule of exhaustion of local remedies. In its decision on Communication 147/95-149/96 Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission indeed indicated that the condition of exhaustion of local remedies cannot apply if the remedies in question are not available, effective or sufficient. The Commission has also established the fact that if the complainant cannot turn to a court of his country because he fears for his life or for that of members of his family, remedies are considered non-existent for him.

In the present case, the Complainants acknowledge that a Commission of Inquiry on extrajudicial executions and acts of torture was set up by the State to investigate several cases of extrajudicial execution including that of the victim; however, they submit that despite the existence of a report of this Commission which indicates that the victim's file is still ongoing, no information was transmitted on the investigative acts carried out and the results of the investigation; assuming it was carried out, to the family or to the NGOs that followed the case. Consequently they consider that three (3) years and (7) seven months after the occurrence of the facts (26 August 2010), these remain unpunished and that the procedure is unduly prolonged. The Respondent State indicated that a Commission had been created to investigate various cases including that of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo and that a file had been opened in his name. Consequently, what now matters for the Commission is to analyse the procedure set in motion by the Respondent State, in light of the arguments on admissibility put forward by the Complainant and in light of the responses and arguments provided by the Respondent State and of the latter's obligations.

The promptness of the procedure to establish responsibility starting with the investigation is undoubtedly a key factor. The Commission notes that three (3) years and (7) seven months seems to be a long period for an investigation that is not yet closed. However, it is not so much the prolongation in itself that is in question, but it is the normal or abnormal nature of the prolongation of the local remedies set in motion that should be sought. In this regard, the Commission has already emphasised in its decision on Communication 293/04- Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa /Zimbabwe, the need to take into consideration the circumstances of the case and the reasons put forward to justify the prolongation of remedies in order to determine whether the prolongation is normal or abnormal. The Commission will therefore examine, in light of the applicable legal instruments, the facts and the circumstances of the case, whether the remedies in question have been prolonged in a normal or abnormal manner.

The Commission notes on the one hand that the Respondent State did not respond to the Complainants' allegation that in certain more complex cases, the competent authorities conducted the prosecution and the trial with speed.

From the Respondent State's arguments listed above, it appears that the non-conclusion or slowness (notably of the investigation which it says is ongoing) is linked to the failure of the victim's family members and the witnesses to appear and testify at the prosecutor's office. However, the Complainants have maintained since their initial submissions that no information on the investigative acts carried out; nor the results of the investigation was communicated to the family members. Moreover, despite all the steps undertaken by the family and the NGOs, the authorities refused to hand over the victim's body without providing any explanation and discouraged them from pursuing steps in this case at the risk of bringing trouble upon themselves; this therefore implies that no summons was received either by the family members or by the other persons concerned and may suppose a manifest will of the State not to pursue the case.

Faced with this disagreement between the parties on the materiality of the summonses made, the Commission must first rule on the question of the burden of proof. The burden of proof lies in principle on the one who accuses or makes the allegation, therefore on the Complainants. However, as emphasised by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the Ahmadou Sadio Diallo case (Republic of Guinea v. Democratic Republic of the Congo), it would be wrong to consider this principle, inspired by the adage onus probandi incumbit actori, as an absolute rule. The Commission agrees with the ICJ: "...that, as a general rule, the applicant cannot be required to prove the negative fact it asserts. A public authority is generally able to demonstrate that it has followed the appropriate procedures and respected the guarantees required by law – if such was the case – by producing documents that prove the acts that have been carried out".

The Commission notes in this regard that the Respondent State did not place in the file the material proof of the summonses made. In the present case, the Complainants allege a negative fact (the absence of summons) the proof to the contrary of which should logically be in the possession of the Respondent State. Indeed, if summonses were actually made, it was for the Respondent State to provide the documents attesting to the existence of these summonses and their notification to the parties. The Respondent State, although aware of the Complainants' allegation regarding the absence of summons, placed no evidence in the file.

In any event, the Commission notes that the Public Prosecutor's Office, through the prerogatives linked to the exercise of public prosecution, must in principle have the necessary means to compel the appearance of any person whose hearing is necessary in the examination of a file. According to the United Nations Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extra-legal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions, the investigating authority must have the power to oblige persons suspected of being involved in cases of executions to appear and testify including witnesses. In the same vein, the Commission notes that Law No. 1/10 of 03 April 2013 revising the Code of Criminal Procedure in Burundi provides in its Articles 79, 82, 83, 335 and 336, a list of diligent actions (warrant for arrest, referral before the competent judge, summons to appear) that the Public Prosecutor's Office may implement to bring persons summoned to appear. The Respondent State has however not indicated what diligent actions were implemented in accordance with its obligations, to hear the witnesses for the prosecution and for the defence in this case. Publicising a case as the State indicates cannot replace these legal means.

In view of the nature of the alleged violations, which requires a prompt investigation in order to establish responsibility, and in the face of the absence of sufficient justification by the Respondent State to explain the slowness of the investigation concerning the death of the victim Jackson Ndikuriyo since August 2010 and the lack of communications concerning the actions undertaken and the results of the investigation or at least the first results, demonstrates that the State did not take all the measures to deal with this case with all the required speed, which in the present case constitutes an undue prolongation of remedies.

The Complainants argue the lack of will of the State to establish responsibility for the crime in the present case and the dysfunction existing within the judicial apparatus. The Respondent State did not respond specifically to these allegations. The Commission has, in its jurisprudence, indicated that a remedy that has no chance of success does not constitute an effective remedy and that a remedy is sufficient when it is capable of giving satisfaction to the Complainant. The Commission notes the prolonged nature of the remedies in the present case; it also notes the latter's attempts to discourage all the persons who had tried to move the investigation forward. Although having stressed that it had opened an investigation into the victim's case, the State has not provided elements to contradict the Complainants' statements as to its lack of will to do justice.

As to the dysfunction relied upon by the Complainants, the Commission notes that it emerges even from the Complainants' allegations that Burundian justice functioned fully in other cases and that the Complainants do not describe sufficiently how the alleged dysfunction is an obstacle in the present case.

In sum, the Commission concludes that the allegation that the State lacks the will to establish responsibility can be admitted in view of the arguments provided by the Complainants and the absence of contrary proof from the Respondent. As for the dysfunction of the entire judicial apparatus of Burundi, the Commission finds that it cannot be established in view of the elements provided by the Complainants.

The Complainants argue that no investigative act was in reality carried out by the judicial authorities as no information was communicated on this and the victim's family was never contacted or heard in the course of the investigation. The Commission considers that the Respondent State was well aware of the Complainants' allegations and that if it alleges the contrary, it should have provided proof that summonses were actually sent. In the absence of evidence showing the minimum actions undertaken, notably the effectiveness of the summonses, the Commission considers that there is thereby an ineffectiveness of local remedies, notably of the investigative acts or investigations carried out. The Complainants' argument that it is dangerous to exhaust local remedies.

The complainants submit that it is dangerous for the family to seek to obtain justice from Burundian justice, particularly following thinly veiled threats uttered by the authorities both against it and against the various persons concerned by the file. They also maintain that Jackson Ndikuriyo was killed while he was held by the police, that the Director General of the Police had declared on the radio that the body would not be returned to the family and that the victim "had got only what he deserved" refusing to hear of a decent burial. Furthermore, all the persons who sought to obtain justice for these crimes were directly threatened and had their liberty infringed. Finally, even before his death the victim had been forced to live in hiding owing to increasingly pressing death threats against him.

In its jurisprudence, the Commission has already stressed the fact that when remedies prove dangerous for the Complainant, it would not be reasonable to ask him to exhaust them. In the case 147/95-149/96 Sir Dawda K. Jawara v. The Gambia, the Commission indicated that: "The existence of a local remedy must be sufficiently certain, not only in theory but also in practice, failing which it will be neither available nor effective. Consequently, if the complainant cannot turn to the court of his country because he fears for his life or for that of members of his family, local remedies are considered non-existent for him".

Furthermore, the Principles on the Effective Prevention and Investigation of Extra-legal, Arbitrary and Summary Executions provide that: "Complainants, witnesses, those conducting the investigation and their families shall be protected from violence, threats of violence or any other form of intimidation. Those potentially implicated in extra-legal, arbitrary or summary executions shall be removed from any position of control or power, whether direct or indirect, over complainants, witnesses and their families, as well as over those conducting investigations."

Moreover, in its decision on Communication 205/97 Kazeem Aminu v. Nigeria, where the victim was forced to live in hiding to escape persecution by the security services, the Commission decided to exempt him from exhausting local remedies.

From all the foregoing, it emerges that the question that arises is whether the risks mentioned are legitimate or well founded. To this end, it is appropriate to take into account in the analysis the nature of the alleged violations, the profile of the alleged perpetrators and the context surrounding the case in order to assess whether or not the risks incurred by the Complainants if they brought proceedings are well founded.

On the nature of the alleged violations, the Commission notes their serious character. The need has already been emphasised, in cases of allegations of serious crimes such as torture and homicide, to ensure protection capable of providing the victims or their relatives with the guarantees necessary to bring legal action. In the present case, the facts reported by the Complainants concerning the victim, Jackson Ndikuriyo, allege serious violations notably the infringement of the right to life.

Next, as regards the profile of the alleged perpetrators, the case under analysis as presented shows prima facie an involvement of the law enforcement and security forces of Burundi, particularly the police who had uttered threats against the victim and in whose hands he died, which makes the fears of anyone wishing to file a complaint more understandable.

As for the context, the facts reported mention growing pressure and constant threats against the victim before his death, which contributed to creating an environment of apprehension and fear for the family. The Complainants have indeed placed in the file reports mentioning the situation of vulnerability of the relatives and the family, notably due to the position of the persons alleged to be responsible for the facts who are members of the National Police, enjoying significant means of pressure to prevent steps from being initiated before national courts against them. Moreover, the Complainants also report that there is no legal and judicial framework for the protection of victims and witnesses in Burundi, this information being supported by the concluding observations of the Committee against Torture in 2007 following the examination of the report of Burundi. The Respondent State in its brief on admissibility does not mention the existence of the legal and institutional framework for the protection of victims and witnesses in Burundi nor the effectiveness of such a framework if it existed. In its note on provisional measures, the State vaguely indicated that the victims' families are protected like other citizens without further arguments on this point. This assertion supports the allegation of the absence of particular protection in the case of certain serious crimes and this is likely to terrify the victims and witnesses of atrocious crimes.

Finally, as regards Article 56(6) of the African Charter which prescribes that the Communication must "be submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized of the matter", it should be further emphasised that in the present case, the parties agree on the fact that local remedies have not been exhausted. Having already established the fact that the remedies are unduly prolonged and not being able to identify in the Respondent State's code of criminal procedure the time limit for the investigation of such a file, all the more so as the State does not give the list of investigative acts carried out and does not clearly indicate at what stage of the investigations the file stands, the Commission should count the time for its seizure from the moment when the Complainants should reasonably have realised the undue prolongation of local remedies.

The Complainants alleged that in August 2012, the Commission of Inquiry set up by the Prosecutor General of the Republic to shed light on the cases characterised as extrajudicial execution or torture indicated that the case of Jackson Ndikuriyo would have been the subject of an investigation. Nevertheless, no file reference number; nor the acts carried out within the framework of the investigations, nor the results of the investigation, had been communicated to them. They also report that more than three years and seven months (3 and 7) since the occurrence of the facts, no family member or witness has been heard in this case.

In its submissions on admissibility the Respondent State did not provide elements contradicting or justifying this, merely indicating that a judicial file in the victim's name existed at the level of the Prosecutor General's Office of the Republic.

Unlike the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and the American Convention on Human Rights which set a specific time limit for the submission of communications: six months, the African Charter only provides that communications must be submitted "within a reasonable period" which is not defined. The Commission therefore treats each case on its merits to set a reasonable period.

Although in the case of Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Republic of Sudan the Commission declared that the expiry of two years and five months or twenty-nine months without any reason or justification was considered unreasonable. The Commission had also noted that "when a Complainant has a valid and compelling reason for not submitting his complaint to the Commission's examination, the latter has the responsibility, in the interest of fairness and justice, to grant the Complainant an opportunity to be heard."

In the present case, the Respondent State itself acknowledges that the case is still pending before the courts; the Complainants seized the Commission on 09 June 2014 for, among other reasons, the undue prolongation of the procedure, notably an investigation that has lasted for more than 3 years without any results. The Commission therefore considers that the time within which it was seized is reasonable.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the African Charter.

The Complainants allege the violation of the following articles of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter) 4, 5, 6, 9 (2), read together with Article 1 as well as, 7 (1) (a), 18 (1) and 26.

The Complainants submit that the provisions of Article 4 of the African Charter which guarantees to every human being the right to respect for his life and the integrity of his person have been violated by the Respondent State, which failed in its duty to protect human life against gratuitous or arbitrary actions of public authorities and private persons.

For the Complainants, two main elements emerge from the jurisprudence of the African Commission that make it possible to characterise an infringement of the right to life as an extrajudicial execution. First, the execution must have been committed by an agent of the State or with the consent of the latter. In addition, the execution must follow an arbitrary trial - inappropriate, unfair, unpredictable or unlawful - or not be preceded by any consent.

They maintain that the African Commission has recognised that extrajudicial executions constitute a violation of the right to life protected in Article 4 of the African Charter. Consequently, they consider that when an infringement of the right to life has been caused by an agent of the State following an arbitrary trial or outside any judicial procedure, it is an extrajudicial execution, whatever the motivations and intentions of those responsible or the conditions surrounding the infringement.
They also add that the Commission has already characterised as extrajudicial execution deprivations of the right to life committed by State agents outside the framework of trials.

They emphasise the obligation of States to investigate effectively and diligently infringements of the right to life, as well as their responsibility to protect all persons under their jurisdictions against non-State actors, notably the duty to take preventive operational measures to protect a person whose life is in danger from the criminal acts of another person".

The victim suffered an infringement of his right to life, having been found dead on 27 August 2010 on the outskirts of the Musigati Police Station after having been arrested by the police and while he was in a police vehicle with the Commissioner and other police officers. The criminal nature of his death is not contested by the authorities, who would moreover have opened a judicial file to that effect.

Furthermore, according to the complainants, the extrajudicial nature of Mr Ndikuriyo's death is clearly established. Indeed, while the victim was with other persons in the vehicle when it was allegedly caught in an ambush, he alone lost his life following the bullets fired at the police car which, moreover, showed no impact of bullets or the slightest scratch.
Finally, several inconsistencies were highlighted in the versions of the authorities' representatives and no investigation was opened to identify the alleged perpetrators.
In view of the foregoing, the Commission is therefore requested to find the violation of Article 4 by the State of Burundi.

Under Article 5 of the African Charter "[e]very individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited."

The Complainants submit that Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo was a victim of torture, cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment as well as a serious infringement of his right to dignity and legal personality as enshrined in Article 5 of the African Charter.

They assert that the African Commission considers the right to human dignity as "a fundamental right which all human beings must enjoy without any discrimination whatsoever, irrespective of their mental capacities or incapacities, as the case may be. It is therefore a natural right that every human being is obliged to respect, by all means, and which also confers on every human being the duty to respect it".

They add that the Commission has adopted a broad interpretation of the notion of dignity, considering that Article 5 of the Charter protects not only the physical person of the victim but also the minimum economic and social circumstances required for human existence. They add that it is generally accepted that legal personality has a natural origin and derives from the very essence of the being to which it is attached. Thus the right to legal personality embodies the notions of human dignity and integrity of the person, entailing a right to legality. It is a right to have rights, respect for which is a necessary prerequisite for the realisation of all individual rights.

Thus, serious infringements of the life and integrity of a person who is removed from the protection of the law constitute violations of dignity and legal personality, which is the case of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo.

Indeed, the day after his arrest, the body of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo was found not far from the Police Station, whose Commissioner allegedly asserted in a public statement that the latter had accidentally lost his life during an ambush set against the police. However, his remains were left at the site for an entire night and were not handed over to his family so that it could proceed to a dignified burial. In this, he was denied in his very essence, which implies a violation of his dignity and legal personality. Moreover, the circumstances of his death and the treatment accorded to his remains tend to reinforce the thesis of extrajudicial execution in the person of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo as the complainants maintain.

They further consider that the family of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo was a victim of torture, following the loss caused by the victim's death which plunged his family, particularly his wife and his three children, into deep suffering and moral distress. To this is added the uncertainty prevailing over the circumstances of the victim's death together with the authorities' refusal to hand over the body to them in order to allow them to bury him with dignity and to mourn.

In support of their arguments, they submit that the Human Rights Committee has consistently recognised in its jurisprudence that "the anguish and distress that the disappearance [...] caused to his entire close family" constitutes a violation of Article 7 of the Covenant on Civil and Political Rights with regard to the victim's relatives.

The Complainants also maintain that the State did not respect the positive obligations arising from the rights protected in Article 5 of the Charter, namely, to take the necessary measures to prevent the extrajudicial execution of Mr Jackson Ndikuriyo and the abandonment of his body at the place of his execution for an entire night, as well as by not putting in place "effective solutions in a transparent, independent and effective legal system" and by not pursuing effective and independent investigations relating to these allegations.
The Complainants request to be heard by the Commission on this ground and that it find the violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

Article 6 of the African Charter provides that every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law.

The Complainants recall that in its jurisprudence, the African Commission analyses Article 6 on two distinct and complementary components; the right to liberty and the right to security of the person. The right to liberty benefits every individual and constitutes a fundamental condition for the enjoyment of other rights and "to be deprived of it is a fact that appears to have a direct and undesirable effect on the enjoyment of several other rights, ranging from the right to a family and to a private life, through freedom of assembly, association and expression, to the right to freedom of movement".

It therefore presupposes the right to be free from any constraint, subject to compliance with the law.
