Kingdom of Lesotho, indicating that to be characterised as disparaging or insulting, the language used by the Complainant must unequivocally demonstrate the Complainant's intention to bring the State and its institution into disrepute. Thus, for example, in Communication Ligue Camerounaise des Droits de l'Homme v. Cameroon, the Commission considered as insulting terms such as ""Paul Biya must answer for crimes against humanity", "thirty years of a neo-colonial, criminal regime, embodied by the Ahidjo/Biya duo", "torturing regime" and "governmental barbarisms"" and declared the Communication inadmissible.

Another fundamental aspect that must be considered in defining the disparaging or insulting nature of the statements made by the complainant within the framework of Article 56(3) of the Charter is respect for the right to freedom of expression. In other words, the provisions of Article 56(3) of the Charter must be interpreted in parallel with Article 9(2) of the Charter which enshrines the right to expression. More particularly, it is necessary to know within what limits the institutions of the State may be criticised without violating the right to freedom of expression, or to know the limits of the right to freedom of expression. Thus, while being aware of the fact that the prohibition of disparaging and insulting terms is fundamental in diplomatic, courteous and respectful relations between parties appearing before it as well as respect for the institutions of the State, the Commission must also not ignore the existence of the right to freedom of expression protected by the Charter.

As the Commission has already expressed in Communication Zimbabwe Lawyers for Human Rights and the Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa v. Zimbabwe, "a balance must be struck between the right to express oneself freely and the duty to protect State institutions to ensure that, while discouraging abuse of language, the African Commission is not otherwise violating or restraining the enjoyment of other rights guaranteed by the African Charter such as, in this case, the right to freedom of expression". The commission considers that there is no harm in criticising in good faith or making a respectful comment on an action of a State institution as long as the intention is not to discredit it.

Thus, for example, in Communication Bukweri Land Claims Committee v. Cameroon, the Commission found that the Complainant may allege, among other things [...], that the President of the Republic exercises extraordinary powers so as to influence the judicial system and that the judicial system is partial and lacks independence. The same analysis was retained by the Commission in the communication Congress for Democracy and Justice (CDJ) v. Gabon. In that communication, the Commission concluded that by asserting that the Constitutional Court is not independent, the Complainant was merely describing his perception and the opinion he had of the Constitutional Court, and that consequently this did not constitute disparaging or insulting language within the meaning of Article 56(3) of the Charter. Moreover, a communication raising human rights violations contains, by its very nature, allegations giving a negative reflection of the State and its institutions.

In the present case, referring to the preceding examples, the African Commission finds nothing in the Complainant's various observations as noted by the Respondent State that would justify invoking Article 56(3) of the Charter to find the Communication inadmissible on the ground of the use of disparaging or insulting language. The Commission considers that the complainant may allege - as is the case here - that France, the United States and the European Union requested the publication of the results, polling station by polling station, and that this will never be done. The Commission does not share the view of the Respondent State which maintains that this position would mean that the Complainant wished to show that the Constitutional Court of the Gabonese Republic is not credible. On the contrary, this is merely the Complainant's perception of the functioning of the Gabonese Constitutional Court which in no way constitutes an intention to discredit it.

Whether this perception is true or false is another matter; but this does not in any way diminish the requirement of Article 56(3) of the Charter. In particular, a statement may be false without being insulting or disparaging. In the present case, to prove that the Complainant's allegations are disparaging or insulting, the Respondent State seems to show that, contrary to what the Complainant says, the Constitutional Court carried out the systematic verification of all the electoral minutes polling station by polling station. It reiterates that this Court proceeded to the recount of votes before proclaiming the results of the presidential election in accordance with the law. Admittedly, the Respondent State has the right to prove that the Complainant's allegations are false; it is even possible that these allegations are false as the Respondent State indicates. But this proof cannot be taken into account in the interpretation of Article 56(3) of the Charter. What would be of interest in the present case is rather to show how the terms used by the Complainant would be disparaging or insulting by proving above all the Complainant's intention to undermine the integrity of the Gabonese Constitutional Court.

The same analysis applies to the other passages of the Complainant's brief considered by the Respondent State as constituting disparaging and insulting language. Thus, for example, the Commission does not see how it is disparaging or insulting towards the Respondent State to say that "a pre-report drawn up by the Mission to Observe the management of the election dispute, under the auspices of the African Union is published in the press". The same is true of other passages extracted from the Complainant's observations by the Respondent State and which the latter considers disparaging or insulting.

The Commission observes that these are mere allegations of the Complainant describing his understanding or opinion on the functioning of the Gabonese Constitutional Court. Thus, for example, he criticises the failure to respect the adversarial principle (see the extracts from pages 21/35 and 22/35 of the complainant's brief as noted by the Respondent State); the independence and impartiality of courts (see the complainant's statements on page 23/35 of his brief as noted by the Respondent State); the absence of objective impartiality of the constitutional court (see the complainant's statements on pages 26/35 and 29/35 of his brief as noted by the Respondent State). The wording of these paragraphs simply expresses the Complainant's opinion on the Gabonese judicial system through the Constitutional Court and is far from being disparaging or insulting.

From all these observations, the Commission concludes that such statements do not constitute disparaging or insulting language within the meaning of Article 56(3) of the Charter. The objection that the communication was allegedly not submitted within a reasonable period since the exhaustion of local remedies

Article 56(6) of the African Charter provides that a communication must be submitted within a reasonable period after the exhaustion of local remedies or from the date on which the Commission is seized of the matter. Unlike the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms and the American Convention on Human Rights, which provide a specific time limit for the submission of communications, which is six months, the African Charter provides only that communications must be submitted "within a reasonable period" without however indicating the length of a reasonable period.

However, as the Complainant noted, in Communication Michael Majuru v. Zimbabwe, aligning itself with the practice of similar regional human rights instruments such as the Inter-American Commission and Court and the European Court, the Commission considered that 6 months seemed to be the usual norm. On the ground by which the Complainant contests the jurisprudence of Communication Majuru v. Zimbabwe

In the present case, the Complainant does not agree with this interpretation of the Commission. He considers that the Commission's reasoning which sets the length of the reasonable time within the meaning of Article 56(6) of the Charter at 6 months is not convincing because "it sets a condition which does not appear therein". He alleges that Articles 60 and 61 of the Charter to which the Commission refers to make this interpretation invite the Commission to take international law into consideration in a general manner and that the latter does not enshrine a 6-month period for seizing an international judicial or quasi-judicial body. He maintains that in the absence of a general principle of international law and of international custom, the uncertainty arising from Article 56(6) must remain because it was intended by the States that drafted the Charter and accepted by those that ratified it.

The Commission recalls that it is vested with the prerogatives of interpreting any provision of the Charter by virtue of Article 45(3) of the same Charter. On the basis of these prerogatives, it has, in many cases, tried to determine the meaning and scope of the various provisions of the Charter in response to the complaints submitted to it. Thus, by virtue of this power conferred on it by the Charter, an interpretation by the Commission becomes a precedent that other institutions or partners of the African Union must follow. The Commission itself must follow its interpretation when called upon to give its opinion on allegations of human rights violations.

In this perspective, complaints submitted before the Commission must also conform to the guidelines laid down by the latter in its earlier decisions. In particular, since the case of Majuru v. Zimbabwe in 2008, the Commission has always considered that 6 months constitute the reasonable time within the meaning of Article 56(6) of the Charter. Thus, in seizing the Commission, a Complainant cannot deliberately ignore an interpretative orientation of the Charter that the latter has developed for the sole reason that he is not convinced by its reasoning.

In the present case in particular, the Complainant indicates that in the "absence of any power of constraint, they [the Commission's decisions] will be applied only on the express condition of being in conformity with the international law in force". The Commission considers that this cannot constitute a valid excuse for not complying with an already established practice which has acquired a certain legal force. On the ground that the existence of good and compelling reasons may justify exceeding the reasonable time according to the Commission's jurisprudence

The Commission agrees with the Complainant that where there are good and compelling reasons which prevented a complainant from submitting the complaint in a timely manner, the complaint must be examined in a spirit of fairness and justice. Thus, in Communication Darfur Relief and Documentation Centre v. Republic of Sudan, the Commission considered that the provisions of Article 56(6) make it possible to render the party complaining of a prejudice suffered at the hands of a State more vigilant and to discourage delay by potential Complainants. It reiterated, however, that "where there is a good and compelling reason" why a complainant does not submit his complaint to the Commission for examination, it is incumbent upon the Commission, in a spirit of fairness and justice, to give him the opportunity to be heard.

On the basis of this jurisprudence, the Commission agrees with the complainant on the analysis according to which the usual standard of 6 months that it has retained and considered as a reasonable time must not have the effect of excluding the admissibility of a communication submitted later on account of particular circumstances. Thus, each case must be treated according to its own circumstances. In the present case, the last decision rendered by the Constitutional Court dates from 15 November 2016 and the Commission was seized on 13 February, that is 15 months after the exhaustion of local remedies. It is then for the Commission to determine whether there are particular circumstances which would justify exceeding the 6 months forming part of the Commission's practice as a reasonable time.

In the present Communication, the complainant maintains that there are compelling reasons which would justify exceeding the usual six-month period. He mentions that the only available local remedy did not meet the "imperative of fairness and justice" advocated by the Commission in the case Institute for Human Rights and Development in Africa and Others v. DRC. However, the Commission considers that the arguments put forward by the Complainant as having hindered the submission of the complaint are not convincing. In particular, the Commission does not see how the absence of fair trial guarantees in the 2 applications filed by the victim before the Constitutional Court could influence the delay in seizing the Commission.

In this regard, the Commission shares the view of the Respondent State that after the last decision of the Constitutional Court, the Complainant had the latitude to seize it. The Complainant does not provide the Commission with evidence justifying particular circumstances which would have placed the victim in a total impossibility of seizing the Commission. The presence of Mesdames MBORANTSUO and AGONDJO within the Constitutional Court and the violation of the adversarial principle by the Constitutional Court on which the Complainant relies as being able to justify the delay in seizing the Commission cannot succeed as such. This justification merely points to irregularities encountered during the applications that the Complainant lodged before the Constitutional Court. Whether or not these irregularities existed or affected the decision of the Constitutional Court matters little. Indeed, this would in no way justify the delay in seizing the Commission within the time limit set by its jurisprudence. On the contrary, a prudent person, a victim of such kinds of judicial irregularities, would not fail to respect the time limits allotted to him to pursue potential remedies, such as the one pursued before the Commission.

Rather, the Complainant could have shown the circumstances occurring after the last decision of the Constitutional Court that would have made it impossible to seize the Commission within the 6 months following the decision of the Constitutional Court. In the absence of this evidence, the Commission's jurisprudence commands that the Communication be declared inadmissible. Thus, for example, in Communication Michael Majuru v. Zimbabwe, the Commission found that the arguments put forward by the Complainant as having hindered the submission of the complaint did not seem convincing because the complainant had not, among other things, provided medical evidence indicating that he suffered from mental problems, [...]. Consequently, it declared it inadmissible.

On the contrary, proof of the existence of particular circumstances which would have hindered the submission of the Communication suffices to derogate from the principle of the 6-month period that has been retained as a reasonable time. Thus, for example, in Communication Obert Chibhamo v. Zimbabwe, the Commission took note of the fact that the Complainant did not reside in the Respondent State and that it took him time to settle in the new destination before lodging his complaint before the Commission. Consequently, it concluded that even if it were to adopt the practice of other regional bodies of considering that six months is a reasonable time for submitting complaints, it does not consider that the communication was submitted contrary to Article 56(6) of the Charter; the application having been submitted 10 months after his flight.
In this respect, the Commission concludes that the reason put forward by the Complainant according to which the delay was due to the absence of fair local remedies is not convincing.

The other elements put forward by the complainant as constituting exceptional circumstances do not sufficiently prove that he was unable to submit his communication to the Commission. In particular, he mentions the threats weighing on the victim and his close political and family supporters. While not denying that these threats existed and continue to exist, the Commission does not find in the file any element which would justify that they were of a nature to hinder the seizure of the commission. Indeed, despite these alleged threats, the victim seems to have always continued to go about his political activities; as evidenced by certain passages of the complainant's own brief where he states that on 25 July 2017 the victim was "returning from a diplomatic tour in France and other European countries".

After analysis of the documents in the file, it also appears to the Commission that the threats alleged by the Complainant intensified in the first moments close to the election date. In other words, they were not continuous so as to extend to this period of 15 months that the Complainant waited to seize the Commission. In particular, the Commission notes that whereas the elections took place on 26 August 2016, the threats against the Complainant and his supporters occurred in the period from 31 August 2016 to 5 September 2016. Another resurgence of threats occurred when the victim was returning from his tour in Europe on 25 July 2017, that is 10 months after the first series of threats. The Commission finds that this period of calm could have been used by the Victim to seize the Commission.

Moreover, the need for much more than 6 months in order to reach a political settlement of the problem put forward by the Complainant does not constitute, also in the eyes of the commission, an exceptional circumstance. The Commission shares the view of the Respondent State that an international mediation, once envisaged, would not prevent the seizure of the Commission. International mediation being political in nature, it does not exclude a quasi-judicial procedure such as that before the Commission. Thus, the Commission is of the view that the one does not exclude the other and is not suspensive of the other. Even in a post-electoral context, international mediation is not an exclusive measure that would prevent a party, after the exhaustion of local remedies, from seizing the Commission within a reasonable time. What is more, the Commission considers that political mediation is not a local judicial remedy in the legal sense of the term.

On the basis of these developments, it emerges that the reasons put forward by the Complainant are neither good nor compelling to justify exceeding the 6-month period necessary for filing a complaint before the Commission.

In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. Declares the Communication inadmissible for failure to comply with Article 56(6) of the African Charter. Adopted by the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights at its 70th Ordinary Session held virtually from 23 February 2022 to 9 March 2022
